prerequisites: Access to real customers or micro-creators who are also customers
steps: Cast real customers or micro-creators who are also customers for testimonial and UGC content.
Avoid actors or unrelated personas presented as customers.
Avoid framing the ad as the brand and customer against a shared rival; that competitive framing reads as hostile, not relatable.
Carry organic on-camera faces into paid creative where they already resonate.

test.method: A/B test real-customer creative against staged or actor-led creative.
test.read_point: After the standard creative test window

title: Only use named, checkable, relevant credentials near a claim
hypothesis: If claims on a PDP or ad only carry a named, checkable, relevant credential, then authority-based trust is earned honestly instead of borrowed from an unrelated or unverifiable title.

signal.check: A claim carries an unnamed expert, an unrelated celebrity, or a title the shopper cannot verify.

expected_effect.size: unknown; mechanism-based, apply as a credibility filter

risk.note: A claims-review rule.

prerequisites: A real, named, relevant expert or credential
steps: Audit every authority claim on PDPs and ads for a named, checkable, relevant credential.
Remove any title, expert or celebrity endorsement that cannot be verified or is unrelated to the claim.
Prefer a credential that concedes a minor point honestly before making the main claim.
Use a real store footprint or track record as an authority signal where relevant.

test.method: Review claims quarterly against the credential standard.

title: Only show scarcity or a deadline that is true right now
hypothesis: If every stock count, deadline or restock message shown is checkably true, then scarcity converts honestly and does not create legal or trust risk from a fake or resetting claim.
does_not_apply_when: A brand that does not actually sell out or run a real time-limited offer; scarcity there should not be used at all

signal.check: A countdown, stock count or restock message is live that does not match real inventory or a real fixed deadline.

expected_effect.size: unknown; mechanism-based, apply only where the constraint is real

risk.note: A resetting countdown or a fake stock count is a consumer-law risk in some markets, not just a trust risk.

prerequisites: Real-time inventory or a fixed sale end date
steps: Audit every scarcity or deadline element on the site and in ads.
Tie each one to real stock data or a real fixed end date.
Kill any countdown that resets or any stock count not backed by inventory.
Never use scarcity to imply better performance, only availability.

test.method: Compare conversion with true scarcity messaging removed vs kept.
test.read_point: After enough sessions for a stable read

title: Show a real premium tier or item first to anchor the rest of a pricing page
hypothesis: If a real premium tier or item is shown first on a pricing page or upsell, then the rest of the lineup reads as fairly priced by genuine contrast, without a fake 'was' price.

signal.check: A pricing page or upsell flow does not lead with a real premium option, or uses a fabricated 'was' price to create the contrast.

expected_effect.size: unknown; mechanism-based, applied honestly in a 3-tier ladder and anchor-high-then-downsell pattern in this playbook's examples

risk.note: A real premium anchor is honest; a fake 'was' price is not.

prerequisites: A genuine premium tier or item to lead with
steps: Design or confirm a real premium tier or item exists in the lineup.
Place it first on the pricing page or as the first upsell offer.
Order post-purchase upsells from highest to lowest price.
Never fabricate a 'was' price to manufacture the contrast.

test.method: A/B test premium-first ordering against the current order.
test.read_point: After enough orders for a stable read

title: Pre-commit a spend ceiling before any competitive bid
hypothesis: If the team sets a spend ceiling before any competitive bid (an ad auction, inventory buy or sponsorship deal), then auction-fever style overcommitment does not happen mid-negotiation.

signal.check: A competitive bid or negotiation is about to start with no pre-agreed ceiling written down.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a discipline rule

risk.note: A pre-commitment discipline.

steps: Before any competitive bid or negotiation, write down the maximum acceptable price.
Share the ceiling with everyone involved in the negotiation beforehand.
Do not exceed it in the moment, even under pressure.
Run the time-travel question ('knowing what we now know, would we make this call again?') on any launch or bet before funding it further.

test.method: Track whether any bid exceeded its pre-set ceiling.
test.read_point: After each competitive bid or negotiation

title: Avoid stacking conflicting persuasion cues on one step
hypothesis: If we avoid stacking an aggressive countdown next to heavy unrelated proof on the same step, then credibility is not reduced by cues that clash instead of reinforcing each other.

signal.check: One page or ad stacks urgency, heavy social proof and an authority claim all at once.

expected_effect.size: unknown; mechanism-based, apply as a design constraint

risk.note: A design simplification.

steps: Audit any page or ad using more than 2 persuasion cues at once.
Pick the single most relevant cue for that step instead of stacking every available cue.
Test the honest, simplified version against the stacked version.
Never apply a persuasion cue before the baseline page mechanics (clarity, load time, checkout flow) already work.

test.method: A/B test a single-cue version against the current stacked version.
test.read_point: After enough sessions for a stable read

title: Do not cut pre-sale spend on a lagged October ROAS read
hypothesis: If we treat weak short-window ROAS in October and early November as a lagging indicator, not a real weak signal, then we do not shrink the top-of-funnel audience right before the sale needs it to be biggest.
does_not_apply_when: A flat-demand subscription store with no Q4-weighted sales calendar

signal.check: Short-window ROAS looks weak in October or early November and a spend cut is being considered.

expected_effect.size: the 1-day vs 30-day click gap was about 40% normal and about 80% in November in one agency's accounts

risk.note: Cutting pre-sale spend based on a lagged read can shrink the audience the sale needs most.

prerequisites: At least one prior year of both short-window and long-window ROAS data
steps: Pull the brand's own 1-day vs 30-day click ROAS gap from a prior peak period.
Expect short-window ROAS to look weaker than usual in October and early November.
Do not cut spend based on the short-window number alone during this period.
Re-read performance on the longer window once enough time has passed for it to settle.

test.method: Compare short-window and long-window ROAS for the same spend in prior years.

title: Front-load about a third to 40 percent of the Q4 budget into September and October
hypothesis: If about 31 to 43% of the September-to-December budget is spent in September and October, then the account has an established audience and learning phase before CPMs and competition spike in November.

signal.check: The September-October budget share of the Sep-to-Dec total is well under the brand's own calibrated range and CPMs are expected to spike in November.

expected_effect.size: portfolio range cited: 31 to 43% of Sep-to-Dec budget in Sep and Oct; CPMs rose about 25 to 30% above October from about November 12

risk.note: Front-loading commits budget earlier; treat the range as a portfolio calibration, not a fixed target.

prerequisites: A written September-to-December budget
steps: Set the total September-to-December budget.
Allocate roughly a third to 40 percent of it to September and October, calibrated to the brand's own prior-year pattern.
Treat November as a harvesting month for reach, not the main buying month.
Update the plan each year rather than carrying last year's CPM assumption forward.

test.method: Compare front-loaded years against non-front-loaded years' peak results.
test.measure: spend share by month vs peak revenue

title: Decide profit play or inventory play before setting the peak's CAC tolerance
hypothesis: If the peak sale's objective (maximize contribution profit, or clear C-grade stock) is decided and written down before setting CAC tolerance, then the media team is not pulled in two directions during the sale.

signal.check: The peak sale is being planned without a written objective (profit vs inventory clearance) and CAC tolerance.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a decision-clarity rule

risk.note: A planning decision made before the sale starts.

prerequisites: Inventory grading and margin data
steps: Decide with the founder whether the sale's objective is contribution profit or clearing C/D-grade stock.
Write down the CAC tolerance that objective implies.
Communicate the objective to the media team before the sale weekend.
Avoid a tiered offer that tries to serve both objectives at once, since it tends to underperform either pure play.

test.method: Confirm the written objective and CAC tolerance exist before the sale starts.
test.measure: presence of a written objective and CAC tolerance

title: Apply the 3 peak corrections: attribution, cohort quality and margin
hypothesis: If we correct the peak CAC forecast for attribution lag, November cohort quality and discount-adjusted margin, then the plan is not built on a distorted base.

signal.check: A peak-season CAC allowance is set without correcting for attribution lag, November cohort repeat rate, or discount-adjusted break-even ROAS.

expected_effect.size: one 10-brand sample found November cohorts repeated at 38.5% at 6 months vs 63% for February, though 2 of 10 showed no gap

risk.note: A forecasting correction step.

prerequisites: Prior-year attribution window comparison
6-month repeat by acquisition month for 2 prior years
Gross margin by SKU
steps: Derive an attribution multiplier from the brand's own prior-year short vs long click window gap.
Check the brand's own November cohort 6-month repeat rate against a normal month.
Model discount-adjusted break-even ROAS per offer tier.
Combine all 3 into a corrected November CAC allowance before finalizing the plan.

test.method: Compare the corrected CAC allowance to the naive one.
test.read_point: Before the peak plan is finalized

title: Scale peak spend on marginal contribution margin with written numeric gates
hypothesis: If peak spend scales on a 3-day rolling marginal contribution-margin rule with written gates instead of a fixed morning target, then the team reacts to the real marginal economics instead of an average CAC that can hide a bad marginal CAC.

signal.check: Peak spend decisions are made against a fixed daily target time (like an 8am check) rather than a written 3-day rolling marginal CM3 rule.

expected_effect.size: example: average CAC under a $400 limit at $392 while marginal CAC ran about $1,000

risk.note: Scaling on average CAC alone during a peak can mask a much worse marginal CAC.

prerequisites: Ability to track marginal CM3 by day or by hour
steps: Write the rule before the peak: 3-day rolling marginal CM3 improving means increase, flat means hold, 2 consecutive poor reads mean decrease.
Build per-hour delayed-attribution multipliers since spend peaks earlier than revenue.
Read conversion rate by hour as a less-lagged signal than revenue.
Use revenue-to-spend elasticity only to justify a cut, never to justify scaling, since it is observational.

test.method: Apply the written rule daily during the peak window.
test.read_point: Daily during the peak, reviewed every 3 days

title: Set base and stretch peak budgets with pre-agreed numeric gates
hypothesis: If the peak plan enters with base and stretch budgets and pre-agreed numeric gates, then the team can move between them or pull back without needing a live approval call mid-sale.

signal.check: The peak budget is a single fixed number to spend, not a base and stretch range with written gates.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a planning-structure rule

risk.note: A planning step; the gates themselves are the rollback mechanism.

steps: Set a base budget and a stretch budget for the peak.
Write numeric gates (a CM3 floor, a marginal CAC ceiling, or a ROAS band) that decide movement between them.
Agree the gates with the founder before the peak starts.
Treat the stretch budget as a ceiling to deploy against incremental returns, never a spend target.

test.method: Track which gate triggers during the peak and whether the response matched the plan.
test.measure: gate triggers vs actual spend response
test.read_point: During and immediately after the peak

title: Forecast peak creative volume from spend divided by a realistic per-ad ceiling, with a tail buffer
hypothesis: If peak creative volume is forecast as peak daily spend divided by a realistic per-ad spend ceiling, with extra tail-buffer ads planned, then the account has enough ads that can actually hold the spend instead of assuming a handful of winners will carry it.

signal.check: The peak spend target has been set without checking whether enough ads exist that can each hold the implied per-ad spend.

expected_effect.size: example: a $150k peak day at $10 to 12k per ad needs 12 to 18 ads that can each hold that spend; the bottom 80% of ads held about 54% of one portfolio's spend

risk.note: If required volume exceeds production capacity, lower the spend target or raise production before locking the plan.

prerequisites: Historical per-ad spend ceiling for the account
steps: Estimate the brand's own realistic per-ad daily spend ceiling from history.
Divide peak daily spend target by that ceiling to get the minimum number of ads needed.
Add a tail buffer of extra ads, since the bottom 80% of ads still carries a meaningful share of peak spend.
If production or page-limit capacity cannot meet the number, lower the spend target or raise capacity before locking the plan.

test.method: Count ads actually holding meaningful spend during the peak vs the forecast.
test.measure: number of ads at or near the per-ad ceiling

title: Never turn off evergreen campaigns for a sale; duplicate and badge winners instead
hypothesis: If evergreen campaigns stay live and winning ads are duplicated and badged with the sale offer instead of pausing evergreen, then the account does not lose the 50 to 60% of Black Friday spend that evergreen typically carries.

signal.check: A plan exists to pause evergreen campaigns during the sale to make room for new sale-specific campaigns.

expected_effect.size: evergreen is cited as carrying 50 to 60% of Black Friday spend in one portfolio

risk.note: Turning off evergreen is called the single biggest peak mistake in this source; it can be hard to recover the learning phase mid-peak.

prerequisites: List of current evergreen winners
steps: List every evergreen campaign that must not be turned off for the sale.
Duplicate the best performers, including some fatigued ones, and badge them with the sale offer.
Judge peak creative on CTR and CPC at the ad-set level, not ROAS at the ad level, since the discount corrupts the ROAS read exactly when the most data is generated.
Add sale messaging to catalog and dynamic ad copy as well.

test.method: Track evergreen campaign status and CTR/CPC through the peak.
test.measure: ctr and cpc at the ad-set level

title: Pre-build the full offer ladder with pages and creative loaded before the sale starts
hypothesis: If the full offer ladder (GWP, referral, free shipping, bundle, deepest discount) is pre-built with landing pages and creative loaded and trade-number triggers set, then the team can pivot the offer mid-sale without producing anything live.

signal.check: The peak sale plan has one fixed offer with no fallback ladder, pages or triggers pre-built.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a preparation rule to prevent offer fatigue and live production scrambles

risk.note: A pre-production task; lock the offer sequence before producing launch and deadline assets.

prerequisites: Margin data to price each tier of the ladder
steps: Design the full offer ladder: GWP, referral, free shipping threshold, bundle, deepest sitewide discount.
Build the landing page and creative for every rung of the ladder in advance.
Set trade-number triggers for when to move to the next fallback.
Lock the offer sequence before producing final launch and deadline creative.

test.method: Confirm every rung of the ladder is pre-built and ready before the sale.
test.measure: count of ladder rungs with pages and creative ready

title: Prep Google as a peak preparation platform, not a weekend scaling lever
hypothesis: If Google titles, assets, promotion feeds and Merchant Center pricing are updated well in advance and budget is not raised on Google over the sale weekend based on its ROAS alone, then Google spend is not mistaken for incremental demand it is mostly just capturing.

signal.check: Google ROAS looks strong during the sale weekend and a budget raise is being considered based on that alone.

expected_effect.size: unknown; strength during the weekend is described as mostly captured demand from Meta and brand search

risk.note: A preparation and restraint rule.

prerequisites: Merchant Center and PMax access
steps: Update titles, assets, promotion feeds and Merchant Center pricing well before the sale.
Treat cost caps as a diagnostic tool during the peak, not the main scaling lever.
Do not raise Google budget over the weekend based on ROAS alone.
Recheck the current Merchant Center and PMax settings before the peak, since these change often.

test.method: Compare Google's incremental read (from a prior holdout) to its reported ROAS during the peak.
test.read_point: During and after the peak weekend

title: Sign 3PL and 4PL paperwork and size support and inventory before the peak, not during it
hypothesis: If 3PL and 4PL paperwork, inventory buffer and support capacity are confirmed on a fixed pre-peak date, then a missing document or capacity gap does not cause an inventory seizure or a support collapse during the busiest weeks of the year.

signal.check: 3PL or 4PL paperwork, inventory buffer or support capacity has not been checked against a fixed pre-peak date.

expected_effect.size: one example lost a $130M acquisition offer after a missing 4PL document caused a full inventory seizure on Black Friday two years running

risk.note: A missed document or capacity gap during peak can be catastrophic and is very hard to fix mid-event.

prerequisites: A list of every region's 3PL and 4PL paperwork requirements
steps: List every region's required 3PL and 4PL paperwork.
Confirm every document is signed by a fixed pre-peak date, not during the event.
Size inventory buffer and support headcount against the expected spike.
Confirm restock lead time and decide in advance whether to protect stock into December.

test.method: Run the operations checklist against the fixed pre-peak date.
test.measure: count of outstanding items on the checklist
test.read_point: On the fixed pre-peak checklist date, at least 4 to 6 weeks before the sale

title: Prepare a deliberate Q5 offer for the cheapest media window of the year
hypothesis: If a specific offer is prepared for the roughly December 16 to 31 window, then the store captures the cheapest media of the cycle deliberately instead of dumping leftover budget with no plan.

signal.check: No specific offer or creative is planned for the December 16 to 31 window beyond leftover Black Friday assets.

expected_effect.size: described as the cheapest media of the cycle, but do not carry last year's CPMs into this year's forecast

risk.note: A planning task; check current-year macro conditions before assuming last year's cheap-media pattern repeats.

prerequisites: Q5-specific offer and creative
steps: Design a specific offer for the December 16 to 31 window, separate from Black Friday leftovers.
Check the current year's macro conditions (rates, inflation, ad inventory) rather than assuming last year's cheap CPMs repeat.
Prepare creative and landing pages ahead of the window.
Launch the Q5 offer as a deliberate push, not a leftover-budget dump.

test.method: Compare Q5 CPM and ROAS to the rest of Q4.
test.measure: cpm and roas_blended in the Q5 window
test.read_point: During and after the Q5 window

title: Never credit a channel launched into a seasonal peak with the peak's own lift
hypothesis: If a channel launched right before or during a seasonal peak is not credited with the peak's lift without a causal design, then a normal seasonal spike does not get mistaken for proof the new channel works.

signal.check: A new channel launched in October or November is being credited with the peak's revenue lift with no lift test, geo-lift or CausalImpact design behind it.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a discipline rule

risk.note: A discipline rule for post-peak reporting.

steps: Note the launch date of any new channel relative to the seasonal peak.
Do not credit that channel with revenue growth in the same window without a causal design.
Run a proper lift test, geo-lift or CausalImpact analysis before crediting or funding it further.
Extend the measurement window post-peak to capture lagged conversions before drawing conclusions.

test.method: Run a causal test on the new channel outside the peak window.
test.measure: incremental lift attributable to the new channel
test.read_point: After the causal test completes, typically 4 or more weeks post-peak

title: Default to profit and supplier terms before debt, and debt before equity
hypothesis: If growth is funded from profit and supplier terms first, debt second, and equity only for a specific opportunity cash flow cannot buy fast enough, then the brand keeps control and kills losing bets faster because no outside money props them up.
does_not_apply_when: A genuinely inventory-heavy or capital-constrained model that may need outside capital regardless

signal.check: A capital raise or debt facility is being discussed before supplier terms and profit reinvestment have been fully used.

expected_effect.size: one example progressed supplier terms from none to 15, 30, 45 and 60 to 90+ days before any revolver

risk.note: A sequencing decision on how to fund growth.

prerequisites: Current supplier terms and cash position
steps: List current funding sources in order: profit reinvestment, supplier terms, a revolver or recap, a strategic minority partner, investor capital, a secondary or sale.
Push supplier terms and profit reinvestment as far as they reasonably go first.
Before taking on debt or equity, name the specific opportunity it funds that cash flow cannot buy fast enough.
For any investor, ask whose money it is, what return they need, and over what time horizon.

test.method: Review the funding stack before any new capital decision.
test.measure: share of growth funded by profit and terms vs debt or equity

title: Match the working-capital tool to the timing gap, cheapest first
hypothesis: If we match a revolver, recap, PO factoring or supplier terms to the specific timing gap they solve, then the brand does not take on debt or equity for a problem a cheaper tool would fix.

signal.check: A financing decision is being made without first checking whether supplier terms or PO factoring would solve the same timing gap more cheaply.

expected_effect.size: conservative leverage cited at 2 to 3x EBITDA vs 6 to 7x seen pre-2022

risk.note: Debt taken without genuine confidence the business works is a short-term patch that can compound the underlying problem.

prerequisites: Cash conversion cycle and supplier terms data
steps: Identify the specific timing gap (smoothing cash flow, a large PO, taking value off the table).

Match it to the cheapest tool that solves it: supplier terms and safety stock first, then a revolver for smoothing, then PO or receivables factoring for a specific large order, then a recap only to take enterprise value off the table.
Model the debt load a lender or buyer would place on the business and whether it survives a downturn before accepting it.
Avoid funding first-purchase losses with debt unless the operator is genuinely dialed in on the unit economics.

test.method: Compare the cost of the chosen tool against the cheaper alternatives before signing.
test.measure: effective cost of capital by tool

title: Bring in a CFO or fractional finance lead around $1M in revenue, not the year before a sale
hypothesis: If a CFO or fractional finance lead joins around $1M in revenue instead of the year before a sale, then financial models and clean books exist well before they are urgently needed.

signal.check: The store is past roughly $1M revenue with no CFO, fractional finance lead, or real financial model in place.

expected_effect.size: one brand had no financial models until about a year before a sale interview and calls that a gap

risk.note: A hiring decision.

steps: Hire a fractional or full-time finance lead once revenue passes about $1M.
Build financial models and a set of books that close fast and would pass an audit.
Add a banker or acquisition-experienced finance advisor once a sale becomes a real possibility.
Do not wait until a year before a planned exit to start this.

test.method: Check whether books close within a set number of days and would pass a basic audit.
test.measure: days to close books; audit readiness

title: Vet single-source suppliers with MFN clauses, backup capacity or vertical integration
hypothesis: If single-source suppliers carry most-favored-nation clauses, backup capacity, or are vertically integrated where the input is the moat, then a supplier problem does not become an existential brand problem.

signal.check: A core input or SKU relies on a single supplier with no MFN clause, backup capacity plan, or certification vetting.

expected_effect.size: one brand nearly lost its business when a larger customer bought out its sole manufacturer's capacity

risk.note: Supplier diversification and MFN clauses take time and negotiating leverage to arrange.

prerequisites: A supplier map by SKU and input
steps: Map every SKU and key input to its supplier count.
For single-source relationships, negotiate an MFN clause and confirmed backup capacity.
Vet contract manufacturers on capacity and certifications, and split across facilities once volume allows.
Treat vendor relationships as mutual, not as pure leverage extraction.

test.method: Audit single-source exposure and backup plans quarterly.
test.measure: share of SKUs with a single, unbacked supplier

title: Require the 1+1=3 test and an enterprise-value check before any strategic minority sale
hypothesis: If a strategic partnership or minority equity sale only proceeds when it closes a capability gap the brand cannot build itself and visibly raises enterprise value, then the deal is worth the dilution instead of a shortcut to a full sale.

signal.check: A minority equity or strategic partnership deal is being considered without a clear 1+1=3 capability gap or an enterprise-value test.

expected_effect.size: one example sold about 30% for logistics and distribution capability and reports enterprise value tripling in about 6 months

risk.note: Expect the partner to influence product and channel decisions even as a minority holder; set exclusivity and exit terms first.

prerequisites: A named capability gap the brand cannot build alone
steps: Name the specific capability gap (distribution, logistics, manufacturing) the brand cannot build itself.
Confirm the partner closes that gap and would visibly raise enterprise value.
Set exclusivity and exit terms before signing.
If the test fails on either count, consider a full sale instead of a partial one.

test.method: Track enterprise value and capability gap closure after the deal.
test.read_point: 6 to 12 months after the deal closes

title: Treat exit multiples as founder heuristics to verify, never as an assumed outlier band
hypothesis: If any cited exit multiple is labelled as a founder heuristic and checked against current market conditions, then a founder does not plan around an outlier deal as if it were the norm.

signal.check: A valuation or exit plan cites a specific multiple without checking whether it is current and whether it applies to this brand's category and structure.

expected_effect.size: bands cited: dropshipping about 1 to 2x EBITDA, non-subscription ecommerce about 3 to 6x, subscription higher, outlier deals up to about 3 to 5x revenue or 30x EBITDA

risk.note: A verification habit before planning around any multiple.

steps: Label any cited exit multiple as a founder heuristic, not a fact.
Check current market conditions for the brand's category and structure before using it.
Focus on the real value drivers: recurring revenue, hard-to-win customers, scale, growth trajectory, and a buyer whose network lifts the earnout.
Build cash flow and operating skill first; design for a specific multiple only once close to a real process.

test.method: Compare the cited multiple against current comparable deals before using it in planning.

title: Remove key-person risk deliberately before it is tested by a crisis
hypothesis: If a leadership team, a defined CEO-replacement archetype, and celebrity or creator deals with 3-year minimums are built before a crisis, then the brand does not stop selling if one person leaves or one partner's public profile changes.

signal.check: The brand's sales, brand name, or a major creative asset depend heavily on one person with no named backup or succession plan.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a risk-reduction rule

risk.note: Building a leadership team and succession plan takes real time and cost, but the alternative risk is high.

steps: List every point where one person's absence would stop sales (founder, a single dominant creator, a celebrity partner).
Avoid naming the brand after one person or over-relying on one creator or celebrity.
Define the CEO-replacement archetype the stage needs before a hire is urgent, and run any hire through a roughly 6-month trial.
Set celebrity or creator equity deals on a 3-year minimum with a plan for their public profile changing.

test.method: Audit key-person exposure points quarterly.
test.measure: count of unmitigated key-person exposure points

title: Kill a structurally dead product line fast, but don't confuse it with a temporarily slow one
hypothesis: If a structurally dead product line is wound down quickly instead of chased with more marketing, then cash is protected, but the same decisiveness must not be applied to a category that is only temporarily slow.

signal.check: A product line's core reason to exist has genuinely disappeared (a regulatory change, a trend that fully ended) and the team is still funding it at scale.

expected_effect.size: one example wound down a suddenly-dead revenue line and laid off about 2,000 staff; competitors that kept scaling that same revenue are described as bankrupt or delisted

risk.note: Winding down a line too early on a merely slow (not dead) category can destroy a line that would have recovered.

prerequisites: Clear evidence the line's core demand driver is structurally gone, not just slow
steps: Distinguish a structurally dead line (the core reason to buy has genuinely disappeared) from a temporarily slow one.
For a confirmed dead line, wind it down decisively rather than trying to rescue it with marketing.
For a slow-but-viable line, apply patience (see the multi-year patience idea) instead.
Document the evidence behind the call either way.

test.method: Review the evidence for 'dead vs slow' before any wind-down decision.
test.measure: documented evidence trail for the call
test.read_point: Before any major SKU or category wind-down

title: Build a peer and mentor network before a growth-stage crisis hits
hypothesis: If a founder builds a peer and mentor network before a crisis, then advice is available for growth-stage problems that become rarer and harder to find guidance for as the brand scales.

signal.check: The founder has no active peer or mentor network and is currently facing a decision with no precedent inside the company.

expected_effect.size: one founder called on named peers during a sellout crisis

risk.note: A relationship-building habit.

steps: Identify 3 to 5 founders or operators a stage or two ahead in a comparable category.
Build the relationship before a crisis, not during one.
Bring growth-stage problems to this group as they arise.
Remember no single operator sees every problem alone.

test.method: Track how many major decisions used outside input from the network.
test.measure: count of decisions run past the peer network

title: Hold a warranty, damage and product-liability reserve as its own cost line
hypothesis: If a physical-goods store holds a warranty, damage and product-liability reserve as its own line, then a claim or recall does not become a surprise cash event on top of normal operating costs.
does_not_apply_when: A store with no physical product or negligible liability exposure

signal.check: No warranty, damage or product-liability reserve line exists in the cash model for a physical-goods store.

expected_effect.size: unknown; no source in this folder covers this, verify against the brand's own claim and defect history

risk.note: A reserve-setting task.

prerequisites: Historical defect rate and claim data
steps: Pull historical defect rate, warranty claims and any liability incidents.
Size a reserve line based on that history and category norms.
Add it to the cash model alongside the other founder and capital decision lines.
Review the reserve size annually or after any claim.

test.method: Compare actual claims against the reserve annually.

title: Question a competitor's P&L or letter the same way you'd question your own
hypothesis: If a competitor's public P&L or shareholder letter is read by checking the contribution-margin definition, the ARR annualization month, the LTV horizon versus the oldest real cohort, and what funds any cash-flow claim, then the teardown does not copy a number that would not survive its own scrutiny.

signal.check: A competitor teardown is using a public P&L, letter or interview figure without checking its definitions and funding basis.

expected_effect.size: one disclosed example gave a contribution-margin definition and a Q2 net margin figure that were internally unreconciled

risk.note: A read-only skepticism check.

prerequisites: A competitor's public filing, letter or interview
steps: Check how contribution margin is defined in the source.
Check what month any ARR figure was annualized from.
Check the LTV horizon claimed against the oldest real cohort age.
Check what is funding any cash-flow-positive claim before treating any figure as reliable.

test.method: Apply this checklist to every competitor figure before using it in a teardown.
test.measure: count of figures that failed the checklist

title: Classify a competitor's ad account as creating demand or harvesting it
hypothesis: If we tag a sample of a competitor's ads by awareness stage and celebrity or influencer share, then we can tell whether their account creates new demand or only harvests existing fame, which decides what is actually transferable.

signal.check: A competitor teardown recommends copying an ad strategy without checking whether that account depends on fame, retail scale or press the brand under review lacks.

expected_effect.size: one competitor ran about 96% of ads in the bottom 2 awareness stages with no cold-prospecting fallback, a strategy legitimate only with fame most brands lack

risk.note: A read-only classification of public ads.

prerequisites: A scrape of 40 or more of the competitor's public ads
steps: Tag a sample of 40 or more competitor ads by awareness stage.
Count the share carrying a celebrity or influencer name.
Ask whether any cold-prospecting creative in the sample would survive if the outside engine (fame, retail, PR) stopped.
Classify the account as creating or harvesting demand before recommending any pattern from it.

test.method: Complete the classification before writing teardown recommendations.
test.measure: share of ads by awareness stage and celebrity presence
test.read_point: Before the teardown report is finalized

title: Map competitor creative against a fixed format taxonomy and score the 8 beats
hypothesis: If we map a competitor's creative against a fixed format taxonomy and score a sample of scripts on the 8 beats (hook, problem, mechanism, proof, objection, offer, risk reversal, CTA), then the teardown captures the pattern of what works structurally instead of copying the actual script.

signal.check: A teardown is reviewing competitor creative without a fixed format taxonomy or script-beat scoring.

expected_effect.size: one competitor's script was cloned across 3 personas with only the persona and destination changed

risk.note: A read-only analysis; never reproduce the competitor's actual script or copy.

prerequisites: A scrape of the competitor's live ad creative
steps: Define a fixed format taxonomy (for example editorial, portrait, product grid, carousel, UGC).
Map the competitor's ad sample against that taxonomy.
Transcribe a sample of scripts and score them on the 8 beats.
Count voiceover vs silent and measure median and maximum live-ad age.
Note what the taxonomy misses, such as founder or store content.

test.method: Complete the format map and script scoring before the teardown report.
test.measure: format share and average beat-completeness score
test.read_point: Before the teardown report is finalized

title: Audit where a competitor routes paid traffic and which of their pages get none
hypothesis: If we audit the share of a competitor's ads landing on a homepage, grid, persona page, advertorial or PDP, and note which built pages get zero traffic, then the teardown finds real routing patterns to test instead of copying page copy.

signal.check: A teardown discusses a competitor's landing strategy without checking the actual share of ads by destination type.

expected_effect.size: one competitor sent about three quarters of paid traffic to collection grids; another had a built page with no ads pointed at it at all

risk.note: A read-only audit.

prerequisites: A scrape of the competitor's ad library with landing URLs
steps: Tag each ad by destination type: homepage, category grid, persona page, advertorial or quiz, PDP.
Compute the share of ads by destination type.
Note any built page with no ads pointing to it.
Only treat a category grid as a viable paid destination if the brand under review can staff a daily-owner merchandising process, as fast fashion typically does.

test.method: Complete the destination audit before the teardown report.
test.measure: share of ads by destination type
test.read_point: Before the teardown report is finalized

title: Audit a competitor's proof numbers for internal consistency, then run the same audit on your own
hypothesis: If we check whether a competitor's same-day ad claims (customer counts, ingredient counts) match their own disclosed totals, and run the same check on our own claims, then a compliance gap is caught before a platform or regulator finds it.

signal.check: A proof number (customer count, review count, ingredient count) appears in ads or on the PDP without a recent cross-check against the brand's own internal records.

expected_effect.size: one competitor's same-day ads claimed 3 different customer counts against one disclosed figure

risk.note: An unaddressed inconsistency is a compliance and trust risk, not just a competitor teardown finding.

prerequisites: A sample of the brand's own live ads and PDP claims
steps: Pull a sample of same-day ad and PDP claims with a proof number.
Compare them against the disclosed or internally recorded true figure.
Flag any inconsistency for correction before a platform or regulator does.
Run this audit on the brand's own claims as a standing quarterly check, not only on competitors.

test.method: Run the consistency audit quarterly on the brand's own claims.
test.measure: count of inconsistent proof numbers found

title: Separate what is transferable from a competitor teardown from what is not
hypothesis: If a teardown explicitly separates transferable patterns (structure, mechanism, format mix, routing) from non-transferable assets (a unique financing facility, a celebrity equity deal, a fame-dependent strategy), then recommendations do not assume the brand under review has resources it does not have.

signal.check: A teardown report recommends copying a competitor pattern without stating whether the underlying resource (financing, fame, celebrity deal) is available to this brand.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a report-structure discipline

risk.note: A reporting discipline.

prerequisites: Completed awareness, format and destination audits
steps: List every pattern found (script structure, offer stacking, persona pages) as a candidate.
For each, name the resource it depends on (financing, fame, celebrity deal, retail scale).
Mark it transferable only if the brand under review has or can build that resource.
Route each transferable pattern to its owner folder as a hypothesis to test on the brand's own traffic, never as a copy.

test.method: Review the transferable list against the brand's actual resources before testing any pattern.
test.measure: count of patterns confirmed transferable vs not
test.read_point: Before the teardown report is finalized

title: Count competitor concept diversity at peak season, not just asset count
hypothesis: If a peak-season competitor scrape counts distinct creative concepts instead of just total asset count, then the teardown captures how many real ideas a competitor tested, not how many variations of one idea they shipped.

signal.check: A competitor scrape reports total ad count for the peak season without counting distinct underlying concepts.

expected_effect.size: one large brand shipped 429 unique assets from only 3 concepts, flagged as not advisable at smaller scale

risk.note: A read-only scrape.

prerequisites: A scrape of competitor peak-season ads
steps: Scrape competitor ads and pages from the prior peak season.
Group them by distinct underlying concept, not by asset count.
Compare concept count across competitors of different sizes.
Use the count as a signal for next year's own concept-count planning, not a target to match exactly.

test.method: Repeat the scrape and concept count each peak season.

title: Use free demand barometers to filter a category or creator before committing
hypothesis: If Amazon best-seller rank and Google Trends are checked for a consistent upward line before committing to a category or a long creator contract, then a short-lived spike is not mistaken for a real trend.

signal.check: A new category or a 6 to 12 month creator contract is being committed to without checking Amazon BSR or Google Trends first.

expected_effect.size: unknown; these are directional filters, they show interest but not margin

risk.note: A free, read-only screening step.

steps: Check Amazon best-seller rank trend for the category or comparable products.
Check Google Trends for the category term and for any creator being considered for a long contract.
Look for a consistent upward line, not a single spike.
Remember neither tool shows margin; use them as a filter, not a full validation.

test.method: Track BSR and Trends for the committed category or creator after the decision.
test.measure: trend direction vs the pre-decision read

title: Do all arithmetic in code and keep totals separate from breakdowns
hypothesis: If every ratio and total is computed in code from raw data rather than by hand or read off a platform breakdown, then breakdown numbers (age, placement, audience splits) are not mistaken for the incremental return at the margin.

signal.check: A key metric or budget decision was computed by hand or copied directly from a platform's breakdown view rather than from a code-based calculation on raw data.

expected_effect.size: unknown; an operating discipline, not a metric target

risk.note: A process discipline.

prerequisites: Access to raw order and ad-spend data
steps: Compute period ROAS and other ratios as total value divided by total spend, in code, from raw data.
Do not restructure a campaign based on a platform breakdown (age, placement, audience segment) alone.
Keep totals and breakdowns in separate views so they are never confused.
Show any missing input as unavailable, never as zero.

test.method: Audit a sample of recent decisions for whether the number behind them was code-computed.
test.measure: share of decisions backed by a code-computed number

title: Treat every threshold in this bank as a hypothesis until the brand's own data confirms it
hypothesis: If every benchmark or threshold used in planning is checked against the brand's own data before being acted on, then a founder figure, agency average or hypothetical example does not get treated as a fact for this specific brand.

signal.check: A benchmark or threshold from an external source is being used in a plan without checking it against the brand's own recent data.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a verification habit

risk.note: A verification habit.

steps: Before using any external benchmark, pull the brand's own equivalent number.
Compare and note the gap, if any.
Use the brand's own number for the actual decision; use the benchmark only as a sanity check.
Flag any benchmark with no supporting brand data as unverified in the plan document.

test.method: Audit a sample of recent plans for unverified benchmarks.
test.measure: share of used benchmarks checked against brand data

title: Move fast on internal bets, slow down and test on anything customer-facing
hypothesis: If internal bets move fast on directional evidence while customer-facing changes (a new market, a new checkout, a full billing-cycle switch) are tested incrementally, then a 'flip the switch' launch does not break something a customer depends on.

signal.check: A customer-facing change (checkout, billing cycle, a new market launch) is planned as a single full switch rather than an incremental test.

expected_effect.size: one 'flip the switch' international launch broke its cross-border integration; a wholesale switch to quarterly billing is called dangerous by a separate source

risk.note: Some customer-facing switches (billing cycle, checkout provider) are hard to unwind once live for existing customers.

steps: Classify a planned change as internal (creative, targeting, internal process) or customer-facing (checkout, billing, market launch).
For internal bets, move on directional evidence without waiting for full certainty.
For customer-facing changes, run an incremental or segmented test before a full rollout.
Keep a pre-change baseline so the before-and-after comparison is clean.

test.method: Run the customer-facing change on a segment before a full rollout.
test.measure: cvr_checkout_to_order or the relevant metric on the test segment

title: Timestamp every structural change and keep a pre-change baseline
hypothesis: If every structural change (a pricing change, a new offer structure, a platform migration) is timestamped with a kept pre-change baseline, then the CAC and LTGP series can be compared cleanly before and after.

signal.check: A recent structural change was made with no recorded date or pre-change baseline to compare against.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a record-keeping discipline

risk.note: A record-keeping habit.

steps: Log the date of every structural change to pricing, offer, platform or channel.
Save the CAC and LTGP series as they stood immediately before the change.
Compare the before and after series at the appropriate lag (60 to 180 days for cash levers).
Keep the log accessible for future diagnosis, not just the change that prompted it.

test.method: Review the change log against the CAC/LTGP series at each stage review.
test.measure: number of changes with a clean before/after comparison available

title: Follow the SKU the data picks over the launch plan, even if it raises COGS
hypothesis: If the hero SKU the data actually picks is followed instead of the one the original launch plan favored, even when it raises COGS, then the brand builds around a genuinely strong product instead of forcing a weaker one to succeed through marketing.

signal.check: Sales data clearly favors a different SKU than the one the launch plan or marketing calendar is built around.

expected_effect.size: a strong product with mediocre marketing can still win; the reverse rarely works

risk.note: A prioritization shift, not a live risk on its own.

prerequisites: Sales data by SKU
steps: Review sales and repeat data across all active SKUs, not just the planned hero.
Identify the SKU the data actually favors, even if it carries higher COGS.
Shift marketing calendar and creative focus to that SKU.
Improve the winning SKU further (ingredient, quality) even if it raises cost, when it drives stickiness.

test.method: Compare marketing-weighted revenue for the data-picked SKU vs the originally planned hero.
test.measure: revenue and repeat rate for the data-picked SKU

title: Default to tracked codes and links over a zero-attribution creator program
hypothesis: If we default to codes, URLs and a post-purchase survey for creator programs and only allow a zero-attribution program when DTC share is small with a large creator bench, then most stores get an attributable read instead of a vague blended one.
does_not_apply_when: A brand with DTC under about 5% of revenue and a bench big enough that a 7-day window misses real purchases

signal.check: A creator program runs with no codes, links or survey attribution and DTC is the majority of revenue.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a conflict-resolution default

risk.note: A tracking-method decision.

steps: Check the brand's DTC share of revenue.
If DTC is the majority, require codes, links and a post-purchase survey on every creator deal.
Only allow a zero-attribution, blended-signal program if DTC share is small and the creator bench is large.
Never recommend zero attribution on the strength of a competitor's example alone.

test.method: Compare code-attributed vs blended-signal reads for a sample of creator deals.
test.read_point: After 8 to 12 weeks of the program

title: Never cut branded search on attributed ROAS alone; run a holdout first
hypothesis: If branded search is never cut purely on its attributed ROAS, and a holdout is run first, then a low-awareness brand does not lose real captured demand while a high-awareness brand still gets to cut unneeded spend once its own holdout confirms it.
does_not_apply_when: A brand with strong organic awareness whose own holdout has already confirmed branded search is not incremental

signal.check: Branded search spend is being cut or capped based on its attributed ROAS with no holdout test run.

expected_effect.size: one high-awareness brand's own holdouts supported capping branded search near 1% of marketing spend

risk.note: A holdout test before any structural cut.

prerequisites: Ability to run a branded-search holdout
steps: Run a branded-search holdout test before making any cut.
Exclude brand terms from PMax and report brand separately regardless of the holdout result.
Cut based on the brand's own holdout result and awareness level, not a borrowed percentage.
Protect branded search by default until the holdout says otherwise.

test.method: Run the branded-search holdout for at least 4 weeks.

title: Scale budget in about 20% steps by default; reserve doubling for small validation tests
hypothesis: If budget scales in about 20% steps by default and doubling is reserved for small-dollar validation tests, then learning phases and profit are protected at real scale while early demand tests can still move fast.
does_not_apply_when: A very small validation test ($10 to 200 a day) where doubling is a demand test, not a scaling decision

signal.check: Budget is being doubled on a meaningful campaign (above small validation-test size) rather than stepped up gradually.

expected_effect.size: doubling is described as breaking at 6-figure spend; 20% steps are the standard scaling pace

risk.note: Doubling budget on a scaled campaign can reset the learning phase and spike CPA.

steps: For any campaign above small validation-test size, scale budget in roughly 20% steps.
Only double budget inside a small, bounded validation test where the return ratio holds at each step.
Check current platform learning-phase and budget-change guidance before scaling, since this changes over time.
Watch for the return ratio breaking at each step and pause the increase if it does.

test.method: Compare cpa stability under 20% steps vs doubling on a test campaign.
test.measure: cpa stability after each budget step
test.read_point: After each budget step, typically 3 to 7 days

title: Let the brand's own signals pick organic-first or paid-from-day-1, not a fixed rule
hypothesis: If we run the cheap validation gates in order (list test, organic outlier, small paid test) and let the results decide the sequence, then the brand does not force an organic-first or paid-first approach that does not fit its category or resources.

signal.check: The brand has picked organic-first or paid-from-day-1 as a fixed philosophy without testing which one its own early signals support.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a conflict-resolution default

risk.note: A sequencing decision informed by cheap early tests.

steps: Run the list-threshold test, then the organic-outlier test, then the small paid test in order (see the staged demand validation idea).
Let the strongest signal from these tests decide whether to lean organic-first or paid-from-day-1.
Do not adopt either sequence as a fixed rule from a competitor's story alone.
Revisit the sequencing choice once real data replaces the early signal.

test.method: Compare organic and paid signal strength from the staged tests.
test.read_point: After the staged validation tests complete

title: Require a named backup for ads, fulfilment, finance and customer service at any headcount
hypothesis: If every brand keeps a named backup for ads, fulfilment, finance and customer service regardless of how lean the team is, then a lean-generalist team does not stop shipping or collecting cash if one person is out.

signal.check: No named backup exists for at least one of ads, fulfilment, finance or customer service.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a resilience rule regardless of team size

risk.note: A staffing and cross-training task.

steps: List the current owner of ads, fulfilment, finance and customer service.
Name a backup (internal cross-training or an external contractor) for each function.
Keep headcount growth below revenue growth even while adding these backups.
Treat pushback from a strong hire surrounded by weaker colleagues as a retention risk to manage, not ignore.

test.method: Test each backup by having them cover the function for a short period.
test.measure: whether the function ran without the primary owner

title: Only fund an unmeasured brand-intuition line once past the performance ceiling
hypothesis: If unmeasured 'brand intuition' spend is only allowed once a brand is past its pure-performance ceiling (roughly $1M to $20M) and has cash to lose, then intuition-led spend does not fund an early, resource-constrained brand's guesswork.
does_not_apply_when: An early or resource-constrained brand, for which rigorous measurement should apply instead

signal.check: Unmeasured spend justified by 'intuition' or 'brand feel' exists at a brand still under its pure-performance ceiling or without spare cash.

expected_effect.size: the pure-performance ceiling is cited around $1M to $20M revenue in one agency's client base

risk.note: A gating rule for unmeasured spend.

prerequisites: Confirmed stage placement (C1-C4)
steps: Confirm the brand is past its own performance-scaling ceiling before allowing any unmeasured brand-line spend.
Confirm the brand has spare cash it can afford to risk on unmeasured spend.
Match every other decision's measurement tier to its size using the reliability ladder.
Never fund an unmeasurable channel on intuition alone at an early stage.

test.method: Check stage placement and cash position before approving any unmeasured spend line.
test.measure: presence of the two gating conditions
test.read_point: Before any brand-line budget is approved

title: Default to bundles and AOV-distribution thresholds; treat hero-SKU gating as a reversible test
hypothesis: If bundles and thresholds set from the AOV distribution are the default offer architecture, and pulling a hero SKU from direct sale is only run as a written, reversible test, then most stores get a safer AOV lever while a genuinely coveted hero SKU still gets a real, bounded trial.
does_not_apply_when: A consumable category where a stockpile-style gift threshold could kill reorder frequency

signal.check: A hero-SKU gating offer is being planned as a permanent default rather than a bounded, reversible test.

expected_effect.size: one case moved AOV from about $65 to $100 by gating a hero SKU; the safer default (bundles, thresholds) has a wider evidence base

risk.note: Hero-SKU gating is higher risk; write a revert condition before testing it.

prerequisites: AOV distribution data
steps: Set the default offer architecture to bundles and thresholds set from the brand's own AOV distribution.
Only test hero-SKU gating if the hero is genuinely coveted and the economics survive giving it away as a gift.
Write a revert condition before launching a hero-gating test.
Keep the cheapest SKU out of paid entirely as a separate, low-risk lever.

test.method: A/B or phased test of the chosen offer architecture.
test.read_point: After 2 to 4 weeks of live orders

title: Gate any long-payback subscription plan on a written funding source and stop condition
hypothesis: If a longer payback period is only allowed with a named funding source, proven cohort evidence and a written stop condition, then a brand does not copy a financed competitor's payback window without the financing that made it survivable.
does_not_apply_when: A brand with proven non-dilutive or patient capital and cohort data that reaches the claimed payback horizon

signal.check: A subscription plan targets a payback period beyond the brand's own short-payback gate without a named funding source or stop condition.

expected_effect.size: one competitor's 6 to 8 month payback was funded by a facility paying 70% of each cohort's marketing; its own teardown says not to copy the window

risk.note: Funding a long payback without the matching financing structure can drain cash quickly.

steps: Gate spend on the brand's own short payback by default (A9, A10).
If the founder wants a longer payback, require a named funding source in writing.
Require cohort evidence that actually reaches the claimed payback horizon, not a projection.
Set a written stop condition before launching the longer-payback plan.

test.method: Track payback months against the written stop condition.

title: Apply the honest-urgency gate before any CRO test adds proof or scarcity
hypothesis: If urgency and proof are only tested on ambiguous, cold-traffic steps with a true backing claim, and never as a default add-everywhere reflex, then CRO tests do not reduce credibility with stacked or fake cues on high-intent or premium traffic.
does_not_apply_when: High-intent branded traffic or a premium page, where urgency and heavy proof can read as desperate

signal.check: A CRO backlog adds urgency or proof to every page as a default tactic without checking traffic type or claim truth first.

expected_effect.size: unknown; the honest version can lose to no urgency on confident buyers, so both should be tested

risk.note: A CRO test-design gate.

steps: Before testing urgency or proof, check the traffic type (cold and uncertain vs high-intent or premium).
Confirm any urgency or proof claim is real before testing it.
Ban resetting countdowns, seller-typed counts and staged rivals outright, regardless of test results.
Test the honest version against no urgency at all, since it can lose on confident buyers.

test.method: A/B test honest urgency/proof against no urgency on the same page.
test.read_point: After enough sessions for a stable read by traffic type

title: Plan creative for the peak's spread tail; let winners concentrate the rest of the year
hypothesis: If creative volume is planned for a spread tail during the peak window and allowed to concentrate on winners the rest of the year, then the account matches the real Pareto pattern of each period instead of applying one rule year-round.

signal.check: The account applies the same concentration strategy (heavy winner concentration or heavy spread) in both the peak window and the rest of the year.

expected_effect.size: one portfolio found the bottom 80% of ads held about 54% of Black Friday spend, unlike a normal period's concentration on the top few ads

risk.note: A seasonal planning switch.

prerequisites: Historical Pareto data for the account by period
steps: Plan for concentrated spend on a few winners during a normal scaling period.
Plan for a spread tail of many ads during the peak window, since offer and discount drive more of the variance then.
Use ad-set budget controls that allow this switch by period.
Review the actual Pareto split after each peak to recalibrate next year's plan.

test.method: Compare spend concentration in the peak window vs a normal month.
test.measure: share of spend held by the top 10% of ads, by period
test.read_point: After the peak window and again after a normal month

title: Carry the conservative 30% figure for the data-integrity audit claim, not the 80% headline
hypothesis: If we carry the more conservative, transcript-stated figure (about 30%) for how often data integrity is the real bottleneck, rather than a source's own unsupported 80% headline, then planning is not anchored to an inflated claim.

signal.check: A plan cites an 80% figure for how often measurement is the root cause of a performance problem, sourced from a title rather than a stated method.

expected_effect.size: the source's own transcript states about 30%, not the 80% in its title; no published method exists for either

risk.note: A citation-accuracy check.

steps: When citing this claim, use the transcript-stated 30% figure, not the headline 80%.
Flag the true share as unknown pending any published methodology.
Still run the data-integrity checklist regardless of which figure is used, since the checklist itself is the useful part.

test.method: Not applicable as a live test; a citation-accuracy rule.
test.measure: which figure is cited in internal materials

title: Require flows and a subscription option from day one; schedule the deliberate retention phase later
hypothesis: If cheap retention infrastructure (welcome and abandoned-cart flows, a subscription option, cohort tracking) is required from day one while the deliberate, resourced retention phase is scheduled for the $1M to $10M stage, then no store delays the cheap wins waiting for the big program.

signal.check: A store has no welcome flow, abandoned-cart flow or subscription option live, or has delayed a deliberate retention phase past proven acquisition with no reason given.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a conflict-resolution sequencing rule

risk.note: A sequencing rule combining 2 conflicting source recommendations.

steps: Launch welcome and abandoned-cart flows, a subscription option (for a consumable), and cohort tracking from day one, regardless of stage.
Schedule the deliberate, resourced retention phase (starting with the offer structure) once acquisition is proven, roughly at the $1M to $10M stage.
Set retention expectations by category repeat band, not a universal target.
Do not delay the cheap infrastructure waiting for the resourced phase to start.

test.method: Confirm cheap infrastructure is live regardless of stage; track repeat_rate_90d once the deliberate phase starts.
test.read_point: Cheap infrastructure checked at launch; repeat rate reviewed quarterly once the phase starts

title: Test the founder against an expert or hired face rather than assuming either wins
hypothesis: If founder-led content is tested against a niche expert or credible hired face on the brand's own traffic, then the brand picks the format that actually performs instead of assuming founder content is always right or always a liability.

signal.check: The brand has committed to founder-led content or an expert-face strategy as a fixed rule without testing the alternative.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a conflict-resolution test, results vary by founder and category

risk.note: Never make the brand depend on one face either way; keep the key-person risk mitigation in place regardless of the test winner.

prerequisites: Ability to produce both founder-led and expert or hired-face creative
steps: Produce a comparable batch of founder-led and expert or hired-face creative.
Test both against the same audience and offer.
Pick the format that performs, but never depend on one person's continued involvement.
Revisit the test periodically as the brand and audience evolve.

test.method: A/B test founder-led vs expert-face creative.
test.read_point: After the standard creative test window

title: Require a foot-traffic model and a break-even-in-4-walls test before any retail store
hypothesis: If any planned physical store passes a foot-traffic model and a break-even-in-4-walls test first, then a location does not get chosen on brand-control preference alone when a high-traffic mall location would perform better.
does_not_apply_when: A store already generating strong controlled foot traffic in its category (a true retail destination brand)

signal.check: A retail location decision favors a standalone flagship over a high-traffic mall location without a foot-traffic model or break-even test.

expected_effect.size: one brand's standalone stores lost money even in prime locations while high-traffic malls broke even or profited

risk.note: A retail lease is a large, hard-to-reverse commitment.

prerequisites: Foot-traffic data for candidate locations
steps: Model expected foot traffic for each candidate location.
Model a break-even-in-4-walls case (rent, staffing, expected sales) for each.
Prefer a retail-as-a-service or pop-up test before committing to a lease.
Choose based on the model, not brand-control preference alone.

test.method: Run a retail-as-a-service or pop-up test in the top candidate location first.
test.measure: actual foot traffic and sales vs the model
test.read_point: After the pop-up or test period, typically 4 to 12 weeks

title: Set founder-meeting strategy in a sale process from the stated exit intent
hypothesis: If founder presence in buyer meetings is set from the stated exit intent (a clean exit vs staying on) rather than a default habit, then the buyer prices the deal on the intended outcome instead of assuming continuity that is not planned.

signal.check: A sale process is underway with a default founder-presence approach that has not been checked against the actual exit intent.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a process-design rule requiring deal-advisory review

risk.note: Requires legal and deal advisory review before finalizing the approach.

prerequisites: A stated exit intent from the founder
steps: State the exit intent clearly: a clean exit, or staying on in some capacity.
For a clean exit, consider limiting founder presence so the buyer does not price in 'the magic' of a retained stake.
For a staying-on scenario, use founder engagement to build buyer confidence as standard M&A guidance suggests.
Review the chosen approach with deal advisory counsel before the process starts.

test.method: Not a live metric test; a process-design decision reviewed with advisors.
test.measure: advisor sign-off on the founder-presence strategy

title: Fix the angle first for an underperforming ad; fix the offer first for an underperforming business
hypothesis: If an underperforming single ad is diagnosed by testing the angle first and an underperforming business overall is diagnosed by checking the offer first, then the fix matches the scale of the problem instead of applying one rule to both.

signal.check: An underperformance issue is being fixed with the wrong-scale lever: rebuilding the offer for one weak ad, or testing angles for a business-wide profit problem.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a diagnosis-scale rule

risk.note: A diagnosis-scope rule.

steps: For a single underperforming ad, test the angle before the offer, persona or format.
For a business-wide profit or CAC problem, check the offer architecture before touching individual ad angles.
Do not apply the ad-level fix order to a business-level problem or vice versa.
Route the fix to the matching owner folder (creative for angle, offers for the offer).

test.method: Track which fix (angle or offer) resolved the issue at each scale.
test.measure: ctr or cvr_overall after the matched fix
test.read_point: After the standard test window for the fix applied

title: Keep the cash-constrained exception to the LTGP:CAC-above-3 rule
hypothesis: If a brand with LTGP:CAC above 3 is allowed to hold spend rather than being told to 'ramp harder' when it cannot fund the inventory a faster ramp needs, then a cash-constrained but efficient brand is not pushed into an inventory crisis by a generic scaling rule.
does_not_apply_when: A brand with LTGP:CAC above 3 and no cash constraint, which should scale harder

signal.check: LTGP:CAC is above 3 and a plan says to scale harder without checking whether the brand can fund the resulting inventory buy.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a conflict-resolution exception

risk.note: A gating check before a scale-up recommendation.

prerequisites: Cash model from procedure 4.1
steps: When LTGP:CAC is above 3, check the cash model for whether the brand can fund the inventory a faster ramp needs.
If it cannot, keep spend where it is and treat the ratio as a sign of underinvestment to revisit once cash allows.
If it can, scale harder as the ratio suggests.
Document which case applies before recommending either path.

test.method: Check the cash model before any scale-up recommendation when LTGP:CAC is above 3.
test.measure: whether the cash model supports the inventory buy
test.read_point: Before any spend-increase recommendation at this ratio

title: Let the account's job (find new customers vs harvest an existing audience) decide creative rotation speed
hypothesis: If a harvest-only distribution account rotates creative fast while an account that must find new customers holds winners with quick replenishment, then rotation speed matches the account's real job instead of copying whichever competitor is loudest.

signal.check: Creative rotation speed has been set by copying a competitor's cadence without checking whether the account's job (find new customers vs harvest an existing audience) matches.

expected_effect.size: one harvest-only account turned over its account roughly every 3 weeks with a 24-day max ad age; a customer-finding account held winners with quick replenishment instead

risk.note: A creative-cadence decision.

steps: Name the account's real job: finding new customers, or harvesting an existing warm or famous audience.
For a harvest-only account, rotate creative fast.
For an account that must find new customers, hold winners and replenish quickly rather than rotating on a fixed schedule.
Recheck the account's job periodically as the brand's audience and channel mix change.

test.method: Compare CAC and frequency under the chosen rotation speed.
test.read_point: After one full rotation cycle under the chosen approach

title: Default retail distribution to wide availability; use an exclusive only as a bounded launch tactic
hypothesis: If retail distribution defaults to wide availability and an exclusive deal is only used as a bounded launch tactic with a planned end and a plan for other retailers' reaction, then the brand gets both broad access and the occasional FOMO benefit of a real exclusive.

signal.check: A retail exclusivity deal is being considered as a permanent strategy rather than a bounded launch tactic.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a conflict-resolution default

risk.note: An exclusivity deal can strain relationships with other retailers if not planned for.

steps: Default to wide retail availability as the standard approach.
Consider an exclusive deal only for a specific launch, with a clear end date.
Plan in advance for how other retailers will react once the exclusive ends.
Revisit wide distribution once the exclusive period ends.

test.method: Compare sell-through during and after the exclusive period.
test.read_point: At the planned end of the exclusive period

title: Pick a channel strategy by supply, shareability and measurement fit, not the loudest founder
hypothesis: If a channel strategy (Meta-dependent vs Meta-avoidant, for example) is picked by checking creator supply, product shareability and measurement needs, then the brand does not copy a founder's channel philosophy that fits a different product or era.

signal.check: A channel strategy decision cites one founder's public story as the justification without checking creator supply, product shareability or measurement needs for this brand.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a conflict-resolution check

risk.note: A decision-check step.

steps: Check the brand's own creator supply and cost.
Check how shareable the product genuinely is on organic formats.
Check the brand's measurement needs and whether a low-attribution channel strategy fits them.
Pick the channel mix these checks support, not the mix a louder founder's story implies.

test.method: Review the 3 fit checks before committing to a channel strategy.
test.read_point: Before finalizing the channel mix plan

title: Build one monthly growth model sheet tying the P&L, cash and cohorts together
hypothesis: If the P&L waterfall, acquisition ratios, cohort table, cash model and forecast all live in one monthly sheet, then every other procedure reads from the same numbers instead of each team rebuilding its own version.

signal.check: The P&L, CAC/LTGP table, cash model and forecast currently live in separate, disconnected files or dashboards.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a consolidation task, not a metric lift

risk.note: A one-time build, then a monthly maintenance task.

prerequisites: 12 months of order, cost, spend, inventory and opex data
steps: Build the P&L waterfall tab with dollars and percent of net revenue, new and returning columns.
Build the acquisition tab: spend by channel, new customers, CAC, first-purchase GP, AMER, MER.
Build the cohort tab: cumulative GP per customer at day 30, 90, 180, 365, LTGP:CAC, payback.
Build the cash tab with the 6 levers as named inputs.
Build a forecast tab with its own error band, and a dashboard tab with the headline metrics.
Mark every cell with a missing input as unavailable, never zero.

test.method: Rebuild the sheet monthly and check it against a manual spot-check.
test.measure: sheet accuracy vs a manual spot-check

title: Run a monthly pass/fail unit-economics health check with a named binding reason
hypothesis: If a monthly pass, hold or stop call is made on unit economics with a named binding reason and next procedure, then a spend increase is never approved just because nobody explicitly said no.

signal.check: Spend increases are approved without a monthly documented pass/hold/stop check on GP:CAC, LTGP:CAC, payback, AMER vs MER, cash and opex.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a governance process

risk.note: A monthly review process.

prerequisites: Growth model sheet built for at least 3 trailing months
steps: Read first-purchase GP:CAC and LTGP:CAC against the bands.
Read payback months and the 6-month cohort GP:CAC trend.
Read AMER vs MER, ending cash and CCC, and opex as percent of revenue.
Output a pass, hold or stop call with the single binding reason and the next procedure to run.

test.method: Run the check every month before any spend-increase approval.
test.measure: pass/hold/stop outcome and its binding reason

title: Run a quarterly stage review against the measurement, creative, structure and team checklist
hypothesis: If the brand's measurement layer, creative tier, account structure, channel sequencing and team are checked against its actual revenue and spend stage every quarter, then gaps are caught before the next stage boundary, not after.

signal.check: No quarterly review exists comparing the brand's measurement, creative, structure and team against its stage requirements.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a governance process

risk.note: A quarterly review process.

prerequisites: Trailing 12-month revenue and current monthly spend
steps: Place the brand in its revenue and spend band.
Check measurement layer, creative and production tier, account structure and channel sequencing against the stage requirements.
Check team: founder still running ads, finance capability, decision-loop size, opex sized for a past peak.
Output a priority list of gaps to close before the next stage boundary.

test.method: Run the review every quarter and track gap closure.

title: Run a next-best-dollar channel mix review with inflators stripped before reallocating
hypothesis: If every channel's read is stripped of view-through, existing-customer and halo inflation before ranking, then the next dollar goes to the channel with real headroom instead of the channel whose number was inflated the most.

signal.check: Channel budget decisions rank channels by raw attributed ROAS without stripping view-through, existing-customer or halo inflation first.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a review procedure

risk.note: A review procedure; each reallocation carries its own confirmation window.

prerequisites: Spend and new-customer revenue by channel
steps: Compute AMER and, where available, incremental AMER per channel.
Strip view-through, existing-customer conversions and any halo event from each channel's read.
Check for overlap between channel pairs before scaling either.
Rank by incremental AMER relative to break-even and allocate the next dollar to the channel furthest below its frontier.

test.method: Run this review before any quarterly budget reallocation.
test.measure: other:amer by channel after stripping inflators

title: Write a full peak-season plan at least 70 days before the sale
hypothesis: If the full peak plan (objective, corrections, budget, creative volume, offer ladder, pacing, operations checklist) is written at least 70 days before the sale, then production, inventory and paperwork all have enough lead time to be ready.
does_not_apply_when: A flat-demand subscription store with no meaningful Q4-weighted sales calendar

signal.check: The peak season is under 70 days away and no written plan covering objective, budget, creative volume, offer ladder and operations exists yet.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a planning-deadline rule

risk.note: Missing this deadline compresses production, inventory and paperwork lead time.

prerequisites: Prior-year peak data
steps: Set a hard planning deadline at least 70 days before the sale.
