Write the objective, the 3 corrections, base and stretch budgets, creative volume plan and offer ladder by that date.
Confirm the operations checklist (3PL/4PL paperwork, inventory buffer, support capacity) by the same date.
Circulate the written plan to every team involved before production starts.

test.method: Check plan completeness against the 70-day deadline each year.
test.measure: days before the sale the plan was completed
test.read_point: At the planning deadline each year

title: Run a structured brand teardown intake before acting on any competitor pattern
hypothesis: If a teardown always runs through context and finances, awareness classification, format mapping, destination audit, offer audit, consistency audit and a transferable-vs-not list in that order, then no step gets skipped and no competitor copy gets reproduced.

signal.check: A competitor teardown is being used to justify a change without having run the full structured intake procedure.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a procedure completeness rule

risk.note: A read-only procedure; never reproduce competitor copy, products, faces or page text.

prerequisites: A scrape of the competitor's public ad library and pages
steps: Complete the context and finances read, applying the P&L skepticism check.
Complete the awareness-stage tag and creating-vs-harvesting verdict.
Complete the format map, script scoring, destination audit and offer audit.
Complete the consistency audit and the transferable-vs-not list.
Route each transferable pattern to its owner folder as a hypothesis to test on the brand's own traffic.

test.method: Check the teardown report against all 6 steps before it is used.
test.read_point: Before the teardown report is finalized

title: Write a capital and ownership memo with a downside case for every option before any founder decision
hypothesis: If every founder capital decision (raise, sell, partner, hire a CEO, take debt) goes through a written memo listing options in order of dilution with a downside case for each, then no option gets chosen without its risk being stated first.

signal.check: A major capital or ownership decision is being made without a written memo listing options in order of dilution and a downside case for each.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a decision-documentation procedure

risk.note: The memo recommends; the founder decides, and legal, tax and deal advice is required before signing.

prerequisites: Cap table, current debt terms, personal and company objectives, exit intent
steps: State the decision and the objective it serves.
List options in order of dilution and cost, cheapest first.
For any debt or equity option, model the leverage multiple and the downturn case.
State the downside case for every option, including doing nothing.
End with the legal, tax and deal advice line before anything is signed.

test.method: Not a live metric test; a documentation completeness check.
test.measure: presence of a downside case for every listed option

title: Run the death-spiral response protocol the moment CAC and volume diverge
hypothesis: If the death-spiral response (freeze spend, confirm the read, split the P&L, decompose CAC, work the ratio not the funding, check opex, route dead stock) runs as soon as the pattern is confirmed, then the spiral is interrupted before CAC roughly doubles.

signal.check: CAC is rising with falling new-customer volume and revenue, or LTGP:CAC is below 1, and no structured response has started.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a response protocol, not a stated recovery size

risk.note: Freezing spend increases can feel uncomfortable but is the first step; do not raise budget to hold revenue during this response.

prerequisites: Confirmed death-spiral pattern from the CAC/LTGP series check
steps: Freeze spend increases immediately; do not raise budget to hold revenue.
Confirm the read is real by stripping view-through and existing-customer conversions.
Run the 2-P&L split and document any funding route with a limit.
Decompose CAC into CPC and conversion rate, and CPC into CTR and CPM, to find the weak surface.
Work the ratio (offer, margin, or CAC), not just the funding source.
Check opex creep separately and set a 60 to 180 day confirmation window.

test.method: Run this protocol as soon as the death-spiral pattern is confirmed.
test.measure: cpa and new-customer volume trend after each step
test.read_point: Weekly during the response, with a 60 to 180 day full confirmation window

title: Recompute the existing-customer ad budget in dollars, not as a percent of spend
hypothesis: If the existing-customer ad budget is computed as customers times target frequency times CPM in dollars, then it does not silently grow or shrink just because total ad spend changed.

signal.check: Existing-customer ad spend is set as a fixed percent of total budget rather than computed from customer count, target frequency and CPM.

expected_effect.size: one source frames the calculation as customers x target frequency x CPM, with frequency under about 7 to 8 as the target range

risk.note: A budgeting-method change.

prerequisites: Existing-customer count and target frequency
steps: Get the existing-customer count eligible for retargeting.
Set a target frequency (recommendation under about 7 to 8 over a defined window).
Compute the dollar budget as customers x target frequency x CPM.
Replace any percent-of-spend rule for this budget with the computed dollar figure.

test.method: Compare actual existing-customer spend to the computed figure monthly.

title: Forecast new-customer revenue from a regression of daily spend, with its own error band
hypothesis: If new-customer revenue is forecast from a regression of daily AMER on daily spend over roughly a year, with peak outliers removed and an honest error band, then the forecast is not treated as more precise than it really is.

signal.check: New-customer revenue forecasts are quoted as a single number with no error band and no regression method behind them.

expected_effect.size: unknown; treat any forecast's stated accuracy claim skeptically rather than assuming it

risk.note: A forecasting-method improvement.

prerequisites: About a year of daily spend and AMER data
steps: Pull about a year of daily spend and AMER data.
Remove peak outliers and sub-floor days from the regression input.
Regress daily AMER on daily spend to forecast new-customer revenue.
Report the forecast with its own error band, not a borrowed accuracy claim from another source.

test.method: Compare forecast to actual new-customer revenue monthly.

title: Size a new-concept test budget at 3 to 5 times target CPA and read at about 1 week
hypothesis: If a new creative concept test is budgeted at about 3 to 5 times the target CPA and read at roughly 1 week (longer for a smaller, slower account), then a concept is not killed or kept on too little data.

signal.check: A new concept test is being judged on a budget under about 3 times target CPA or before the test window has run its course.

expected_effect.size: reference: 0 to 1 conversions at 3x CPA cuts, 2 extends, 3 to 4+ keeps; test window about 1 week, or 3 to 4 days for a large fast account and 10 to 14 days for a small slow one

risk.note: A test-sizing rule.

prerequisites: A defined target CPA
steps: Set the new-concept test budget at 3 to 5 times the target CPA.
Set the read window at about 1 week, adjusted for account size and speed.
Apply the conversion-count decision rule (cut, extend or keep) at the read point.
Do not judge a concept before its budget and window are both reached.

test.method: Run each new concept to the full sized budget and window before judging.
test.read_point: At the end of the sized test window

title: Do not treat a Meta scaling campaign as worth its own structure below about $400 a day
hypothesis: If a dedicated scaling campaign is only stood up once plateaued spend reaches about $400 a day, then account complexity is not added before there is enough spend to justify it.

signal.check: A dedicated scaling campaign structure exists for a plateaued ad set spending well under about $400 a day.

expected_effect.size: one agency cites a scaling campaign as worth it from about $400 a day plateaued spend, not at about $60

risk.note: A structural simplification rule.

steps: Check plateaued daily spend on any campaign being considered for a dedicated scaling structure.
Keep it inside the existing testing structure below about $400 a day.
Only split it into its own scaling campaign once it plateaus above that level.
Consolidate back down if spend later falls below the threshold.

test.method: Track plateaued spend before splitting into a scaling structure.
test.measure: plateaued daily spend vs the $400 threshold

title: Add a brand spend line once performance spend shows diminishing returns past $30 to 40k a day
hypothesis: If a brand-spend line (measured differently from direct-response spend) is added once performance spend shows diminishing returns past roughly $30 to 40k a day, then spend keeps growing through a channel that does not need to hit a direct ROI bar.

signal.check: Performance spend is showing diminishing returns above roughly $30 to 40k a day and no brand-spend line exists yet.

expected_effect.size: diminishing returns on brute-force performance are cited as appearing past about $30 to 40k a day

risk.note: Brand spend where ROI is unmeasurable requires founder buy-in that it will not be judged on the same bar as performance spend.

prerequisites: Confirmed diminishing returns on current performance spend
steps: Confirm performance spend is genuinely showing diminishing returns near this range, not just a temporary dip.
Set aside a brand-spend line with its own budget, separate from the performance budget.
Agree with the founder that this line is judged differently, not on direct ROI.
Size the brand line initially small and grow it as liquidity allows.

test.method: Track total addressable spend and blended CAC after adding the brand line.
test.measure: total spend absorbed and blended cpa
test.read_point: One quarter after the brand line launches

title: Cap subscription churn target under 5% and expect peaks at day 1, about 28, and 31 to 45
lever: subscription churn target and peak mapping
hypothesis: If a subscription program sets a target churn under 5% and maps expected cancellation peaks at day 1, about day 28 and days 31 to 45, then retention effort targets the actual peak cancellation windows instead of a flat monthly campaign.

signal.check: A subscription program has no churn target under 5% and no cancellation-day mapping showing where churn actually peaks.

expected_effect.size: one brand moved churn from 24% to 17% toward a goal under 5%, with peaks at day 1, about 28, and 31 to 45

risk.note: A targeting and mapping exercise.

prerequisites: Subscription cancellation data by day
steps: Map cancellation rate by day since subscription start.
Identify the brand's own peak cancellation days, expecting clusters near day 1, about 28, and 31 to 45.
Build a retention intervention (a check-in, a value reminder, an offer) timed to just before each peak.
Set a churn target under 5% and track progress toward it.

test.method: Track churn rate and cancellation-day distribution monthly.

title: Check the marketing-to-revenue ratio against the brand's stage band before trusting a stage placement
hypothesis: If the marketing-to-revenue ratio (typically 8 to 20% of revenue, up to 50% in high-margin periods) is checked against the revenue-based stage placement, then a mismatch (spend band far ahead of or behind the revenue band) is caught before applying the wrong stage's plan.

signal.check: A stage plan has been applied based on revenue alone without checking whether the marketing-to-revenue ratio matches the expected range for that stage.

expected_effect.size: marketing-to-revenue ratio cited at 8 to 20% typically, up to 50% in high-margin periods

risk.note: A cross-check on stage placement.

prerequisites: Trailing 12-month revenue and current monthly marketing spend
steps: Compute marketing spend as a percent of trailing revenue.
Compare it to the 8 to 20% typical range for the stage.
If it is far outside that range, investigate why before trusting the revenue-based stage placement.
Recalibrate the stage plan to the brand's own ratio rather than the generic band.

test.method: Recompute the ratio at each stage review.
test.measure: marketing spend as percent of revenue

title: Recheck welcome-discount depth against the 10-to-20-percent no-extra-gain-at-30 finding
hypothesis: If welcome-discount depth is periodically rechecked against the finding that 10 to 20% converts well with no added gain at 30%, then the brand does not keep deepening a discount past the point where it stops helping and starts hurting margin.

signal.check: The welcome discount is at or above 30% and has not been tested against a shallower depth in the last year.

expected_effect.size: one brand found a 10 to 20% welcome discount converted well with no added gain at 30%

risk.note: A recurring test, not a one-time change.

steps: Check the current welcome discount depth.
If it is 30% or deeper, test a 10 to 20% version against it.
Compare conversion rate and true gross margin between the two depths.
Adopt the shallower depth if conversion holds, to protect margin.

test.method: A/B test the current discount depth against a 10 to 20% version.
test.read_point: After enough new-customer volume for a stable read

title: Check that first-order contribution margin has not drifted negative as CPMs rise
hypothesis: If first-order contribution margin is tracked over time rather than assumed stable, then a slow drift from positive to negative as CPMs rise is caught before it compounds into a structural loss on every new customer.

signal.check: First-order contribution margin has not been recalculated in the last year despite known CPM increases.

expected_effect.size: one unsourced industry report cited first-order contribution margin moving from about plus $9 to about minus $29 over roughly a decade

risk.note: A recurring calculation check.

prerequisites: True gross margin and CAC by month
steps: Compute first-order contribution margin (first-order gross profit minus CAC) monthly.
Track the trend over the last 12 to 24 months.
If it is drifting toward zero or negative, treat it as an early warning alongside the death-spiral check.
Address it through the same levers as the death-spiral response: offer, margin or CAC.

test.method: Track first-order contribution margin monthly.

title: Treat a reported multi-touch or first-click tool's brand-search credit with suspicion
lever: multi-touch tool skepticism for brand search
hypothesis: If a first-click or multi-touch attribution tool's recommendation to redirect budget into brand search is checked against a holdout before acting, then budget is not moved into a channel that tool is structurally biased to favor.

signal.check: A multi-touch or first-click attribution tool is recommending more brand-search budget with no holdout confirming the recommendation.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a tool-bias caution

risk.note: A verification step before acting on tool output.

steps: Note when an attribution tool recommends more brand-search or first-touch-heavy spend.
Run or recall the brand's own branded-search holdout result before acting.
If no holdout exists, treat the tool's recommendation as unverified, not a fact.
Prefer the reliability-ladder tier match (A24) over a single tool's output.

test.method: Compare the tool's recommendation against the holdout result.
test.measure: gap between tool-recommended and holdout-confirmed incremental value
test.read_point: Whenever a brand-search budget change is proposed

title: Check existing-customer spend concentration when ROAS is healthy but topline is flat
hypothesis: If a healthy blended ROAS next to flat topline is checked for existing-customer or unconverted-follower spend concentration first, then the account is not scaled further on a ROAS that will dry up once that pool is exhausted.

signal.check: Blended ROAS looks healthy but total revenue is flat, and existing-customer ad frequency has not been checked.

expected_effect.size: audits found existing-customer frequency of 20 to 100 exposures a month in some accounts, with about 10 as a rough gut-check ceiling

risk.note: A diagnostic check; treat a frequency cut as a hypothesis to confirm with a lift test.

prerequisites: Frequency and spend by audience segment
steps: Check existing-customer ad frequency over the trailing 30 days.
Check the share of spend and of 'cold' conversions that are actually existing customers or an unconverted organic following.
If concentration is high, treat it as the likely reason ROAS looks healthy while topline is flat.
Confirm with a lift test before cutting existing-customer spend, since the cut itself is a hypothesis.

test.method: Run a lift test on existing-customer spend before cutting it.
test.read_point: After the lift test completes, typically 2 to 4 weeks

title: Time international and mass-retail entry to operational fit, not just demand
hypothesis: If international and mass-retail entry are timed to operational triggers (revenue scale, localized site and creative ready, inventory buffer for POs) rather than demand alone, then a 'flip the switch' expansion does not break checkout, fulfillment or a retail relationship.
does_not_apply_when: A brand still well below the roughly $10M+ stage where this expansion decision is not yet live

signal.check: An international market or mass-retail entry is being planned without a localized site, localized creative, or an inventory buffer for the first purchase order.

expected_effect.size: one brand's international expansion broke its cross-border integration after launching without localization first

risk.note: A broken international launch or a missed retail PO can damage the relationship for years.

prerequisites: Localized site and creative
Inventory buffer sized for the first PO
steps: Confirm the revenue and operational scale that typically supports this market or retail channel.
Localize the site, checkout and creative before any spend goes into the new market.
Prove sell-through digitally or with one retail chain before adding more doors or markets.
Size an inventory buffer for the first purchase order so a missed PO does not end the relationship.

test.method: Run the new market or retailer as a bounded pilot before a full rollout.
test.read_point: Before the pilot launches, then reviewed after it

title: Prove sell-through with one retail chain before adding more doors
hypothesis: If sell-through is proven with one national retail chain before pitching more doors, then the brand has real evidence and inventory discipline before expanding retail exposure.
does_not_apply_when: A DTC-only brand with no retail ambitions

signal.check: A retail pitch to multiple chains is planned before sell-through has been proven with a single chain.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a sequencing rule from founder self-reports on retail entry

risk.note: A missed retailer PO or overproduction miss can lose the account for good.

prerequisites: Digital sell-through and brand recognition evidence
steps: Build digital sell-through and brand recognition evidence first.
Pitch and prove with one national or regional chain before adding more.
Overproduce carefully around the first major PO to avoid a stockout at the retailer.
Expect buyer turnover roughly every 2 years at large retailers and plan the relationship accordingly.

test.method: Track sell-through rate at the first chain before pitching a second.
test.measure: inventory_turns and sell-through at the first retailer
test.read_point: After the first full retail season

title: Treat TikTok Shop and creator-commission arbitrage as a fast-shifting, impulse-price-fit channel
hypothesis: If TikTok Shop and creator-commission programs are run as a separate track fit to impulse pricing and re-checked monthly for changing economics, then the brand catches the arbitrage while it lasts instead of over-committing to a channel that shifts fast.
does_not_apply_when: A high-AOV or considered-purchase brand where this channel's impulse-price fit does not apply

signal.check: TikTok Shop or creator-commission spend is treated as a stable, permanent channel with no monthly economics recheck.

expected_effect.size: one brand's TikTok Shop win correlated with about a 30% lift on Amazon, Target and Walmart

risk.note: Economics here are described as shifting monthly; verify current policies and payouts before scaling.

steps: Run TikTok Shop affiliate as a separate track from the general organic creator program.
Fit the price point to impulse buying, generally under about $29 to 39.
Recheck current TikTok Shop affiliate economics and policies monthly, since they shift often.
Watch for spillover lift on other retail and marketplace channels as a secondary signal, not the main justification.

test.method: Track TikTok Shop revenue and spillover lift on other channels monthly.

title: Audit revenue and creator concentration by channel and diversify before a crisis forces it
hypothesis: If revenue share by channel, retailer and creator is audited continuously and diversified deliberately, then losing one channel does not threaten the business the way it did for a brand caught with most of its revenue in one place.

signal.check: No recent audit exists of revenue share by channel, top retailer or top creator, and one of these holds a large majority of revenue.

expected_effect.size: one brand came within about a week of a 50% layoff after losing its largest channel

risk.note: Diversifying deliberately before a crisis is far cheaper than being forced into it afterward.

prerequisites: Revenue tagged by channel, retailer and creator
steps: Compute revenue share by channel, top retailer and top creator.
Set a threshold the brand is comfortable with and flag any share above it.
Build a deliberate diversification plan (new channel, new retailer, broader creator base) for any flagged concentration.
Repeat the audit quarterly, not just after a scare.

test.method: Track concentration share over time as diversification efforts run.

title: Audit a competitor's offer and price discipline: median price, entry price, and ad vs off-ad language
hypothesis: If a teardown checks median price, whether the entry price is advertised, discount and risk-reversal language in ads vs off-ad, and the tier ladder and default selection, then real offer patterns are found instead of assuming the competitor's ads represent their whole pricing strategy.

signal.check: A teardown discusses a competitor's pricing without checking median price, entry price visibility, or ad vs off-ad discount language separately.

expected_effect.size: one competitor showed 0% of ads mentioning price or discount while running a 10% off-ad email capture and other risk-reversal off-ad

risk.note: A read-only audit.

prerequisites: A scrape of the competitor's ad library and site pricing pages
steps: Record the competitor's median price and whether the cheapest entry price is ever advertised.
Compare discount and risk-reversal language used in ads vs off-ad (email, checkout).
Map the tier ladder and which tier is the default selection.
Note any monthly-equivalent price display for a longer commitment and flag it for a compliance check before considering it.

test.method: Complete the offer and price audit before the teardown report.
test.measure: documented price and discount pattern by surface
test.read_point: Before the teardown report is finalized

title: Route around Meta's per-Page ad cap with regional or whitelisted Pages
hypothesis: If duplicate, regional or whitelisted Pages carry the overflow once a Page nears Meta's active-ad cap, then a high-volume account keeps testing new concepts instead of being forced to pause or delete live ads to make room.

signal.check: Active ad count on the brand Page is approaching Meta's stated per-Page cap (roughly 300 to 500 active ads) and ads are being paused only to free up room for new tests.

expected_effect.size: unknown; removes a volume ceiling rather than lifting a rate

risk.note: A cosmetic Page-management change; verify current Meta Page-cap mechanics before relying on it, since UI and limits change.

prerequisites: A brand Page already near the active-ad cap
Enough creative volume that the cap is the binding constraint, not creative supply
steps: Confirm the account is actually hitting the active-ad cap, not just running many ads
Stand up a second brand-styled Page (duplicate) or a country-specific Page for a region already segmented by country
Route new tests to the new Page instead of pausing live ads on the original
Check whether a self-created third-party-styled Page (whitelisting) fits the brand's compliance posture before using it
Re-verify the current cap and Page rules in Meta's own documentation before scaling this pattern

test.method: Track active ad count per Page against the cap before and after adding the new Page.
test.measure: count of ads paused solely to free up cap room
test.read_point: Monthly, or whenever a Page approaches the cap

title: Run a retrospective causal-impact model when no advance geo-lift exists
hypothesis: If a retrospective counterfactual model estimates what revenue would have done without a channel or spend change, then a brand that never ran a forward geo-lift test can still get a directional incrementality read instead of relying on raw attribution.

signal.check: A channel or spend change already happened with no advance holdout, and the only available read is attributed ROAS.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a directional read, not a controlled experiment

risk.note: A modeling exercise on historical data; does not touch live spend, but a wrong model input can mislead a real decision if treated as certain.

prerequisites: Daily revenue and spend history covering a period before and after the change
Someone able to run a counterfactual time-series model
steps: Pick a channel or spend change with a clear before and after date
Build or run a counterfactual time-series model on the pre-change period to project what would have happened without the change
Compare actual post-change revenue to the model's projection
Treat the gap as a directional incrementality estimate, not a proven causal result
Flag the read as unverified until a real forward holdout can confirm it

test.method: Compare a counterfactual model's projection against actual results for at least one past channel change.
test.measure: modeled incremental revenue vs attributed revenue for that change
test.read_point: Once per major retrospective read; before repeating the same spend decision

title: Set bid and cost caps at the ad-set level, never the individual ad
hypothesis: If cost caps, bid caps and other bidding controls are only ever set at the ad-set level, then the account's optimization signal is not fragmented by conflicting ad-level settings that Meta's system does not fully honor.

signal.check: Any cost cap, bid cap or manual bid setting exists at the individual ad level rather than the ad set.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a structural correction, not a rate lift

risk.note: A settings change inside the ads manager; fully reversible.

prerequisites: Access to the ad account's bidding settings
steps: Audit every active ad set for any bidding control set at the ad level
Move any cost cap, bid cap or manual bid to the ad-set level
Confirm the ad-set-level setting is inherited correctly by every ad inside it
Document the change so future team members set new controls at the correct level

test.method: Audit bidding settings once, then check on any new campaign launch.
test.measure: count of ad-level bidding controls found and corrected
test.read_point: At account structure review, and on every new campaign build

title: Verify true incremental headroom before chasing a high-blended-ROAS placement
hypothesis: If a placement or segment with a high blended ROAS is checked for real incremental headroom before a dedicated campaign is built for it, then spend does not chase a number that Meta's own system has already tried to capture and is not finding more of.

signal.check: A team is about to build a new dedicated campaign or ad set based on a breakdown report showing one placement, age band or region far outperforming the account average.

expected_effect.size: unknown; prevents a wasted structural change

risk.note: A verification step before a change, not a change itself.

prerequisites: Access to the platform's breakdown report and enough spend history to test incrementality
steps: Pull the breakdown report and note the outperforming segment
Check whether the account has already tried pushing more spend into that segment and what happened
If no test exists, run a small, time-boxed spend increase into that segment alone and read the result before building permanent structure around it
Only stand up a dedicated campaign if the small test shows real incremental lift, not just a repeat of the same blended number

test.method: Run a small spend increase into the outperforming segment before committing structure to it.
test.measure: incremental revenue from the test spend increase vs the segment's blended ROAS
test.read_point: Before any new campaign is built off a breakdown report

title: Run the 5-question diagnostic before restructuring any ad account
hypothesis: If product-category count, margin spread, non-overlapping persona count, region count and creative throughput are answered before touching account structure, then the resulting structure matches the business instead of copying a template built for a different brand.

signal.check: An account restructure, consolidation or segmentation change is being considered without first answering the five diagnostic questions.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a decision-quality precondition, not a metric lift

risk.note: A planning exercise before any live change; the actual restructure carries its own separate risk.

prerequisites: Basic knowledge of product categories, margin by category, persona count, regions sold into and current creative output
steps: Count distinct product categories and their margin spread
Count genuinely non-overlapping personas, not just demographic slices
Count regions or countries actively sold into
Estimate current creative throughput per month
Only then decide whether consolidation or segmentation fits, instead of defaulting to a template

test.method: Answer the five questions in writing before any restructure and compare the resulting plan to the prior default template.
test.measure: whether the five answers changed the planned structure

title: Skip a dedicated website-visitor retargeting campaign for most accounts
hypothesis: If a dedicated website-visitor retargeting campaign is skipped by default and the audience-segment breakdown is checked instead, then most accounts avoid adding structure that the existing testing and scaling campaigns already cover.

signal.check: The account is considering or running a standalone website-visitor retargeting campaign without having checked the audience-segment breakdown first.

expected_effect.size: unknown; removes unneeded structure for the stated majority of accounts

risk.note: A structural simplification; reversible by re-adding the campaign if the breakdown later shows a real gap.

prerequisites: Access to the platform's audience-segment breakdown report
steps: Pull the audience-segment breakdown (new, engaged, existing) on current campaigns
Check whether warm and engaged visitors are already being served meaningfully by the existing testing and scaling structure
If coverage looks adequate, do not stand up a dedicated retargeting campaign
Keep a small, frequency-capped existing-customer campaign separate, sized to the brand's own repeat-purchase profile

test.method: Compare account performance with and without a dedicated website-visitor retargeting campaign on a subset of spend.
test.measure: incremental revenue from the dedicated campaign vs its spend
test.read_point: Before adding a website-visitor retargeting campaign, and quarterly if one already exists

title: Never add creative to a winning ad set; launch new tests in a fresh set
hypothesis: If a currently winning ad set is left untouched and new creative for that same concept is launched in a separate new ad set, then the winning set's learning phase and delivery are not disrupted by an unrelated new-ad reset.

signal.check: A team is about to add a new ad into an ad set that is already hitting its KPI.

expected_effect.size: unknown; avoids a self-inflicted performance dip

risk.note: A workflow rule, not a spend change; fully reversible.

prerequisites: A defined KPI per ad set so 'winning' is unambiguous
steps: Check whether the target ad set is currently hitting its KPI
If yes, do not add, remove or edit ads inside it
Duplicate the concept or launch the new creative variant in a new ad set instead
Reserve free editing of ads for ad sets that are already underperforming, where there is no working sequence to protect

test.method: Track post-edit performance of ad sets that were hitting KPI before and after this rule is enforced.
test.measure: rate of performance dips following an in-set creative addition
test.read_point: Ongoing, at every creative launch decision

title: Avoid multi-creative-per-ad formats to keep per-creative attribution
hypothesis: If ads are built one creative per ad rather than bundled into a single multi-asset ad unit, then the team can still tell which specific creative is driving results and keep iterating on it.

signal.check: The ad account is using or considering a feature that lets multiple creative assets rotate inside one ad unit.

expected_effect.size: unknown; preserves the ability to iterate rather than lifting a rate

risk.note: A format choice; reversible, though it may mean fewer active ad slots against the per-Page cap.

prerequisites: Access to ad creation settings
steps: Identify any ads currently using a bundled multi-creative format
Estimate how much of current spend or results comes from those ads
Rebuild the strongest performers as single-creative ads where attribution matters most
Reserve the bundled format only for cases where the per-Page ad cap forces it and attribution loss is accepted

test.method: Compare iteration speed and win-rate on single-creative ads versus bundled ads over a testing period.
test.measure: concepts iterated per month, by ad format

title: Score every cross-sell and upsell on the combined take-rate, lift and margin formula
hypothesis: If every cross-sell or upsell candidate is scored on take rate percent times AOV lift times gross margin percent as one combined number, then a lower-margin but better-fit, higher-take-rate add-on is not passed over for a higher-margin one that few customers actually buy.

signal.check: Upsells or cross-sells are picked or ranked using only one input (margin, take rate, or AOV lift) rather than the combined formula.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a selection method, not a guaranteed lift

risk.note: A scoring and ranking exercise; no live change until a new offer is actually placed.

prerequisites: Take rate, AOV lift and gross margin data for each current or candidate add-on
steps: List every current and candidate cross-sell or upsell
Record take rate percent, AOV lift and gross margin percent for each
Multiply the three into one combined incremental-contribution-profit score
Re-rank all offers by that combined score, not by any single input
Swap the top offer into the highest-visibility slot and re-measure after a fixed window

test.method: Compare incremental contribution profit before and after re-ranking offers by the combined formula.
test.measure: incremental contribution profit per offer slot
test.read_point: One full sales cycle after re-ranking

title: Match upsell placement and complexity to the customer's funnel friction
hypothesis: If in-cart offers stay simple and high-margin, checkout offers stay low-friction and non-product, and post-purchase offers anchor high before downselling, then each offer matches how much friction the customer will tolerate at that exact step.

signal.check: Upsell offers are placed and worded the same way regardless of whether the customer is in-cart, at checkout, or post-purchase.

expected_effect.size: unknown; benchmark ranges cited by the source, not measured on a real brand

risk.note: A merchandising and copy change on existing funnel steps; reversible.

prerequisites: Ability to edit cart, checkout and post-purchase offer placements
steps: Audit current offers at each of the three funnel steps
In-cart: keep one simple, high-margin offer per slot
Checkout: use only low-friction, non-product add-ons, kept simple
Post-purchase: lead with the highest-value offer first, then downsell if declined
Track take rate and revenue-per-visit separately for each step after the change

test.method: Compare take rate and revenue-per-visit at each funnel step before and after matching placement to friction.
test.measure: take rate and RPV per funnel step
test.read_point: One month after the placement change

title: Track post-purchase upsell revenue-per-visit against a 10 to 15 percent benchmark
hypothesis: If post-purchase revenue divided by post-purchase funnel visits is tracked against a 10 to 15 percent benchmark, then a post-purchase upsell program has a concrete target instead of being judged only by whether it exists.

signal.check: A post-purchase upsell page or flow exists with no tracked revenue-per-visit metric, or RPV is well under 10 percent.

expected_effect.size: 10 to 15 percent of AOV, per the source's own benchmark

risk.note: A measurement and offer-tuning exercise on an existing flow.

prerequisites: A post-purchase upsell page or flow already in place, with visit and revenue tracking
steps: Instrument post-purchase page visits and post-purchase revenue separately
Calculate RPV as post-purchase revenue divided by post-purchase visits
Compare against the 10 to 15 percent benchmark
If below benchmark, test a higher-value anchor offer or a better-matched add-on before adding more offers

test.method: Track RPV monthly against the benchmark.

title: Segment exit-intent offers by the exact stage the customer is exiting from
hypothesis: If browsing exits get a generous return incentive, cart-abandon exits get a small nudge, and checkout-abandon exits get risk reversal instead of a discount, then exit-intent spend is not wasted discounting a customer who was already about to buy.

signal.check: The same exit-intent offer, usually a flat discount, is shown regardless of whether the visitor is browsing, has items in cart, or is at checkout.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a segmentation change, not a guaranteed lift

risk.note: A pop-up and offer logic change; fully reversible.

prerequisites: Exit-intent tooling that can detect funnel stage (browse, cart, checkout)
steps: Split exit-intent triggers into three stages: browse, cart-abandon, checkout-abandon
Show a generous, low-commitment incentive on browse exits
Show a small nudge, not a deep discount, on cart-abandon exits
Show risk reversal such as free shipping, not a discount, on checkout-abandon exits
Measure conversion and margin impact separately per stage

test.method: Compare conversion rate and discount cost per stage before and after the segmented offers.
test.measure: cvr_checkout_to_order and discount cost per exit stage

title: Sell the gift-with-purchase item at its own retail price to frame it as added value
hypothesis: If the gift item in a gift-with-purchase offer is also sold at its own retail price on the site, then the offer can be framed as a stated dollar value added for the customer instead of a vague 'free gift' that looks cheap or invented.

signal.check: A gift-with-purchase offer names the gift as 'free' with no stated retail value, or the gift is not sold anywhere on the site.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a framing change, not a guaranteed lift

risk.note: The gift item must have a genuine, checkable retail price somewhere on the site or it becomes an invented-value claim.

prerequisites: A gift item that is genuinely sold at its own price, or can be
steps: List the gift item at its own retail price somewhere on the site
Reframe the offer copy from 'free gift' to a stated value, such as '$X value included'
Confirm the gift is genuinely low-cost and well-matched to the customer, not chosen for margin convenience
Track take rate and contribution margin on the reframed offer

test.method: Compare take rate on the offer before and after adding the stated retail-value framing.
test.read_point: One test cycle after the copy change

title: Use waterfall pricing to price a new product and kill it if the price is not viable
hypothesis: If a new product's price is built upward from target net-profit percent through opex, CAC, allowance, shipping and COGS, then a product that cannot clear its numbers at a competitive price is killed before launch instead of underpriced into a loss.

signal.check: A new product's price is set from cost-plus markup (keystone or a fixed multiple) rather than a waterfall build from a target net-profit percent.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a pricing method, not a measured lift

risk.note: A pricing exercise before launch; does not touch a live product unless repricing an existing one.

prerequisites: Estimated COGS, shipping and fulfillment cost, expected CAC, and a target net-profit percent
steps: Set a target net-profit percent for the product
Add back fixed opex percent to get a required contribution-margin percent
Add estimated CAC, a return or discount allowance, shipping cost, and COGS to solve upward for the required price
Benchmark the required price against direct competitors
If the price is far above competitors, either reposition into a niche that can sustain it or kill the product before launch

test.method: Run the waterfall build on the next new-product pricing decision and compare to the price that keystone or a fixed markup would have produced.
test.measure: gap between waterfall price and cost-plus price, and resulting contribution margin

title: Use product repositioning as a zero-cost offer before adding any discount
hypothesis: If the same SKU is repositioned under a new persona and angle before any discount is considered, then a hero-SKU or single-SKU brand gets a genuinely new offer with no margin cost, and any later persona-specific discount has a real audience to attach to.

signal.check: A hero-SKU or single-SKU brand's only lever for a new offer is a discount, with no repositioning attempted first.

expected_effect.size: unknown; source's own examples are single-SKU supplement brands, not benchmarked broadly

risk.note: A creative and landing-page change; no product or pricing change, fully reversible.

prerequisites: A hero SKU with more than one plausible use case, benefit or buyer type
steps: Identify 2 to 3 distinct personas or use cases the current SKU could serve
Build a dedicated angle, headline and landing page for each persona without changing the product or price
Run real spend against each repositioned angle separately
Only add a persona-specific discount or partner offer once a repositioned angle proves it can convert its own audience

test.method: Compare conversion rate on repositioned angles against the original single angle.
test.read_point: One testing cycle per new angle

title: Run a second ad account with different bid logic once spend passes $250k a month
hypothesis: If a second ad account running the same pixel but a different bidding strategy is stood up once spend passes roughly $250k a month, then the brand can win auctions the first account is not entering and is not left exposed to a single account ban or billing failure.

signal.check: All Meta spend runs through a single ad account and monthly spend is near or above $250k, with no backup account in place.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a risk-reduction and reach tactic, time-sensitive per the source

risk.note: Platform behavior around multiple accounts on one pixel changes over time; verify current Meta policy before relying on this at scale.

prerequisites: Monthly Meta spend near or above $250k
A second verified ad account and business manager
steps: Set up a second ad account under the same business manager, sharing the same pixel
Set a different bidding strategy in the second account, such as cost caps instead of maximize-conversions
Run a small share of budget through the second account and compare incremental results
Treat the second account as a standing backup in case the primary account is banned or billing fails
Re-verify current Meta rules on multiple accounts sharing one pixel before scaling this pattern

test.method: Compare incremental auction wins and total reach across both accounts versus the single-account baseline.
test.measure: incremental spend absorbed by the second account without cannibalizing the first
test.read_point: One month after setup, then quarterly

title: Segment ad accounts by billing currency need, not by country
hypothesis: If a brand selling into several countries keeps one ad account per required billing currency and solves country-level reporting with filter rules, then international scaling does not multiply management labor with a separate ad account for every region.

signal.check: A brand is creating or considering a separate ad account for every country it sells into, rather than only where a distinct billing currency is required.

expected_effect.size: unknown; reduces management labor rather than lifting a performance metric

risk.note: A structural change; requires reporting filter rules to replace the visibility a separate account would have given.

prerequisites: Multiple countries or regions of sale
Ability to build filter-based reporting by country inside one ad account
steps: List every country currently or soon to be sold into
Identify which ones genuinely require a separate billing currency
Consolidate countries sharing a currency into one ad account
Build filter rules or saved reports to view performance by country inside the consolidated account

test.method: Compare management time and reporting clarity before and after consolidating by currency instead of by country.
test.measure: number of ad accounts maintained per region sold into
test.read_point: At the next international expansion decision

title: Name and structure every ad set by persona, angle, offer, format and date
hypothesis: If every ad set is named and built around one persona, one angle, one offer and one content type with a launch date, and never by batch or date alone, then wins and losses can be filtered and attributed to a real concept months later.

signal.check: Ad sets are named by batch or launch date alone (for example, 'March 7 creatives') rather than by the concept they test.

expected_effect.size: unknown; improves traceability rather than a rate

risk.note: A naming-convention and account-hygiene change; no spend impact on its own.

prerequisites: Access to rename existing and future ad sets
steps: Define a fixed naming template: persona, angle, offer, content type, launch date
Rename active ad sets going forward under the new convention
Require every new ad set to follow the template before launch
Use the naming fields to filter and compare concept performance later

test.method: Check whether concept-level performance can be filtered and compared six months after adopting the convention.
test.measure: share of ad sets following the naming convention

title: Consolidate retargeting audiences and track only frequency and incremental revenue
hypothesis: If retargeting audiences are consolidated instead of split by product, page or funnel step, and success is judged only on frequency and incremental revenue, then the CPM penalty of over-segmentation is not paid for a marginal conversion-rate gain that rarely justifies it.

signal.check: Retargeting is split into many small audiences by product, page or funnel step, each with its own CPM overhead.

expected_effect.size: unknown; consolidation trades segmentation precision for lower CPM

risk.note: A retargeting-structure change; reversible.

prerequisites: Current retargeting campaigns segmented by product, page or funnel step
steps: List every current retargeting audience and its CPM
Consolidate audiences that are not showing a meaningfully different conversion rate
Set frequency and incremental revenue as the only two KPIs for the consolidated retargeting layer
Re-check CPM and incremental revenue after consolidation

test.method: Compare CPM and incremental revenue before and after consolidating retargeting audiences.
test.measure: cpm and other:incremental_revenue for the retargeting layer

title: Measure DPA performance on incremental attribution, not last-click
hypothesis: If dynamic product ad performance is read on 7-day-click or incremental attribution instead of last-click, and top-of-funnel spend is not cut just because DPA looks strong, then the account does not starve the cold spend that DPA's own results actually depend on.

signal.check: Dynamic product ads (DPA) are reported and judged on default or last-click attribution, and top-of-funnel spend has been cut because DPA showed the best surface-level ROAS.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a measurement correction, not a spend lift

risk.note: A reporting-settings change; no spend change on its own.

prerequisites: Access to the platform's attribution settings and incremental attribution report
steps: Switch DPA reporting to 7-day-click or incremental attribution instead of the default view
Compare the incremental read to the default last-click ROAS
If incremental ROAS is much lower, treat DPA as a mirror of top-of-funnel health, not an independent win
Before cutting top-of-funnel spend, check whether DPA's own incremental ROAS would fall as a result

test.method: Track DPA incremental ROAS alongside top-of-funnel spend over time.

title: Smoke-test angles with a text-overlay image set before building video
hypothesis: If several value-prop angles are tested as a single product photo with only the text overlay changed, before any video is built, then the winning angle is identified for a fraction of the cost of producing multiple full videos.

signal.check: New angles are tested by producing full video creative for each one, with no cheap image-only smoke test to narrow angles first.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a testing-sequence change, not a measured lift

risk.note: A creative-testing workflow change; the winning angle still needs a video build afterward.

prerequisites: One consistent product photo
Several candidate value-prop angles to write as overlay text
steps: Pick one product photo on a plain background and keep it identical across every variant
Overlay a bold text call-out, changing only the message or angle between variants
Launch all variants together in one simple campaign
Read clicks and engagement per variant to identify the winning angle
Only build video for the winning angle, not for every candidate

test.method: Compare cost per validated angle using the image smoke test versus building full video for every candidate.

title: Organize the ad account by story or angle folder instead of funnel stage
hypothesis: If the ad account is organized into one folder per angle holding every image, video and landing-page variant for that story, rather than by prospecting versus retargeting funnel stage, then creative performance can be read and iterated by narrative instead of scattered across stage-based campaigns.

signal.check: The ad account is organized strictly by funnel stage (prospecting, retargeting), making it hard to see all assets belonging to one angle or story together.

expected_effect.size: unknown; an organizational practice tied to current broad-matching platform behavior, not a guaranteed lift

risk.note: Assumes the ad platform's current broad or creative-driven delivery makes strict funnel-stage segmentation less necessary; re-verify this platform assumption before relying on it.

prerequisites: An ad account and asset library that can be reorganized around narrative/angle folders
steps: Define a folder per distinct story or angle currently in market
File every image, video and matching landing-page variant for that angle into its folder
Use the folder structure to review and iterate performance by narrative
Re-verify current platform delivery behavior before assuming this structure fits every account

test.method: Track how quickly the team can find and iterate on all assets for a given angle before and after reorganizing.

title: Match creative cast, setting and language to the exact audience being bought
hypothesis: If an ad's cast, setting and language are matched to the specific audience being targeted, such as regionally-styled creative for a regional buy, then the ad reads as made for that viewer instead of a generic asset served everywhere.

signal.check: The same creative runs against multiple distinct audience segments (region, demographic) with no cast, setting or language variation matched to each.

expected_effect.size: unknown; one operator's reported observation, not a measured benchmark

risk.note: A creative-production and targeting-matching workflow; requires enough creative volume to build audience-specific variants.

prerequisites: Distinct, identifiable audience segments (region, demographic) worth targeting separately
steps: Identify a distinct audience segment currently served generic creative
Build a variant matching that segment's cast, setting or language specifically
Run the matched variant against the generic version to the same segment
Track hook_rate and ctr differences between matched and generic creative

test.method: A or B test audience-matched creative against generic creative for the same segment.
test.measure: hook_rate and ctr, matched vs generic

title: Build ads natively for each placement instead of one reused square asset
hypothesis: If ads are built natively for each placement's actual aspect ratio, with captions and focal point set for that specific frame, then nothing gets cut off or misread the way a single square asset reused everywhere tends to.

signal.check: The same square creative asset is reused across every placement without being reformatted for each placement's actual aspect ratio.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a production-quality fix, not a measured lift

risk.note: A production-workflow change; adds a small amount of editing time per ad.

prerequisites: The ability to export creative in multiple aspect ratios for current placement formats
steps: Identify the placements the ad is running in and their current aspect ratios
Rebuild caption placement and focal point for each specific ratio rather than reusing one square crop
Verify current placement names and ratios before finalizing, since they change
Track ctr on natively-sized placements versus the prior reused-square version

test.method: Compare ctr on native-ratio creative against the same ad run as a reused square asset.

title: Collapse the media-buying pod into one hybrid buyer-strategist role
hypothesis: If the media-buying function collapses from a multi-person pod into one P&L-aware media buyer and creative strategist, supported by a single designer or creator, then decisions move faster because one person owns both the spend and the creative direction driving it.

signal.check: Media buying runs through a multi-person pod (strategist, account manager, buyer, junior buyer, designer) with responsibility split across roles.

expected_effect.size: unknown; one operator's org design, sold by his own agency, weigh accordingly

risk.note: Requires a genuinely capable hybrid hire and existing creative-production support; not proven to work without that backing.

prerequisites: A capable candidate willing to own both spend and creative strategy
A designer or creator to support them
steps: Identify or hire one person capable of owning both media-buying and creative-strategy decisions
Support that person with a single designer or creator rather than a full pod
Give the hybrid role P&L visibility so creative and spend decisions are made together
Track decision speed and account performance under the collapsed structure versus the prior pod

test.method: Track decision latency and account performance before and after collapsing the pod.

title: Set a weekly creative target in concepts and track the real hit rate
hypothesis: If a weekly creative target is set in concepts, not just total ad units, and tracked by how many actually get real spend from the algorithm, then the team knows whether its creative supply is actually converting into live, spending ads, not just raw output volume.

signal.check: Creative output is tracked only as a raw ad count per week, with no tracked measure of how many concepts actually earn meaningful spend.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a cadence-tracking practice, not a measured lift

risk.note: A tracking and planning cadence; adjust the target for season and product-drop calendar.

prerequisites: A defined weekly concept and ad-unit target
The ability to check which ads actually receive algorithmic spend
steps: Set a weekly target in concepts (for example, 10 concepts, 2 ads each)
Adjust the target seasonally for known volume needs (Q4, product drops)
Each week, count new assets launched and how many actually received meaningful spend
Track the hit rate over time to judge whether creative quality or volume is the constraint

test.method: Track weekly concept hit rate over successive weeks.

title: Keep a 30-day creative runway and avoid flooding a thin account
hypothesis: If the account keeps roughly a 30-day runway of ready creative and avoids dumping many new untested ads into an account currently carried by only 2 to 3 proven winners, then the whole account's delivery does not destabilize from too much new, unproven volume at once.

signal.check: A thin account, running mostly on 2 to 3 proven ads, is about to receive a large batch of new, untested ads all at once.

expected_effect.size: unknown; an operator's own observed pattern, not a measured lift

risk.note: A launch-pacing rule; does not reduce total creative output, only paces how it enters the account.

prerequisites: Visibility into how much current spend concentrates on a small number of proven ads
steps: Check how concentrated current spend is on a small number of proven winners
If spend is thin (2 to 3 ads carrying most of it), stagger new ad launches instead of a single large batch
Maintain roughly a 30-day runway of ready-to-launch creative for pacing
Track account-level delivery stability during and after staggered launches versus a prior large-batch launch

test.method: Compare account delivery stability (spend volatility) during staggered launches versus large-batch launches.

title: Pull back paid spend ahead of a scheduled email drop or discount push
hypothesis: If paid spend is deliberately pulled back just ahead of a known email drop, product launch or discount push, then the brand does not pay for demand that its own owned channels were about to capture anyway.

signal.check: Paid spend runs at a flat or increasing pace right before a scheduled email drop, launch or discount push, with no coordinated pullback.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a calendar-coordination tactic, not a measured lift

risk.note: A spend-calendar coordination practice; requires marketing calendar visibility across paid and lifecycle teams.

prerequisites: A shared marketing calendar showing upcoming email drops, launches and discount pushes
steps: Build or check a shared calendar of upcoming email drops, launches and discount pushes
Plan a deliberate paid spend pullback in the days just before each event
Resume normal paid spend once the owned-channel push has run its course
Track total revenue and CAC around the coordinated pullback versus a flat-spend baseline period

test.method: Compare CAC and total revenue during a coordinated pullback period versus a comparable flat-spend period.
test.measure: cpa and total revenue around scheduled owned-channel events

title: Track daily discount rate alongside daily burn to catch hidden margin erosion
hypothesis: If daily discount-as-percent-of-sales is tracked alongside daily ad spend burn, then rising revenue that is actually being bought with a climbing discount rate is caught instead of being read as healthy growth.

signal.check: Daily revenue and ad spend are tracked, but daily discount rate as a percent of sales is not tracked alongside them.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a tracking addition, not a guaranteed margin improvement

risk.note: A reporting addition; no live change to pricing or spend on its own.

prerequisites: Daily order-level data including discount amount and ad spend
steps: Add daily discount-as-percent-of-sales as a tracked line alongside daily ad spend
Plot both together over time, not on separate dashboards
Flag any period where revenue rises while discount rate is also climbing
Investigate whether the revenue growth is actually outrunning the rising discount cost

test.method: Track periods where rising revenue coincided with a rising discount rate and whether margin held.

title: Set a spend threshold for running ads yourself versus hiring a manager
hypothesis: If a founder runs the ad account themselves up to a defined monthly spend threshold, and only then weighs a manager's fee against the test budget it would consume, then a small brand does not give up a meaningful share of an already-thin test budget to a fee before it needs to.

signal.check: A media-management retainer is hired at a spend level low enough that its fee consumes a meaningful share of the available test budget.

expected_effect.size: unknown; one operator's own rule of thumb, not a computed break-even

risk.note: A staffing decision; the exact threshold should be checked against the brand's own numbers, not copied blindly.

prerequisites: Current or planned monthly ad spend
A quoted management fee to compare against
steps: Calculate the management fee as a percent of the current or planned monthly ad spend
If spend is well under a meaningful threshold, default to running the account yourself or using a limited consult instead of a full retainer
Reassess once spend clears a level where the fee is a small share of total spend
Track how much of the test budget a management fee would have consumed at each stage

test.method: Track the management fee as a share of test budget at each spend level before deciding to hire.

title: Segment retention reporting by revenue per recipient and suppress discount-only cohorts
hypothesis: If retention email and SMS reporting is segmented by revenue-per-recipient within cohort (subscriber, repeat non-subscriber, one-time, non-buyer) and cohorts that only ever buy on discount are suppressed from full-price sends, then retention spend is not wasted repeatedly emailing a segment that will not pay full price anyway.

signal.check: Retention email and SMS reporting is blended across all customers with no cohort-level revenue-per-recipient view, and discount-dependent cohorts receive the same full-price messaging as everyone else.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a segmentation practice, not a measured lift

risk.note: A segmentation and reporting change; suppression should be reversible if a cohort's behavior changes.

prerequisites: Order-level and email/SMS send data segmentable by cohort
steps: Define at least four cohorts: subscriber, repeat non-subscriber, one-time buyer, non-buyer
Track revenue per recipient within each cohort separately
Identify cohorts that only ever purchase on a discount trigger
Suppress those cohorts from full-price sends and route them to a different, discount-aware track instead

test.method: Track revenue per recipient by cohort before and after suppressing discount-only cohorts from full-price sends.

title: Build cancellation-flow branches matched to your own top cancellation reasons
hypothesis: If the cancellation flow asks the customer their specific reason and routes each to a different save offer, such as a downgrade for too much product or expectation-setting content for the wrong effect, then save attempts match the real objection instead of every canceling customer getting the same generic discount.

signal.check: The cancellation flow offers one generic discount to every canceling customer regardless of their stated reason for leaving.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a flow-branching change, not a measured lift

risk.note: Requires collecting the brand's own cancellation reasons first, since the specific reasons and best save offers are brand-specific.

prerequisites: A cancellation flow that can branch by selected reason
Collected cancellation verbatims to identify the brand's own top reasons
steps: Collect and cluster real cancellation verbatims to find the brand's own top reasons
Build a selectable reason flow at cancellation, not a single generic offer
Route each reason to a matched save offer (a downgrade, a discount, education content, a win-back offer)
Track save rate by reason and refine the matched offers over time

test.method: Track save rate by cancellation reason before and after adding branched offers.

title: Structure the homepage differently by SKU count
hypothesis: If a single-SKU brand runs a landing-page-style homepage optimized to one CTA, while a multi-SKU brand leads with an offer in the header and the highest-AOV bundle next, then the homepage layout matches how many real decisions the visitor actually has to make.

signal.check: A homepage layout was chosen without reference to whether the brand sells one hero SKU or a wide catalogue, leading to a mismatched structure for the actual decision the visitor faces.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a layout heuristic, not a measured lift

risk.note: A homepage layout change; reversible.

prerequisites: Clarity on whether the brand is effectively single-SKU or multi-SKU for merchandising purposes
steps: Classify the brand as single-SKU-led or multi-SKU-catalogue for homepage purposes
For a single-SKU brand, build a landing-page-style homepage optimized to one clear CTA
For a multi-SKU brand, lead the header with an offer, place the highest-AOV bundle next, then categories and reviews
Test the matched structure against the prior generic homepage layout

test.method: A or B test the SKU-count-matched homepage layout against the prior layout.

title: Test a lifestyle PDP hero image against a plain product-on-white default
hypothesis: If the default plain product-on-white PDP hero image is tested against a lifestyle or in-use shot paired with benefit-led headline copy, then the highest-visibility spot on the page gets a real chance to sell instead of defaulting to a flat catalogue photo.

signal.check: The PDP hero image defaults to a plain product-on-white shot with no lifestyle or in-use alternative tested against it.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a CRO test, not a guaranteed lift

risk.note: A PDP image and copy test; reversible.

prerequisites: A lifestyle or in-use photo of the product
Benefit-led headline copy to pair with it
steps: Identify PDPs currently defaulting to a plain product-on-white hero image
Produce a lifestyle or in-use shot for the same product
Pair it with benefit-led headline copy next to the image
A or B test the new hero image against the plain default

test.method: A or B test the lifestyle hero image against the plain product-on-white default.

title: Ask for exactly one referral, not a broad multi-person ask
hypothesis: If a referral ask requests exactly one specific person rather than several, then the ask feels achievable and converts better than a broad 'tell your friends' request that asks for more than most customers will act on.

signal.check: A referral program or ask requests multiple friends or a broad share, rather than a single, specific referral.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a copy and ask-framing change, not a measured lift

risk.note: A copy change on an existing referral ask; reversible.

prerequisites: An existing referral program or a plan to add one
steps: Identify current referral ask copy and how many people it asks the customer to refer
Rewrite the ask to request exactly one specific referral
Test the single-referral ask against the prior broader ask
Track referral conversion rate under each framing

test.method: A or B test the single-referral ask against a multi-person referral ask.

title: Use a capped-budget, pay-on-approval marketplace for UGC clips
hypothesis: If UGC content is sourced through a marketplace with a capped total budget and a target CPM, paying creators only on approval, then the brand gets a predictable content cost even if a clip goes viral, instead of an open-ended payout tied to reach.

signal.check: UGC or clip-based content sourcing has no capped budget or approval-gated payment structure, risking open-ended cost if content performs unexpectedly well.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a sourcing-structure choice, not a measured lift

risk.note: Requires identifying a current clipping or UGC marketplace and confirming its terms before committing budget.

prerequisites: A clipping or UGC marketplace with capped-budget, target-CPM terms
A defined total budget to cap spend at
steps: Identify a current UGC or clipping marketplace with capped-budget terms
Set a target CPM and a hard total budget cap regardless of how a clip performs
Pay creators only on content approval, not automatically
Track cost per usable asset against the cap over the campaign

test.method: Track cost per usable asset sourced through the capped marketplace versus prior open-ended UGC sourcing.

title: Consolidate a cluttered multi-product routine into one flagship format
hypothesis: If a customer's cluttered multi-step routine is redesigned into one combined flagship product, then the product wins on genuine convenience instead of competing feature-by-feature against a shelf of separate items.

signal.check: The target customer currently juggles several separate products to get one outcome, and no single combined format has been designed to replace that routine.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a product-design method, not a measured lift

risk.note: A product-development decision; taste, form factor and dosing must all genuinely work, not just the consolidation story.

prerequisites: A clearly identified multi-step routine the target customer currently follows
steps: Map every separate product or step in the customer's current routine
Identify which steps can be genuinely and safely combined into one product
Set taste, usability or convenience as a hard requirement alongside efficacy
Test the combined format against the separate routine for stated preference and actual repeat use

test.method: Track repeat purchase and stated preference for the combined format versus continuing the separate routine.

title: Fund third-party clinical validation matched to your subscription term's horizon
hypothesis: If a third-party clinical trial measures outcomes at the exact time horizon a subscription term is sold on, then the term reads as backed by real evidence at that timeframe instead of an arbitrary discount period with no matching proof.

signal.check: A subscription term length is set with no clinical or usage evidence measured at that same time horizon.

expected_effect.size: unknown; an evidence-matching practice, not a measured lift

risk.note: Requires a real, credible third-party trial; confirm which claims are legally publishable in each market before using the results in marketing.

prerequisites: Budget and access to a credible third-party research body
A defined subscription term to validate against
steps: Commission a trial with a named, credible third-party research body rather than relying on anecdote
Measure outcomes at the exact time horizon the subscription term is sold on
Confirm which specific claims are legally publishable in each target market
Use the validated horizon to set or confirm the subscription term length so offer and evidence match

test.method: Track subscription term adoption and churn before and after publishing the matched clinical evidence.
test.read_point: One quarter after publishing the evidence

title: Break your category's default visual color code deliberately
hypothesis: If a brand deliberately picks the opposite color of its category's usual default, then it reads differently on shelf, in feed and on the PDP against every competitor using the expected color.

signal.check: A brand's visual identity uses the same default color convention as most of its category, blending in rather than standing out.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a positioning choice, no measured lift given by the source

risk.note: A brand-identity decision with real switching cost once adopted; not something to test lightly on an established brand.

prerequisites: A clear read on the category's default visual color convention
steps: Identify the color or visual code most competitors in the category default to
Deliberately choose a contrasting color for the brand's core identity
Reinforce the contrast consistently across packaging, ads and partner selection
Track shelf or feed standout (click-through, recall) against the category norm

test.method: Track ctr and unaided recall against category-typical creative using the default color.
test.read_point: One quarter after the identity change

title: Decline retail deliberately while DTC headroom remains, using rejections as leverage
hypothesis: If a brand declines retail offers while it can still name real, unreached DTC headroom, and treats each rejection as leverage for better future terms with a set horizon to revisit, then the decision reads as strategy rather than drift, and eventual retail terms improve.

signal.check: Retail offers are being accepted or declined ad hoc, with no explicit headroom estimate or set horizon for revisiting the decision.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a negotiating-leverage strategy, not a measured lift

risk.note: Requires real, current DTC growth headroom to justify; declining retail with no such headroom is a different, riskier decision.

prerequisites: A current estimate of unreached DTC market headroom
At least one real retail offer to evaluate against it
steps: Estimate the share of the addressable market not yet reached through DTC
Decline retail offers while that headroom remains, stating the reason internally and, where appropriate, to the retailer
Set an explicit horizon (a time or revenue trigger) for revisiting retail
Track whether later retail conversations reference or benefit from the earlier declines

test.method: Compare eventual retail deal terms against what an earlier, un-leveraged acceptance would likely have produced.
test.read_point: At the point retail talks are revisited

title: Structure a top creator or celebrity partnership as long-term equity, not a paid post
hypothesis: If a major creator or celebrity partnership is structured as a multi-year equity stake rather than a one-off paid post, then the partner's payoff is tied to the brand's actual growth instead of a single campaign fee with no ongoing incentive.

signal.check: A brand's biggest creator or celebrity relationships are structured as one-off paid posts with no ongoing stake in the brand's growth.

expected_effect.size: unknown; requires real scale and negotiating leverage; not a template for an early brand

risk.note: Requires proper legal and equity structuring and real existing scale; not available to every brand.

prerequisites: Real traction and negotiating leverage
Legal and equity-structuring support
steps: Identify a partner with genuine, proven affinity for the product, not just reach
Propose a multi-year equity or long-term-aligned structure instead of a single paid campaign
Structure the deal with proper legal and tax advice
Track the partnership's contribution to growth over its multi-year term, not one campaign

test.method: Track attributable growth and content output from the equity partner over the length of the term.

title: Seed product to a partner's inner circle before pitching a commercial deal
hypothesis: If product is seeded to a target partner's inner circle, such as a coach or trainer, and the brand waits for genuine organic adoption before pitching a commercial deal, then any resulting partnership is built on real, unprompted use instead of a cold pitch the partner has no real relationship with.

signal.check: A high-value partner or celebrity is being cold-pitched for a commercial deal with no prior seeding to their inner circle or wider team.

expected_effect.size: unknown; requires product quality that can survive unprompted use, and patience

risk.note: Requires enough product quality to survive unprompted use and enough runway to wait months for organic adoption before pitching.

prerequisites: A product genuinely good enough to earn unprompted repeat use
Identified inner-circle contacts around the target partner
steps: Identify the target partner's inner circle (coach, trainer, team, close staff)
Seed product to that inner circle with no commercial ask attached
Wait for genuine, observable organic adoption before approaching the partner directly
Only then pitch a commercial or partnership deal, referencing the organic use

test.method: Track the conversion rate of inner-circle-seeded partnerships versus cold-pitched ones.
test.read_point: Per partnership attempt, over several months

title: Run top-tier partner relationships personally as founder, not delegated
hypothesis: If the handful of top-tier creator or celebrity relationships are run personally by the founder rather than delegated to staff, then the delicate, high-stakes nature of those relationships is handled with the judgment and authority they require.

signal.check: Top-tier partner or celebrity relationships are delegated to junior staff or account managers with no direct founder involvement.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a time-allocation practice, not a measured lift

risk.note: Consumes significant founder time and does not scale past a small number of top-tier partners.

prerequisites: A small, defined list of top-tier partner relationships worth founder-level attention
steps: Identify the small number of partnerships significant enough to warrant founder-level attention
Have the founder personally manage communication and negotiation for those relationships
Delegate lower-tier creator relationships to the team as normal
Track relationship health and renewal rate for founder-managed versus delegated partnerships

test.method: Compare renewal rate and relationship health for founder-managed versus delegated top-tier partnerships.

title: Tie an experiential giveaway to purchase, built around real partner access
hypothesis: If an experiential giveaway built around genuine access to a brand partner requires a purchase or subscription entry, then the promotion drives measurable orders instead of just growing a list with no purchase requirement.

signal.check: An experiential giveaway or sweepstake is planned with no purchase or subscription requirement to enter, limiting it to a pure awareness or list-growth play.

expected_effect.size: unknown; carries real cost and sweepstakes-compliance burden
