Reassess which stage the business is actually in before adding new tooling, rather than skipping stages

test.method: Track tracking_coverage and event_match_quality against the stage-appropriate checklist for the brand's current revenue band.

title: Build a post-treatment measurement window into pre-season holdout tests
hypothesis: If a pre-season incrementality or holdout test includes a measurement window that extends past the test's official end date, then the delayed incremental lift that keeps showing up afterward, especially large around a peak sale, is captured instead of being missed by closing the read too early.

signal.check: A pre-season holdout or geo-lift test's read is closed exactly at the test's end date, with no extended window to capture delayed conversions that arrive afterward.

expected_effect.size: unknown; category-dependent, with fashion showing far more delayed lift than CPG in the source's cited data

risk.note: Requires the ability to run or read a geo-holdout or similar experiment; extending the window delays how soon a final read is available.

prerequisites: An active or planned pre-season holdout or geo-lift test
steps: Define the test's official intervention window as usual
Extend the measurement window to capture conversions arriving after the test period ends
Compare the extended-window lift against the same-window-only lift to size the delayed-conversion effect
Check whether the category shows meaningfully more delayed lift (as fashion did in the source's data) before deciding how long to extend

test.method: Compare incremental lift measured at the test's original end date against lift measured with the extended window.
test.measure: attribution_gap between original and extended read

title: Build per-hour delayed-attribution multipliers before intraday pacing decisions
hypothesis: If per-hour delayed-attribution multipliers are built and applied before making a push or pull spend decision intraday, and hourly conversion rate is pulled as a supplementary real-time signal, then an early-morning ROAS reading is not mistaken for weak performance when it is really just unbackfilled revenue.

signal.check: Intraday spend decisions during a high-spend event are made from raw hourly ROAS with no correction for the normal lag between spend peaking and revenue backfilling later in the day.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a correction method, not a guaranteed lift

risk.note: Worth building only at spend and offer-rotation frequency high enough to justify the operational load.

prerequisites: Prior-period hourly spend and revenue data to build the multiplier from
steps: Pull historical hourly spend and revenue data to see the typical spend-to-revenue lag pattern
Build a delayed-attribution multiplier for each hour of the day based on that pattern
Apply the multiplier to a raw early-hour ROAS reading before making a push or pull decision
Pull hourly conversion rate as a supplementary, less-lagged signal alongside the corrected ROAS

test.method: Compare decisions made using the corrected hourly read against decisions that would have been made on the raw uncorrected number.

title: Run cost-cap campaigns during a peak sale as a marginal-frontier diagnostic
hypothesis: If cost-cap campaigns, otherwise avoided for their year-round volatility, are run during a peak sale specifically to read what they spend up to, then that ceiling becomes a diagnostic for the account's marginal frontier instead of a full-time scaling mechanism.

signal.check: Cost-cap campaigns are either avoided entirely or run as the main scaling lever, with no use of them as a limited, diagnostic read on the account's marginal frontier during a peak period.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a diagnostic use of a specific bidding tool, not a measured lift

risk.note: This use is specific to a high-spend, high-volatility peak window, not a year-round recommendation.

prerequisites: Ability to run cost-cap campaigns alongside standard maximize-volume campaigns
steps: Run a limited set of cost-cap campaigns alongside standard maximize-volume campaigns during the peak window
Read what the cost-cap campaigns actually spend up to as a signal of the account's marginal frontier
Use that read to decide how hard to push the maximize-volume campaigns
Do not treat cost caps as the account's primary scaling mechanism outside this diagnostic use

test.method: Track how the cost-cap-derived frontier estimate compares to actual marginal returns observed later in the window.

title: Judge creative during a peak sale on CTR and CPC at the ad-set level
hypothesis: If creative during a peak discount period is judged on CTR and CPC at the ad-set level instead of ROAS at the ad level, then a deeply discounted product's inflated ROAS does not get mistaken for creative quality, and a genuinely strong ad on a full-price, slow-moving product is not unfairly judged weak.

signal.check: Creative during a storewide sale is ranked by raw ROAS at the individual ad level, the same way it is judged the rest of the year.

expected_effect.size: unknown; the source frames this as a peak-specific exception, not a year-round practice

risk.note: This is explicitly a sale-period exception; the rest of the year, ROAS remains the right creative signal per this source.

prerequisites: Ad-set-level reporting and CTR/CPC data available during the sale
steps: During the sale window, stop ranking creative by raw ROAS at the ad level
Use CTR and CPC as the primary creative-quality diagnostics instead
Evaluate at the ad-set level rather than the individual ad level to reduce noise from multi-touch and last-click attribution effects
Revert to normal ROAS-based judgment once the sale window ends

test.method: Compare creative rankings produced by CTR/CPC during the sale against the same creative's ranking by ROAS.
test.read_point: During and immediately after the sale window

title: Make every offer static legible at thumbnail size with the offer in the first line
hypothesis: If every offer static is tested by shrinking it to thumbnail size to confirm the discount and deadline are still readable, and the offer or deadline is placed in the first line of ad copy, then the message survives the placements and screen sizes that would otherwise crop or truncate it.

signal.check: Offer creative is approved without a thumbnail-size legibility check, and offer or deadline details sit later in the ad copy where some placements truncate it.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a production QC step, not a measured lift

risk.note: A quick production check before launch; no cost beyond the review step.

prerequisites: Offer creative assets ready for review before launch
steps: Shrink each offer static to thumbnail size and confirm the discount and end date are still readable
Check that 9:16 and other narrow placements do not crop off the offer text
Put the offer and deadline in the first line of ad copy, since some placements truncate longer copy
Reject any asset that fails the thumbnail legibility check before it launches

test.method: Track ctr on thumbnail-checked creative against creative that skipped the check.

title: Write actual sale messaging into DPA and catalog ad copy during a sale
hypothesis: If dynamic product ad and catalog copy is rewritten with real sale messaging during a promotional period, instead of left as generic year-round product copy, then a low-competition, easy win is captured that most competing accounts are not bothering to make.

signal.check: Dynamic product ads and catalog listings run with no sale-specific copy during a promotional period, leaving generic messaging in place.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a competitor scrape found most cold brands skip this, a specific but unverified observation

risk.note: A copy update to existing catalog and DPA feeds; reversible after the sale ends.

prerequisites: Access to edit catalog or DPA feed copy for the sale period
steps: Audit current DPA and catalog ad copy for whether it mentions the active sale at all
Write specific sale messaging (discount depth, end date) into the catalog copy
Confirm the updated copy still displays correctly across placements
Revert to standard copy once the sale period ends

test.method: Compare ctr on catalog and DPA ads before and after adding sale-specific copy.
test.measure: ctr on catalog and DPA ads

title: Route paid traffic to a 3-tier landing structure matched to awareness stage
hypothesis: If cold traffic routes to an education-first advertorial or quiz page, problem- and solution-aware traffic routes to a persona-congruent landing page, and bottom-of-funnel retargeting routes straight to the PDP, then each visitor lands on the page built for how much they already know instead of one generic page trying to serve everyone.

signal.check: Ads at every awareness stage route to the same homepage or generic PDP with no destination logic tied to how cold or warm the traffic is.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a routing architecture, not a measured lift

risk.note: Requires enough traffic volume and personas to justify building and maintaining multiple landing page tiers.

prerequisites: Ads classified by awareness stage
Ability to build persona-specific landing pages
steps: Classify current ads by awareness stage: unaware, problem-aware, solution-aware, bottom-of-funnel
Build or assign an education-first page (advertorial or quiz) for unaware traffic
Build a dedicated, message-matched landing page per persona for problem- and solution-aware traffic
Route bottom-of-funnel and retargeting traffic straight to the PDP
Audit routing periodically to catch any ad still pointed at a mismatched destination

test.method: Compare conversion rate by awareness stage before and after adopting tiered routing.

title: Scale creative volume by varying only the persona on a fixed script
hypothesis: If a winning ad script's mechanism, offer and structure stay fixed while only the persona and its matching landing page change per variant, then creative volume scales quickly because a persona swap alone counts as a genuinely new concept to test.

signal.check: New creative concepts require rebuilding the script, mechanism and offer from scratch each time, slowing volume even though a winning skeleton already exists.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a production method, not a measured lift

risk.note: Requires a genuinely proven script skeleton to hold fixed; swapping persona on a weak script will not fix underlying performance.

prerequisites: A proven winning script skeleton
Multiple distinct personas the product can credibly serve
steps: Identify the current winning ad script's fixed skeleton (hook structure, mechanism, offer, close)
Hold the skeleton fixed and write a new variant changing only the persona and problem framing
Build or assign a matching landing page for each persona variant
Plan creative throughput as roughly proportional to spend, using your own per-creative sustainable spend ceiling

test.method: Track concepts produced per week and average spend sustained per creative unit under persona-swap scaling.
test.measure: other:concepts_per_week and average spend per creative

title: Choose trust elements a competitor could not copy in a week
hypothesis: If every PDP or landing-page trust element is checked against whether a competitor could replicate it within a week, then resources go toward genuinely differentiating proof (a proprietary process, a named advisory board) instead of generic badges and review counts that add little because anyone can copy them.

signal.check: PDP or landing-page trust elements are mostly generic review badges or star counts, with no check on whether a competitor could copy them easily.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a prioritization filter, not a measured lift

risk.note: A prioritization exercise for trust-building investment; does not mean removing generic proof, just not over-investing in it.

prerequisites: An inventory of current trust elements on key pages
steps: List every current trust element on the PDP or landing page
For each, ask whether a competitor could copy it within a week
Deprioritize further investment in easily-copied elements (generic badges, aggregate review counts)
Invest instead in a harder-to-copy element (a named process, a real advisory relationship, proprietary testing)

test.method: Compare conversion rate contribution of hard-to-copy trust elements against generic ones through a test.

title: Restate the guarantee and value props at checkout, not only in cart
hypothesis: If the guarantee, core value props and reviews are restated directly at checkout, not only in the cart step before it, then a location most brands treat as pure transaction gets used as one more chance to hold the sale together.

signal.check: Checkout shows only payment and shipping fields with no restatement of the guarantee, value props or reviews that appeared earlier in the funnel.

expected_effect.size: unknown; the source calls checkout a location most brands rarely use this way, not a measured lift

risk.note: A checkout-page content addition; should not add friction or slow the actual payment flow.

prerequisites: Ability to add lightweight trust content to the checkout page or step
steps: Identify the guarantee, top value props and a compact review element used earlier in the funnel
Add a compact, non-intrusive restatement of these at the checkout step
Confirm the addition does not slow or clutter the actual payment flow
Test checkout completion rate with and without the restatement

test.method: A or B test checkout with and without the trust restatement.

title: Check a P&L's contribution-margin definition before comparing it to a benchmark
hypothesis: If a brand's or competitor's stated contribution margin is checked for whether marketing spend sits above or below that line before comparing it to a benchmark, then a non-standard definition does not get read as if it were the common one, producing a false comparison.

signal.check: A competitor's, partner's or a shareholder letter's contribution-margin figure is compared directly to a standard industry benchmark with no check on how the term is actually defined in that specific report.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a due-diligence step, not a measured lift

risk.note: A reading-comprehension check on financial disclosures; no cost.

prerequisites: The specific P&L or disclosure being read
steps: Find the exact line items included above and below the stated 'contribution margin' or 'contribution profit'
Confirm whether marketing and advertising expense sits above or below that line
Recompute the figure under the standard definition (gross margin minus marketing) if it differs
Only compare like-for-like definitions against a benchmark or your own numbers

test.method: Track how often a recomputed, standardized figure differs materially from the as-reported number.
test.measure: other:comparison_validity gap between as-reported and standardized figures
test.read_point: Whenever reading an external P&L or disclosure

title: Run a 3-question skeptical check before trusting a growth claim
hypothesis: If any ARR, LTV:CAC, or cash-flow-positive claim from a competitor, partner or acquisition target is checked against three questions, which single month was the ARR annualized from, has any real cohort reached the cited LTV:CAC horizon, and what is financing the cash-flow position, then an impressive headline number does not get treated as more solid than it actually is.

signal.check: A growth claim (ARR, LTV:CAC ratio, cash-flow-positive status) from a competitor, partner or acquisition target is being taken at face value with no check on its underlying construction.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a due-diligence checklist, not a measured lift

risk.note: A due-diligence checklist for evaluating an external claim; no cost.

prerequisites: The specific claim and any available underlying disclosure or filing
steps: Ask which single month an ARR figure was annualized from, and compare it to a rolling 3-6 month average instead
Ask whether any actual cohort has reached the horizon a stated LTV:CAC or LTGP:CAC ratio projects to
Ask what, if anything, is financing a claimed cash-flow-positive position
Treat any claim that fails these checks as directional, not confirmed, before acting on it

test.method: Track how often applying the checklist changes the conclusion drawn from a headline growth claim.
test.read_point: Whenever evaluating an external growth claim

title: Increase ad-claim aggressiveness only for colder audiences, and flag the compliance exposure
hypothesis: If claim sharpness and aggressiveness are allowed to increase only as the target audience gets colder, and the resulting compliance exposure at the coldest tier is explicitly flagged and reviewed, then a bigger pattern interrupt for unaware traffic does not slip through with no compliance check simply because it is a small share of total ad volume.

signal.check: Claim aggressiveness varies inconsistently across ads with no deliberate rule tying it to audience temperature, and no extra compliance review on the coldest, most aggressive claims.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a claims-governance rule, not a measured lift

risk.note: Coldest-audience ads carry the most compliance exposure even at low volume; review them with extra scrutiny, not less.

prerequisites: Ads classified by target audience temperature (unaware, problem-aware, solution-aware, most-aware)
steps: Classify current ads by target audience temperature
Allow claim sharpness to increase only for colder-audience ads, not uniformly across the account
Route the coldest-audience, most aggressive claims through an explicit compliance review before launch
Track how many flagged claims get modified or killed at review

test.method: Track the share of coldest-audience ads flagged and modified at compliance review.

title: Pay long-term strategic partners in equity or royalty, tracked as its own P&L line
hypothesis: If a long-term strategic partner, such as an ambassador or key creator, is paid in equity or royalty rather than a fixed per-post fee, tracked as its own named P&L line, then the partner's cost declines as a share of revenue as the business compounds instead of staying fixed regardless of growth.

signal.check: A long-term strategic partnership is paid on a fixed per-post or flat-fee basis, with cost as a share of revenue staying constant or rising as the business grows.

expected_effect.size: unknown; only becomes cheaper if revenue keeps compounding, and depends on landing a partner of real reach

risk.note: Only works if revenue keeps compounding; offers no protection if growth stalls, and requires proper legal and tax structuring.

prerequisites: A strategic partner candidate with real reach
Legal and tax structuring support
steps: Identify a long-term strategic partnership candidate with genuine reach and fit
Propose an equity or royalty structure instead of a fixed fee
Track the partner's cost as its own named line as a percentage of revenue
Pair the deal with ongoing brand-building activity to keep compounding the revenue that deleverages the cost

test.method: Track the partner's cost as a percentage of revenue over successive quarters.

title: Add exactly one missing beat to an under-scripted ad
hypothesis: If an under-scripted ad is upgraded by adding only the single missing beat, of hook, problem, mechanism, proof, objection, offer, risk reversal or CTA, that best fits the brand's existing voice, and risk-reversal phrasing that could invite returns is avoided, then the ad improves without forcing a full rewrite or a return-inviting promise onto a brand that does not want one.

signal.check: An ad scores weak on several of the eight script beats, and the response is either a full rewrite or no change at all, with no targeted single-beat fix considered.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a targeted-fix method, not a measured lift

risk.note: Avoid risk-reversal phrasing that could invite returns (such as 'buy several so you can return the rest') on a brand that does not want that behavior encouraged.

prerequisites: An ad scored against the eight-beat script framework
steps: Score the ad against the eight beats: hook, problem, mechanism, proof, objection, offer, risk reversal, CTA
Identify the single missing beat most likely to move performance without clashing with brand voice
Add only that one beat rather than rewriting the whole script
Check the added beat does not invite unwanted behavior, such as return-inducing risk-reversal phrasing

test.method: Compare performance of the single-beat-upgraded ad against the original and against a fully rewritten version.

title: Name a real, defensible mechanism instead of stacking feel-based adjectives
hypothesis: If a benefit is explained through a specific, real, defensible mechanism, such as a named fabric technology or process, rather than a stack of feel-based adjectives, then the claim persuades at scale and holds up under compliance or acquisition-diligence scrutiny.

signal.check: Product copy relies on stacked feel-based adjectives (soft, buttery, cozy, comfy) with no named, real mechanism behind the claim.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a copywriting technique, not a measured lift

risk.note: Only claim a mechanism that is real and defensible; naming something with no underlying product difference is invented-claim risk.

prerequisites: A real, verifiable product mechanism, process or ingredient to name
steps: Identify a real, specific mechanism, process or material behind the product's key benefit
Give it a clear, specific name if it does not already have one
Pair the name with the functional reason it produces the benefit
Test copy built around the named mechanism against adjective-stacked copy

test.method: A or B test named-mechanism copy against adjective-led copy for the same product.

title: Open a higher-priced product's ad on a felt need before the mechanism
hypothesis: If a higher-priced product's ad opens on a specific, felt need or failure the buyer already recognizes, and only then reveals the named mechanism as the fix, then the ad earns attention through relevance before it earns trust through the solution, instead of opening cold on the product image.

signal.check: Ads for higher-priced products open directly on the product image or a generic lifestyle shot, with no felt-need statement before the mechanism is introduced.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a hook-structure technique, not a measured lift

risk.note: May sit in tension with a purely aspirational brand positioning; confirm fit with brand guidelines before rolling out widely.

prerequisites: A named mechanism to reveal after the felt-need opening
steps: Identify a specific, felt need or failure the target buyer already recognizes
Open the ad by naming that need or failure directly
Reveal the named mechanism immediately after as the fix
Test the need-first structure against a product-first opening for the same product

test.method: A or B test need-first opening structure against a product-first opening for the same offer.

title: Test need-first creative on a lower-risk sub-segment before brand-wide rollout
hypothesis: If a more direct, problem-agitating creative style is tested first on a lower-risk sub-segment, such as a smaller product line, before rolling it out to the brand's main audience, then a positioning-sensitive brand can learn whether the style works without risking its primary aspirational image.

signal.check: A brand considering more direct, need-first creative applies it brand-wide immediately, with no lower-risk sub-segment test first.

expected_effect.size: unknown; one analyst's suggestion, not a tested rule

risk.note: Requires a genuinely lower-risk sub-segment (a smaller line, a less brand-defining category) to test on first.

prerequisites: A smaller, lower-risk product line or segment distinct from the brand's main positioning
steps: Identify a smaller, lower-risk product line or segment to test on first
Run the more direct, need-first creative style on that segment only
Compare performance and brand-sentiment signals against the segment's usual creative style
Decide on wider rollout only after the sub-segment test shows a clear result

test.method: Compare ctr and any available brand-sentiment signal on the sub-segment test against its usual creative baseline.

title: Build a dedicated funnel-stage landing page for a named ambassador or collab
hypothesis: If a named ambassador or collab gets a dedicated landing page built as a real funnel step, with a product carousel and a short story about the collab, rather than a generic photo gallery or the default category grid, then the ad-to-page transition stays congruent and the page actually does conversion work instead of just displaying images.

signal.check: Traffic from an ad naming a specific ambassador or collab routes to a generic grid or a plain image gallery with no dedicated funnel-step page.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a page-build recommendation, not a measured lift

risk.note: Requires likeness and usage rights for the ambassador's imagery in the contract; negotiate what rights are available if a full dedicated page is not possible.

prerequisites: An ambassador or collab partnership with usable imagery rights
Design and dev capability to build a dedicated page
steps: Confirm likeness and usage rights allow a dedicated on-site page for the ambassador or collab
Build the page as a real funnel step: product carousel plus a short story about the collab
Route the naming ad's traffic specifically to this page, not the generic grid
Measure it as a conversion funnel step, not just an engagement asset

test.method: Compare conversion rate on the dedicated collab page against traffic sent to the generic grid.

title: Assign one named daily owner to a category-grid landing page
hypothesis: If one named owner is responsible for reviewing a category-grid landing page daily, tracking which products occupy the top visible slots and whether their winning color and size variants are in stock, then a disproportionate share of traffic aimed at a specific variant does not silently convert worse the moment that variant sells out.

signal.check: Paid traffic lands on a category or collection grid page with no named owner tracking top-slot product placement or variant-level stock daily.

expected_effect.size: unknown; an ownership discipline, not a measured lift

risk.note: Best suited to fast-merchandised categories like fashion where a filtered grid genuinely matches buyer intent; a custom lander may fit better elsewhere.

prerequisites: A category or collection grid page receiving meaningful paid traffic
Variant-level stock visibility
steps: Identify which products currently occupy the top visible slots of the grid page
Assign one named owner responsible for that placement and the page's conversion rate
Track stock at the variant level (specific color and size), not just the product level
Review daily and adjust placement or restock proactively when a winning variant runs low

test.method: Track conversion rate on the grid page against variant stock levels over time.

title: Exclude your lowest-AOV item from paid acquisition creative and entry bundles
hypothesis: If the single lowest-priced item in the catalogue is deliberately excluded from paid acquisition creative and from any entry-price bundle, then acquisition spend is not dragged toward the customers most likely to have the lowest lifetime value.

signal.check: The catalogue's cheapest item appears in paid acquisition ads or in an entry-price bundle with no check on whether it is pulling down AOV and attracting lower-LTV customers.

expected_effect.size: unknown; reverses for a deliberate low-price market-entry strategy, which is a different, intentional choice

risk.note: Does not apply to a brand deliberately running a low-price market-entry play, where a hero SKU (not necessarily the cheapest) may be the intended entry point instead.

prerequisites: Median product price and the single cheapest entry price point for the catalogue
steps: Identify the catalogue's median price and its single cheapest item
Audit current paid acquisition creative and entry bundles for whether the cheapest item appears
Remove the cheapest item from paid creative and entry bundles unless a low-price entry strategy is the deliberate choice
Track aov and new-customer LTV before and after the exclusion

test.method: Compare aov and new-customer ltv_180d before and after excluding the lowest-AOV item from paid creative.

title: Use a spend-threshold free-shipping offer to lift AOV on a premium position
lever: threshold shipping offer for premium brands
hypothesis: If a spend-threshold free-shipping offer, such as free shipping over a set dollar amount, replaces a percentage discount as the AOV lever, then item prices stay intact and the brand's premium position is not undercut by discount language, while still giving the customer a reason to add one more item.

signal.check: A brand positioned as premium or aspirational is considering or running a percentage discount to lift AOV, risking the pricing integrity the position depends on.

expected_effect.size: unknown; framed as low brand risk by the source, not tested with numbers

risk.note: A pricing and shipping-policy change; set the threshold from the brand's own AOV distribution, not a generic number.

prerequisites: Current AOV distribution to set a meaningful free-shipping threshold
steps: Set a free-shipping threshold above current average order value, based on the brand's own AOV distribution
Communicate the threshold on-site and at checkout without discount language
Track AOV and shipping-cost impact after launch
Avoid stacking this with a percentage discount that would undercut the premium framing

test.method: Compare aov before and after introducing the spend-threshold free-shipping offer.

title: Map your own creative library against a fixed format taxonomy to find gaps
hypothesis: If every live creative in your own account is classified into a fixed set of format buckets, then real content gaps become visible instead of assuming raw ad volume already means good format coverage.

signal.check: Creative volume is tracked only as a total count, with no classification into distinct format buckets to check for over-concentration or missing formats.

expected_effect.size: unknown; an audit method, not a measured lift

risk.note: The specific format list should be built for your own category, not copied from another vertical's taxonomy.

prerequisites: A representative sample of the account's current live creative
steps: Define a fixed set of format buckets relevant to your category
Classify every current live ad into one bucket
Check for over-concentration in one or two formats
Identify missing formats and decide deliberately which gap fits the brand's positioning to fill first

test.method: Track format mix and identify newly filled gaps after the audit.

title: Audit your own funnel for a built-but-unused landing page
hypothesis: If every landing page your paid traffic could reach is listed alongside how many ads actually point to it, then a purpose-built page receiving zero traffic is caught and a deliberate decision gets made about reactivating it, instead of it sitting forgotten.

signal.check: The full set of built landing pages has never been audited against actual ad-routing data, so a page with real potential value may be receiving no traffic at all.

expected_effect.size: unknown; an audit practice, not a measured lift

risk.note: Confirm whether a page's dormancy is a past deliberate decision (a retired test) before reactivating it.

prerequisites: A list of all built landing pages and current ad-to-page routing data
steps: List every distinct landing page the funnel could route to
Count how many current ads point to each page
Flag any purpose-built page receiving zero ads
Investigate why before deciding whether to reactivate, retire, or repurpose it

test.method: Track the number of dormant pages found and the decision made for each.

title: Run a CRO fundamentals pass before structural split tests
hypothesis: If a page is checked against CRO fundamentals first, and further gains are only pursued through structural split tests once fundamentals are already in place, with a realistic expectation of roughly 5 to 10 percent incremental uplift rather than a step change, then testing effort goes where real gains are still available instead of chasing a redesign a page does not need.

signal.check: A page redesign is planned or split tests are run with no prior check on whether basic CRO fundamentals (imagery, information architecture, above-the-fold priority) are already in place.

expected_effect.size: 5 to 10 percent incremental uplift is a realistic range once fundamentals are already met, per the source

risk.note: Set the 5 to 10 percent expectation explicitly so a fundamentals-solid page is not judged a failure for not producing a step change.

prerequisites: A page to review against basic CRO fundamentals before planning tests
steps: Check the page against CRO fundamentals: clear imagery, information architecture, above-the-fold priority
If fundamentals are already solid, stop planning a full redesign
Move to targeted structural split tests (such as a selector style or layout element) instead
Set a realistic 5 to 10 percent uplift expectation for these tests, not a step change

test.method: Track actual uplift achieved from structural split tests on a fundamentals-solid page.

title: Size a Meta test's daily budget from a target conversion count and duration
hypothesis: If a test's daily budget is set from the conversion count that counts as significant divided by how many days the test should run, then the budget is sized to reach a real read instead of copying a generic 'X conversions in Y days' platform rule that can be unaffordable across many concurrent tests.

signal.check: New-concept test budgets are set from a fixed platform rule of thumb rather than back-calculated from a target conversion count and chosen duration.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a sizing formula, not a measured lift

risk.note: A budgeting formula; no live spend change beyond normal test sizing.

prerequisites: A target CPA and a chosen number of days for the test
steps: Pick the conversion count that counts as statistically meaningful for this account
Pick how many days the test should run
Daily budget = (target conversions times expected CPA) divided by test duration in days
Compare the result to what a fixed platform rule of thumb would have set, and use whichever is affordable across all concurrent tests

test.method: Compare test read quality and affordability using the formula versus the platform's default guidance.
test.measure: number of concurrent tests affordable at the calculated budget

title: Hand-build 30 to 40 real personas before asking an AI tool for more
hypothesis: If 30 to 40 personas are manually built around problem, desire and buying trigger before an AI tool is asked to generate more, then AI-generated personas add real variety instead of producing generic, averaged output from too few examples.

signal.check: Persona generation starts from asking an AI tool for personas with only 3 to 4 shallow, demographic-only examples already on hand.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a process change to widen creative diversity

risk.note: A research and documentation exercise; no live spend change.

prerequisites: Customer data, reviews, support tickets or surveys to draw real problems and triggers from
steps: Pull real customer language from reviews, support tickets and surveys
Write 30 to 40 personas defined by problem, desire and buying trigger, not demographics alone
Only then feed this set to an AI tool to generate additional variations
Check AI-generated personas against the hand-built set for genuine novelty, not repetition

test.method: Compare concept diversity and hit rate on ads built from AI-assisted personas with and without the 30 to 40 hand-built base.
test.measure: other:concept_diversity and hit rate by persona source
test.read_point: One testing cycle after adopting the practice

title: Build every new ad concept in a fixed order: persona, then angle, then format
hypothesis: If every new ad concept is built by choosing the persona first, then an angle for that persona, and format only last, then the team stops picking a video style or trend before deciding who the ad is actually for.

signal.check: New concepts are started from a format or trend (a video style, a trending sound) rather than from a chosen persona and angle.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a process order, not a measured lift

risk.note: A creative-brief process change; no live spend change on its own.

prerequisites: A defined persona list and angle menu to choose from
steps: Require every creative brief to state the persona first
Require the angle to be chosen next, from a defined menu (problem agitation, contrarian truth, social proof, curiosity gap, comparison, before-after)
Only then choose the format
Reject briefs that start from a format or trend with no persona or angle stated

test.method: Compare hit rate of concepts built in this order against concepts started from a format.
test.read_point: One testing cycle after adopting the order

title: Grade every ad hook on a five-part rubric before it ships
hypothesis: If every hook is checked against clarity, relevance, novelty, specificity and credibility before it ships, then a weak hook is caught before spend is wasted on an otherwise good concept that never gets past the first three seconds.

signal.check: Hooks are shipped without a written quality check, and hook rate is only diagnosed after spend, not before launch.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a pre-launch quality gate, not a guaranteed lift

risk.note: A creative review step; no live spend change on its own.

prerequisites: A written or verbal hook script to review before production
steps: Write out the exact hook line or first 3 seconds before full production
Score it on clarity, relevance, novelty, specificity and credibility
Require at least two of the five to be strong before greenlighting production
Track hook rate after launch against the pre-launch score to calibrate the rubric over time

test.method: Compare hook rate of graded hooks against ungraded hooks shipped before the rubric was adopted.
test.measure: hook_rate by graded vs ungraded hook
test.read_point: One testing cycle after adopting the rubric

title: Build the awareness bridge deliberately and introduce the product late
hypothesis: If the transition from hook to product is built as a gradual awareness bridge and the product is introduced as late as the format allows, then fewer total viewers reach the product reveal but the ones who do convert at a meaningfully higher rate than an abrupt cut to product.

signal.check: An ad cuts from the hook straight to the product with no awareness bridge in between.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a scripting change, not a measured lift on a real brand

risk.note: A scripting and editing change; no live spend impact beyond normal creative testing.

prerequisites: A script or storyboard to review before production
steps: Map the ad's awareness stages: unaware, problem aware, solution aware, product aware
Check the current script for an abrupt cut from hook straight to product
Rewrite the middle section to move gradually through each awareness stage
Push the product reveal as late as the chosen format allows
Compare hold rate and conversion rate against the abrupt version

test.method: A or B test the bridged version against an abrupt-cut version of the same hook and offer.

title: Fix creative fatigue in a fixed preference order before duplicating a post
hypothesis: If a fatiguing ad is first given new hooks on its proven body, then squeezed with a cost cap, then reformatted, and only duplicated into another campaign as a last resort, then the account extends a winner's life with the least added complexity at each step.

signal.check: A fatiguing ad is duplicated into another campaign as the first response, before trying a new hook, a cost-cap squeeze, or a format change.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a remedy sequence, not a guaranteed lift

risk.note: A workflow rule for handling fatigue; each step is reversible.

prerequisites: A way to detect fatigue (rising frequency, falling CTR or hook rate on a previously strong ad)
steps: Detect fatigue via rising frequency or falling CTR/hook rate on a proven ad
First try a new hook on the same proven body
If that fails, move it into a cost-cap campaign to squeeze more short-term spend
If that fails, rotate it into a different format
Only duplicate the post ID into another campaign as the last option, and avoid duplicating the ad set itself

test.method: Track how many fatigue cases are resolved at each step of the sequence versus jumping straight to duplication.
test.measure: share of fatigue cases resolved without a full duplication

title: Choose to squeeze or run an ad lean based on the brand's cash and inventory position
lever: creative pacing tied to cash position
hypothesis: If the decision to squeeze a winning ad hard for fast, short-lived spend or run it lean for a longer life is made from the brand's current inventory and cash-cycle position, and that position is shared with the media buyer proactively, then creative pacing works with the business's cash needs instead of against them.

signal.check: The media buyer decides pacing on a winning ad without knowing the brand's current inventory or cash-cycle position.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a coordination practice, not a measured lift

risk.note: A communication and pacing decision; no cost, fully reversible.

prerequisites: Visibility into current inventory levels and cash position for the media buyer
steps: Share current inventory grade and cash position with the media buyer before scaling a winning ad
If cash is tight or inventory needs to move fast, squeeze the winner hard for short-term spend
If cash and inventory are healthy, run the winner lean for a longer life
Revisit the pacing decision whenever the cash or inventory position changes materially

test.method: Compare winner lifespan and cash outcomes under deliberate pacing versus pacing set with no cash context.

title: Set creative production budget and team size by the brand's spend tier
hypothesis: If creative production budget and headcount scale through named stages, from founder-led content at low spend to a full production team past $100k a month, then production capacity is added when spend can justify it instead of over- or under-investing at the wrong stage.

signal.check: Creative production spend or headcount is fixed regardless of the brand's current monthly ad spend, or was set once and never revisited as spend grew.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a staged plan, not a measured lift

risk.note: A staffing and budget-planning decision; changes should be phased in, not made overnight.

prerequisites: Current monthly ad spend and current creative production cost and headcount
steps: Identify current monthly ad spend and which stage it falls into
At low spend, favor founder-led content and cheap organic validation before paid tests
At mid spend, add a small share of media budget to production and bring in a couple of UGC creators
Past a high-spend threshold, build a full production team and track cost-per-asset and profit-contribution per creator
Revisit the plan whenever monthly spend crosses into a new stage

test.method: Track cost-per-asset and creative output against the stage-appropriate targets after adopting the staged plan.

title: Forecast monthly creative volume from target revenue divided by spend per ad and ROAS
hypothesis: If required creatives per month is forecast as target new-customer revenue divided by average spend per ad times average ROAS, then creative volume planning flexes with the actual revenue goal instead of a flat 'one ad per dollar of spend' rule that ignores the target.

signal.check: Creative volume is planned from a flat rule of thumb (such as one new ad per fixed dollar amount of spend) rather than from the actual revenue target.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a planning formula, not a measured lift

risk.note: A planning exercise; no live change until production output is actually adjusted.

prerequisites: A target new-customer revenue figure, and historical average spend per ad and average ROAS
steps: Set the target new-customer revenue for the period
Pull average spend per ad and average ROAS from recent history
Required creatives per month = target new-customer revenue divided by (average spend per ad times average ROAS)
Compare the result to the flat rule of thumb and to actual production capacity
Adjust the production plan to close any gap

test.method: Compare actual creative output to the formula's required volume each month.
test.measure: planned vs actual creatives per month

title: Consolidate Google Ads campaigns by default; split only for named reasons
hypothesis: If Google Ads campaigns default to one consolidated campaign per product line and only split for brand versus non-brand, geography, margin tier, or a genuinely distinct category, then each campaign keeps enough conversion data to bid accurately instead of learning in isolation on a small dataset.

signal.check: Google Ads campaigns are split by many criteria (audience, keyword theme, product) with no named commercial reason for each split.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a structural correction, not a measured lift on a real brand

risk.note: A structural consolidation; can reset some campaigns' learning phase during the change.

prerequisites: Access to current Google Ads account structure and campaign-level conversion counts
steps: List every active campaign and its monthly conversion count
For each campaign, name the specific commercial reason it exists separately (brand vs non-brand, geography, margin tier, distinct category)
Merge any campaign without a named reason into the closest related campaign
Monitor CPA and ROAS through the consolidation to confirm the merge is not losing signal

test.method: Compare CPA and ROAS at the account level before and after consolidation.

title: Replace single-keyword ad groups with themed topic ad groups on Search
hypothesis: If single-keyword ad groups are replaced with topic ad groups of 10 to 20 themed keywords, then Responsive Search Ads get enough impression volume per group to learn properly instead of being starved by too few keywords per group.

signal.check: Search campaigns still use single-keyword ad groups (SKAGs) with Responsive Search Ads that are not accumulating enough impressions to learn.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a structural fix, not a measured lift

risk.note: A campaign restructure; can reset learning phases for affected ad groups.

prerequisites: An existing Search campaign built on single-keyword ad groups
steps: Group 10 to 20 closely related keywords into one themed topic ad group
Rebuild Responsive Search Ads at the topic level, not the single-keyword level
Migrate ad groups in batches to avoid resetting the whole account's learning phase at once
Track impression volume and CPA per topic group after migration

test.method: Compare CPA and impression volume per ad group before and after migrating from SKAGs to topic groups.
test.measure: cpa and impressions per ad group

title: Structure PMax asset groups by product type with a matching listing group
hypothesis: If PMax asset groups are segmented by product type, each with its own matching listing group and roughly 15 or more products, then spend and creative are matched to the right product set instead of running through Google's single default asset group.

signal.check: A PMax campaign is running on the single default asset group with no product-type segmentation.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a structural fix, not a measured lift on a real brand

risk.note: A PMax restructure; can reset the campaign's learning phase.

prerequisites: A PMax campaign and a product catalogue that can be grouped by type
steps: Group the product catalogue into logical product types
Create one asset group per product type, each with 15 or more products
Build a matching listing group filter for each asset group
Monitor performance per asset group after the split

test.method: Compare ROAS and spend distribution per product type before and after the asset-group split.

title: Set PMax brand exclusions two ways as a redundant fail-safe
hypothesis: If PMax brand exclusions are set both as a brand-list exclusion and as direct negative keywords, then a single broken exclusion does not silently let PMax spend become a retargeting campaign on branded traffic.

signal.check: PMax brand exclusion relies on only one mechanism (either the brand-list exclusion or negative keywords, not both).

expected_effect.size: unknown; a fail-safe, not a measured lift

risk.note: A settings redundancy check; no live spend change.

prerequisites: Access to PMax brand-exclusion and negative-keyword settings
steps: Check whether the brand-list exclusion is set on the PMax campaign
Separately add the brand's own name and common misspellings as direct negative keywords
Periodically re-check both mechanisms are still active, since Meta and Google settings can silently reset
Review the Search Term Report periodically for any brand-term leakage into PMax

test.method: Check Search Term Report for brand leakage on a schedule after setting both exclusions.
test.measure: share of PMax spend on branded search terms

title: Run a low-target-ROAS Standard Shopping feeder under a high-target PMax layer
hypothesis: If Standard Shopping runs as a genuinely cold, low-target-ROAS feeder campaign underneath a higher-target-ROAS PMax layer, then the account reaches cold shoppers Standard Shopping alone would capture cheaply, while PMax still converts on top of that colder traffic instead of mostly re-converting warm shoppers.

signal.check: PMax runs alone with no Standard Shopping feeder, and PMax conversions are suspected to skew heavily toward repeat or warm customers.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a channel-layering strategy, not a measured lift on a real brand

risk.note: Running two overlapping Shopping mechanisms adds account complexity and needs careful budget separation to avoid double-counting.

prerequisites: An active PMax campaign and the ability to run Standard Shopping in parallel
steps: Stand up a Standard Shopping campaign at a deliberately low target ROAS to prioritize reach over efficiency
Keep PMax running at its normal, higher target ROAS on top
Monitor whether PMax's audience report shows less warm-customer skew after adding the feeder
Track combined incremental revenue across both campaigns, not each in isolation

test.method: Compare PMax audience warmth and combined incremental revenue with and without the Standard Shopping feeder.
test.measure: acquisition_volume and PMax audience-report warm share
test.read_point: 30 to 60 days after adding the feeder

title: Rebuild Merchant Center titles around actual converting search terms
hypothesis: If product titles in the Merchant Center feed are rebuilt around search terms that actually convert, with the brand name pushed to the back or dropped if it has no recognition value, then Shopping and PMax listings match what shoppers are really searching for instead of leading with the bare product name.

signal.check: Merchant Center product titles lead with the brand name or a generic product name, with no reference to actual converting search terms.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a feed-optimization tactic, not a measured lift

risk.note: A feed change; should be rolled out in batches, not all at once, to avoid resetting learning account-wide.

prerequisites: A Search Term Report showing which queries actually convert for these products
steps: Pull the Search Term Report to find converting, descriptive query language
Rewrite product titles to front-load that descriptive, converting language
Push the brand name to the back, or drop it if it adds no recognition value
Roll the change out in small batches, watching CTR, CPC and ROAS after each batch

test.method: Compare CTR and ROAS on updated titles versus the prior titles, batch by batch.
test.measure: ctr and roas_prospecting by title batch
test.read_point: Two to four weeks per batch

title: Run a separate Merchant Center feed per currency for every region sold into
hypothesis: If every region sold into gets its own Merchant Center feed in its own currency, then shoppers do not see a mismatched or converted currency display that suppresses click-through and conversion rate.

signal.check: A single shared-currency feed is used for a region where local shoppers see a converted or foreign currency price.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a feed-hygiene fix, not a measured lift

risk.note: A feed-management change; requires ongoing upkeep for each additional region.

prerequisites: Sales into more than one currency region
Ability to publish a separate Merchant Center feed per currency
steps: Identify every currency region currently sold into
Publish a dedicated feed in the correct local currency for each region
Confirm the live shopping listing shows the correct local price, not a converted display
Track CTR and conversion rate by region after separating the feeds

test.method: Compare CTR and conversion rate by region before and after splitting feeds by currency.
test.measure: ctr and cvr_overall by currency region

title: Run a top-down, spend-weighted root-cause process before touching a dropped account
hypothesis: If a performance drop is diagnosed top-down, weighted by each channel's spend share and each campaign's cost rank, before drilling into any single submetric, then time is not spent fixing a small campaign's number that could never move the business result.

signal.check: A performance drop is diagnosed by jumping straight to a flagged submetric (a specific ad's CPC, a specific campaign someone noticed) without first checking whether it matters at the business or channel level.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a diagnostic order, not a measured lift

risk.note: A diagnostic process; no live change until a real fix is applied afterward.

prerequisites: Spend-share and cost data across all active channels and campaigns
steps: Extend the analysis window to avoid small-sample bias before reacting
Check cross-channel spend share first and confirm the channel actually named is the one that moved
Within that channel, sort campaigns by cost and start with the top 5 spenders
Only then drill into ad groups, ads or submetrics inside the implicated campaign
Do not apply a fix until you can state which metric dropped, which submetric drove it, and the root cause

test.method: Track how often a diagnosis reaches the true root cause on the first pass using this order versus jumping to a submetric.
test.measure: share of diagnoses resolved without a wrong first fix

title: Pull conversions by conversion time before judging the last few days of Google data
hypothesis: If Google performance is read using 'conversions by conversion time' instead of the default conversion view, then the last few days do not look artificially weak from reporting lag alone, and no unnecessary change gets made in response to a false dip.

signal.check: A recent dip in Google Ads conversions is being investigated using the default conversion count view for the last 3 to 4 days.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a reporting-view fix, not a measured lift

risk.note: A reporting-column change; no live spend change.

prerequisites: Access to Google Ads custom columns
steps: Add the 'conversions by conversion time' column alongside the default conversion column
Re-check the last 3 to 4 days of performance using the conversion-time view before reacting
Only treat a dip as real once it holds up in the conversion-time view
Make this the default view for any short-window performance check going forward

test.method: Compare how often a short-window dip disappears once viewed by conversion time.
test.measure: share of short-window dips that resolve under the conversion-time view

title: Build a real-time competitor price monitor for Shopping listings
hypothesis: If a competitor's price on a matching product is monitored in near real time and the affected product is deprioritized the moment a competitor undercuts it, then margin is protected without matching every competitor discount dollar for dollar.

signal.check: A Shopping product's CTR or ROAS drops in a pattern matching a competitor's promotion, with no active price-monitoring or response process in place.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a defensive margin tactic, not a measured lift

risk.note: A monitoring and response process; does not require matching competitor discounts.

prerequisites: A way to track competitor prices on matching or near-identical products
steps: Identify the handful of products most exposed to direct competitor price comparison
Set up a price-monitoring check on those products against named competitors
When a competitor undercuts a monitored product, deprioritize or pause the Shopping listing for that product rather than matching the price
Log each event to see how often this protects margin versus losing volume

test.method: Track margin and volume on monitored products through competitor price-cut events, with and without the deprioritize response.
test.measure: gross_margin on affected products during competitor price events

title: Treat Google's 'limited by budget' flag as a signal to check, not proof to act on
hypothesis: If a campaign flagged 'limited by budget' is checked against margin and competitive-saturation evidence before its budget is raised, then a near-universal flag does not get treated as guaranteed unspent profit.

signal.check: A budget increase is being planned or was made based only on the 'limited by budget' flag, with no separate profitability or saturation check.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a verification step, not a measured lift

risk.note: A verification step before a spend decision; no live change on its own.

prerequisites: Margin data per product or campaign, and visibility into competitive saturation (Auction Insights or equivalent)
steps: Note which campaigns are flagged 'limited by budget'
Before raising budget on the strength of the flag alone, check profitability at the current margin
Check competitive saturation via Auction Insights or an equivalent signal
Only raise the budget if the flag is confirmed by real profitable headroom, not the flag by itself

test.method: Track outcomes of budget increases made with and without the added verification step.
test.measure: incremental profit per budget increase, flagged vs verified
test.read_point: 30 to 60 days after each budget increase

title: Offer new affiliates a guaranteed floor or commission tied to a fixed deliverable
hypothesis: If new affiliates are offered a guaranteed monthly floor or a commission rate, whichever is higher, tied to a fixed daily content deliverable, then a creator with no track record has no downside risk to start, and the brand moves them to commission-only once a viral hit clears the floor on its own.

signal.check: New affiliate or creator recruitment offers only a flat per-video fee or commission-only with no floor, discouraging creators with no prior track record from committing.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a recruitment-offer structure, not a measured lift

risk.note: Requires cash flow to cover the floor payments before commission-only creators cover their own cost.

prerequisites: Budget for floor payments to new affiliates
A fixed content deliverable to require in exchange
steps: Set a guaranteed monthly floor payment and a commission rate, paying whichever is higher
Require a fixed daily or monthly content deliverable in exchange for the floor
Track each creator's commission against the floor threshold
Move a creator to commission-only once their commission from a viral piece clears the floor

test.method: Track the share of new affiliates who convert to commission-only and their sustained output after the offer.
test.read_point: One quarter after offering the structure

title: Cut a failed launch price quickly and refund the difference to early buyers
hypothesis: If a launch priced too high is repriced down within days or weeks once weak sell-through is clear, and the price difference is refunded to customers who already bought at the higher price, then demand can be unlocked without eroding trust with the very first customers who took a chance on the brand.

signal.check: A new product launches at a price with weak day-one conversion and no reviews or track record to support it, and the price is either defended too long or cut with no refund to early buyers.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a repricing and trust practice, not a measured lift

risk.note: Pair any repricing-down move with its own margin plan (bundling, upsell, volume); repricing without a margin plan just trades revenue for volume.

prerequisites: The ability to identify and refund early buyers at the original higher price
steps: Confirm weak day-one conversion is a pricing issue, not a product or awareness issue, before repricing
Cut the price to a level the market actually supports
Identify every customer who bought at the original higher price and refund them the difference
Hold the new price and double down on the channel already driving traffic rather than re-testing further

test.method: Track sell-through and customer sentiment before and after the reprice, including reaction to the refund.

title: Maintain a library of recurring UGC content formats instead of one-off briefs
hypothesis: If creators work from a maintained library of recurring content formats, such as street interviews, family reaction videos and voiceover-led hooks, rather than a fresh one-off brief each time, then production scales faster because creators know the shape of what to make without reinventing it every round.

signal.check: Every new creator brief starts from scratch with no reference to a maintained set of proven, repeatable content formats.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a production-efficiency practice, not a measured lift

risk.note: A production-process addition; the library should be refreshed as formats fatigue.

prerequisites: A record of past content formats that have worked
steps: List the recurring content formats that have worked (interview-style, reaction videos, voiceover hooks, and similar)
Document each format's structure so a new creator can follow it without a full custom brief
Brief new creators from the library first, reserving custom briefs for genuinely new concepts
Retire formats from the library once they consistently underperform

test.method: Track content output volume per week before and after adopting a maintained format library.

title: Feed proven hooks into an AI tool to generate a batch of new variations
hypothesis: If hooks that are already proven to work are fed into an AI tool to generate a large batch of new variations, then creator meetings and creative production start from a wide set of testable candidates instead of a handful of hand-written options.

signal.check: New hook ideas are generated only by hand, one at a time, with no use of AI to expand a proven hook into many testable variations.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a generation method, not a measured lift

risk.note: Treat AI-generated hooks as testing material, not finished claims; verify every variation for accuracy before it ships.

prerequisites: At least one proven, currently working hook
Access to an AI text-generation tool
steps: Identify a hook that is already proven to convert
Feed it into an AI tool with instructions to generate a large batch of variations
Bring the batch into creator or creative review meetings as testing material
Track which AI-suggested variations actually convert and recycle winners into the next round

test.method: Track hit rate of AI-generated hook variations against hand-written hooks.

title: Repurpose one content asset across every channel and pay on where it converts
hypothesis: If one piece of content is originated once and tested across every channel, with creator commission paid based on whichever channel it actually converts on, then production effort is not duplicated per channel, and payment reflects real performance instead of the channel it happened to be made for.

signal.check: Content is produced separately and channel-specifically, with no process to test the same asset across multiple channels and attribute commission to wherever it converts.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a repurposing practice, not a measured lift

risk.note: Requires the ability to track and attribute conversion by channel for the same underlying asset.

prerequisites: A content asset produced for one channel
Cross-channel posting and tracking capability
steps: Originate a piece of content on its most natural channel
Repost or adapt the same asset for other channels rather than producing new content per channel
Track which channel the asset actually converts on
Pay creator commission based on the converting channel, not the origin channel

test.method: Track cost per usable asset and per-channel conversion for repurposed content versus channel-specific production.
test.read_point: One quarter after adopting the practice

title: Promote proven creators into a small-salary recruiter and coaching role
hypothesis: If top-performing creators are promoted into a paid recruiter and coaching role, on top of their existing commission, then peer-to-peer recruiting pitches land better than founder outreach, and the creator network can expand without adding founder time to every call.

signal.check: All new creator recruitment and coaching runs through the founder or a small internal team, with no proven creators promoted into a paid role to help recruit and coach.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a role-design practice, not a measured lift

risk.note: Requires identifying creators who are both high-performing and genuinely persuasive with peers, not just prolific.

prerequisites: A pool of proven top-performing creators
Budget for a small base salary in addition to existing commission
steps: Identify top-performing creators willing to take on a recruiting and coaching role
Offer a small base salary in addition to their existing commission
Have them lead outreach calls and onboarding coaching for new creators
Track network growth rate and new-creator retention under peer-led recruiting versus founder-led recruiting

test.method: Compare creator network growth rate and new-creator retention under peer-led versus founder-led recruiting.
test.read_point: One quarter after promoting the first recruiter

title: Deliberately hold back in-stock SKUs from selling out completely
hypothesis: If in-stock SKUs are deliberately marked unavailable before they fully sell out during a demand spike, then future months' ad performance and email sends are protected from the multi-month cost of a total sell-out resetting the ad account's learning phase.

signal.check: A high-demand period is allowed to sell a SKU completely out with no deliberate hold-back, risking a reset of ad-account learning and a gap in future sends.

expected_effect.size: unknown; the source frames a full sell-out as a multi-month cost, not a one-time reset

risk.note: A deliberate revenue trade-off during peak demand; requires real-time inventory visibility to execute in time.

prerequisites: Real-time inventory visibility during a demand spike
steps: Monitor inventory levels closely during any known high-demand event
Set a threshold at which the SKU is marked unavailable before it fully sells through
Communicate the decision internally so paid, email and SMS teams do not keep driving traffic to a soon-to-be-empty SKU
Track ad-account performance and email send continuity through the following months against a period where the SKU was allowed to fully sell out

test.method: Compare ad-account performance and email send continuity in the months following a protected hold-back versus a full sell-out.
test.read_point: Two to five months after the demand spike

title: Pitch prospective creators on vision and their own growth path, not a flat fee
hypothesis: If a founder or proven creator pitches a prospective creator on the brand's ambition and the creator's own potential path, instead of a generic flat-fee-per-video ask, then recruitment converts better because the creator sees a relationship, not a one-off transaction.

signal.check: Creator outreach uses a generic flat-fee, transactional pitch ('$X for a video') with no framing of the brand's vision or the creator's own growth potential.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a pitch-framing change, not a measured lift

risk.note: A recruitment-conversation framing change; no cost.

prerequisites: A founder or proven creator able to speak credibly about the brand's ambition
steps: Replace the generic flat-fee outreach message with a call framed around the brand's vision
Have the founder or a proven creator explain the creator's own potential path within the program
Track signup and activation rate for vision-led pitches against generic transactional outreach
Use a proven creator to deliver this pitch once one exists, since peer credibility lands better

test.method: Compare creator signup and activation rate for vision-led pitches against generic flat-fee outreach.

title: Share real internal metrics with top creators the way you would with staff
hypothesis: If top creators are given real visibility into stock levels, revenue projections and which specific ads are winning or losing, the way an employee would see them, then the relationship reads as a genuine partnership instead of a transactional arrangement, and creators can make better content decisions with real information.

signal.check: Top creator relationships are kept purely transactional, with no visibility into internal metrics like stock levels, revenue projections or which content is actually performing.

expected_effect.size: unknown; requires trust and tolerance for internal numbers reaching outside the company

risk.note: Requires a real tolerance for internal numbers being shared outside the company; reserve for a small, trusted top tier.

prerequisites: A defined top tier of trusted creators
Internal metrics that can be shared safely
steps: Identify a small, trusted top tier of creators for this level of transparency
Share relevant stock levels, revenue projections and specific ad performance data with them regularly
Check whether creators can answer basic brand questions the way an employee could, as a sign the transparency is landing
Track retention and output of this top tier against creators without this level of access

test.method: Compare retention and content output of top creators given internal visibility against those without it.
test.read_point: Two quarters after adopting the practice

title: Classify low-repeat categories and manage them on first-purchase profit alone
hypothesis: If a low-repeat category, such as furniture or homewares, is classified as having near-zero lifetime gross-profit lift, and the business is managed on first-purchase gross profit with a deliberately flat, stable CAC instead of a retention program, then effort is not wasted chasing a repeat-purchase number the category structurally cannot produce.

signal.check: A retention program is being built or funded for a category where customers structurally buy once and rarely again within any realistic window, with no check on whether the category can support meaningful lifetime gross-profit lift.

expected_effect.size: day-365 gross-profit lift benchmarks vary sharply by category, near 0 percent for infrequent-purchase categories per the source's own cited figures

risk.note: This does not mean skip flows or good service; it means not expecting a retention program to move a category-bound lifetime value number.

prerequisites: Historical repeat-purchase data or a reasonable category-based estimate of repurchase frequency
steps: Check the category's realistic repeat-purchase rate and day-365 gross-profit lift, using your own data or comparable category benchmarks
If lift is near zero, manage the business on first-purchase gross profit with a deliberately flat, controlled CAC
Reserve retention-program investment for categories with genuine, demonstrated repeat behavior
Re-classify the category if a genuine repeat behavior later emerges (a new consumable line, a subscription add-on)

test.method: Track whether retention-program spend in a low-repeat category produces any measurable lifetime-value lift.
test.read_point: One year of tracking before continuing or cutting the program

title: Screen out debt or investor funding for acquisition losses below a scale and experience bar
hypothesis: If taking on debt or investor capital specifically to fund a negative LTGP:CAC is screened against the founder's prior scale experience and the business's current revenue level, then a first-time operator at a modest revenue stage does not take on financing risk that the source's own experience says rarely goes well at that stage.

signal.check: A brand with a negative LTGP:CAC is considering debt or investor capital to fund acquisition losses with no explicit screen on the founder's prior experience or the business's revenue stage.

expected_effect.size: unknown; one operator's own stated policy, not a universal rule

risk.note: None of the funding routes fix a structurally negative ratio; they only buy time to fix the underlying LTGP:CAC, and this screen is a risk-management opinion, not a guarantee of outcome either way.

prerequisites: Current LTGP:CAC, revenue level and founder's prior scaling experience
steps: Confirm the LTGP:CAC is actually negative before considering financing to cover it
Check the founder's or leadership team's prior experience scaling a business of this or larger size
Weigh taking on debt or investor capital against this experience and revenue-stage screen, not just the immediate cash need
If the screen fails, prioritize fixing the underlying ratio before seeking financing

test.method: Track outcomes of financing decisions made with and without applying the experience-and-scale screen.
test.read_point: Reviewed at each major financing decision

title: Scope existing-customer retargeting to owned-channel-unreachable segments
hypothesis: If any existing-customer ad spend is scoped to a narrow segment owned channels can no longer reach, such as purchased-and-unsubscribed customers, rather than the whole existing-customer pool, then the spend targets the one slice of existing customers where paid could plausibly be incremental.

signal.check: Existing-customer retargeting spend targets the entire past-purchaser list rather than a narrow segment specifically chosen because owned channels can no longer reach them.

expected_effect.size: unknown; even this narrower segment should still be tested, not assumed incremental

risk.note: Even a narrow, seemingly smart segment should be tested for incrementality, not assumed to work.

prerequisites: A defined existing-customer segment unreachable by email or SMS (such as unsubscribed past purchasers)
steps: Identify the narrow existing-customer segment your owned channels can no longer reach
Scope any existing-customer ad spend to that segment only, not the full past-purchaser list
Run a lift or holdout test on the segment before assuming it is incremental
Cut the spend if the test shows no real incremental lift

test.method: Run a conversion-lift test on the narrow segment to confirm real incrementality.

title: Test incrementality before retargeting an unconverted organic follower pool
hypothesis: If retargeting spend aimed at a brand's own high-intent, unconverted organic followers is tested for incrementality rather than assumed to work, then a short-term high ROAS that will dry up once that finite pool converts is not mistaken for a durable acquisition channel.

signal.check: Paid spend is aimed at a brand's own organic followers who have not yet purchased, producing a strong short-term ROAS with no incrementality test to confirm the spend is actually causing the conversions.

expected_effect.size: unknown; this pool is finite and the resulting ROAS is expected to decline once it converts

risk.note: Treat this similarly to existing-customer retargeting: plausibly more incremental than cold traffic, but still a finite pool, not a scalable channel.

prerequisites: A defined organic follower audience that has not yet purchased
Ability to run a lift or holdout test
steps: Identify the organic follower segment being retargeted with paid spend
Run a lift or holdout test to check real incrementality rather than trusting reported ROAS
Track how the pool size and resulting ROAS trend as more of the segment converts
Plan for the channel's ROAS to decline as the finite pool is exhausted, rather than treating it as durable

test.method: Track ROAS and remaining pool size for this segment over successive months.
test.read_point: Monthly, until the pool is substantially converted

title: Optimize for the lowest profitable ROAS you can acquire at
hypothesis: If a team deliberately targets the lowest ROAS or CPA it can still acquire profitably at, rather than chasing the highest reported ROAS, then it captures more total volume and profit instead of over-optimizing toward a small, already-converting audience that inflates the number.

signal.check: Campaign optimization targets the highest achievable ROAS, favoring a small, already-warm audience over the larger volume available at a lower but still profitable ROAS.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a targeting-philosophy reversal, not a measured lift

risk.note: Requires a clear, confirmed profitability floor (the lowest ROAS or CPA that is still profitable) to target against.

prerequisites: A confirmed break-even ROAS or CPA to use as the profitability floor
steps: Calculate the break-even ROAS or CPA the brand can still profit at
Set campaign targets at that floor rather than the highest achievable number
Track total profitable volume captured at the lower target versus the prior higher-ROAS target
Adjust the floor as margin or CAC conditions change

test.method: Compare total profitable volume and revenue captured under a lowest-profitable-ROAS target versus a highest-ROAS target.
test.read_point: One quarter after the targeting change

title: Check for organic repeat purchase before rebuilding flows to fix retention
hypothesis: If a genuine baseline of unprompted repeat purchase is confirmed before rebuilding email flows to fix a retention problem, then a business with near-zero organic repeat purchase is not sent to an email agency for a flows rebuild that cannot create a habit the product itself has not earned.

signal.check: A brand with a perceived retention problem moves straight to rebuilding email flows, with no check on whether any customers currently return on their own without marketing prompts.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a diagnostic check, not a measured lift

risk.note: If the organic baseline is genuinely absent, treat retention as a product or business-model problem before investing further in flows.
