prerequisites: Repeat-purchase data that can be isolated from flow-attributed revenue
steps: Pull repeat-purchase rate excluding any flow or campaign attribution
Check whether a meaningful share of customers return on their own with no marketing prompt
If a real baseline exists, proceed with a flows rebuild to amplify it
If the baseline is near zero, treat the problem as product or experience-driven before investing in flows

test.method: Track whether a flows rebuild moves repeat purchase when a genuine organic baseline was confirmed present versus absent.
test.measure: repeat_rate_90d after the flows rebuild, by baseline presence

title: Prioritize usage-education content over upsells in post-purchase flows
hypothesis: If post-purchase flows for a complex or instruction-dependent product lead with usage-education content, such as how and when to use it, before any upsell or cross-sell, then the customer experience the flow could have improved is not skipped in favor of an immediate additional ask.

signal.check: Post-purchase flows for a complex or instruction-dependent product go straight to an upsell or cross-sell with no usage-education content first.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a flow-sequencing fix, not a measured lift

risk.note: Applies specifically to products that require explanation of how or when to use them; simpler products may not need this step.

prerequisites: Existing post-purchase flow content to review and resequence
steps: Identify products complex or instruction-dependent enough to need usage explanation
Add or move usage-education content to the front of the post-purchase flow
Move upsell or cross-sell content later in the sequence, after the education content
Track repeat purchase and support-ticket volume before and after resequencing

test.method: Compare repeat_rate_90d and support ticket volume before and after resequencing the flow.

title: Generate repositioning angles with an LLM run on two different models
hypothesis: If the same creative-director prompt for generating repositioning angles is run on two different LLMs using their reasoning modes, then the idea pool roughly doubles because different models return meaningfully different angles from the same product context.

signal.check: New repositioning or persona angles are generated from a single LLM or a single prompt run, with no comparison across models to widen the idea pool.

expected_effect.size: unknown; one narrator's own workflow, not a measured lift

risk.note: Requires access to more than one capable LLM; verify which current models offer a reasoning or 'thinking' mode before relying on model names.

prerequisites: Access to at least two different LLMs
The product's name and website or key benefit information to give as context
steps: Write a prompt asking the model to act as a creative director generating distinct repositioning angles for the product
Require each angle to include the target audience, a hook, and the underlying logic
Run the identical prompt on two different LLMs using their reasoning or 'thinking' mode
Combine both outputs into one angle pool before filtering for brand fit

test.method: Track the number of genuinely distinct, usable angles produced from two models versus one.
test.measure: other:angle_pool_size from single vs dual-model runs

title: Filter out an off-brand or compliance-risky angle before it dominates output
hypothesis: If an LLM-suggested angle that keeps recurring across generated concepts is checked for brand fit and compliance risk, and removed from the prompt when it fails that check, then a single risky or irrelevant theme does not quietly dominate the brand's creative pipeline just because a model keeps suggesting it.

signal.check: An LLM-assisted angle-generation process keeps surfacing the same theme across most outputs, and that theme is used without checking whether it is actually on-brand or compliance-safe for the category.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a governance step, not a measured lift

risk.note: Particularly important in regulated or compliance-sensitive categories, where an appealing but risky recurring theme (such as a prescription-drug-adjacent claim) needs explicit review.

prerequisites: A defined brand-fit and compliance checklist to screen recurring angle themes against
steps: Review generated angle outputs for any theme that recurs across most or all of them
Check that recurring theme against brand fit and compliance guidelines
If it fails the check, explicitly exclude it from the prompt and re-run angle generation
Document why the theme was excluded so future runs do not reintroduce it unreviewed

test.method: Track how often a re-run after filtering still surfaces the excluded theme.

title: Choose SKU repositioning over a new launch to protect cash and inventory
hypothesis: If a broad enough product is repositioned to new personas instead of launching a new SKU, then cash stays out of unsold new-launch inventory and the operational load of a new item (3PL, international complexity) is avoided while spend growth continues on the existing product.

signal.check: A brand is considering a new product launch to open more ad spend capacity, without weighing whether repositioning the existing hero SKU to new personas could achieve the same goal at lower cash and inventory risk.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a build-vs-launch decision framework, not a measured lift

risk.note: Best suited to multi-benefit products broad enough to carry several distinct angles; large-assortment categories (fashion, furniture) may get more value from SKU rotation instead.

prerequisites: A hero SKU broad enough in benefit to support multiple distinct personas or angles
steps: Before committing to a new product launch, check whether the existing hero SKU could instead be repositioned to a new persona
Map the product's genuine benefit pillars to confirm it can credibly support more than one angle
Choose repositioning when cash and inventory risk from a new launch outweighs the benefit of a new SKU
Reserve new launches or SKU rotation for categories that naturally reward catalogue variety

test.method: Track cash and inventory outcomes for a repositioning decision against a comparable new-launch decision.

title: Apply the 1-to-1 rule when cutting fixed OpEx, not marketing spend
hypothesis: If a cash shortfall is addressed by cutting fixed OpEx (staff, software, rent) rather than variable marketing spend, then the cut moves net income and net cash roughly 1-to-1, instead of a marketing cut that also reduces revenue and COGS and can produce a smaller, sometimes negative, net cash effect.

signal.check: A cash-tightening decision defaults to cutting marketing spend, treating it as equivalent to a fixed-cost cut for improving cash position.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a modeled accounting distinction, not measured on a real brand

risk.note: Applies to genuinely fixed costs only; a marketing cut still has its place, just not as a 1-to-1 cash lever.

prerequisites: A cost structure that separates fixed OpEx from variable marketing spend
steps: Before cutting spend to protect cash, classify the candidate cut as fixed or variable
For fixed OpEx (staff, software, rent), expect the cut to move net cash close to 1-to-1
For variable marketing spend, model the resulting revenue and COGS drop before assuming the same 1-to-1 cash benefit
Audit fixed OpEx first for costs added during a past revenue peak and never resized down

test.method: Compare actual net cash change against the modeled 1-to-1 expectation for a fixed-cost cut.
test.measure: other:cash_per_dollar_cut for fixed vs variable cuts

title: Raise maintained markup specifically to release cash from inventory
hypothesis: If maintained markup is raised through supplier negotiation and measured price increases, and the resulting lower inventory requirement is treated as the real prize, then the cash freed by needing less stock to serve the same revenue is captured deliberately instead of the margin gain alone.

signal.check: A markup or price increase is evaluated only for its P&L margin impact, with no check on how much less inventory is now required to serve the same revenue.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a modeled mechanism, not measured on a real brand

risk.note: Check demand elasticity before raising price, so volume does not collapse and offset the markup gain.

prerequisites: Current landed cost, pricing, and inventory-turn data by SKU
steps: Negotiate landed cost with suppliers where possible
Make measured, elasticity-checked on-site price increases
Recompute the inventory required to serve the same revenue at the new margin
Redeploy the freed cash into marketing or the next purchase order rather than leaving it in stock

test.method: Compare inventory required and ending cash before and after the markup change.
test.read_point: One to two inventory cycles after the change

title: Size the next purchase order from actual sell-through, not forecast
hypothesis: If the next inventory purchase order is sized from actual 30-day sell-through rate and real lead time, after cutting SKUs with weak sell-through and poor markup, then cash trapped in slow inventory is released instead of being reinvested into buying more of what already isn't moving.

signal.check: Purchase order sizing is based on optimistic revenue forecasts rather than each SKU's actual recent sell-through rate and real supplier lead time.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a purchasing discipline, not a measured lift

risk.note: Recalculate open-to-buy after every range decision so freed cash is redeployed deliberately, not left idle.

prerequisites: Per-SKU sell-through data over a fixed window and known supplier lead times
steps: Calculate sell-through per SKU over a fixed window (such as 30 days) as units sold divided by units available
Cut or reduce reorder on SKUs with weak sell-through, prioritizing those with poor markup too
Size the next purchase order from actual sell-through and real lead time, not an optimistic forecast
Recalculate open-to-buy after every range decision

test.method: Track days_of_stock and cash released from inventory after adopting sell-through-based purchasing.

title: Audit trending or bestseller badges against real demand, not rank alone
hypothesis: If a trending or bestseller badge is checked against repeat-purchase rate, direct search volume and support-request volume before it is published, then the badge reflects real independent demand instead of a velocity or rank number that shoppers copying other shoppers can produce on its own.

signal.check: A trending, bestseller or 'most loved' badge is shown on a PDP or collection page based only on sales rank or velocity, with no check against independent demand signals.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a verification step, not a measured lift

risk.note: A copy and merchandising audit; no live change beyond removing or keeping an existing badge.

prerequisites: Repeat-purchase, search-volume and support-ticket data by SKU
steps: List every SKU currently carrying a trending or bestseller badge
Check repeat-purchase rate, direct search volume and support-request volume for each
Keep the badge where independent demand signals confirm it
Remove or soften the badge where the ranking looks driven mainly by rank or velocity alone

test.method: Track badge accuracy against independent demand signals on a schedule.
test.measure: share of badges confirmed by independent demand data

title: Concentrate proof and authority cues on the ambiguous funnel steps
hypothesis: If social proof and authority cues are concentrated on cold, unfamiliar-category traffic and ambiguous funnel steps, and reduced on high-intent branded search, then proof does the work where uncertainty is real instead of cluttering a step where the buyer has already decided.

signal.check: The same density of reviews, badges and authority cues appears on every funnel step regardless of whether the traffic is cold and uncertain or high-intent branded search.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a placement change, not a measured lift

risk.note: A page-layout and content-placement change; reversible.

prerequisites: Traffic-source segmentation by certainty level (cold vs branded/high-intent)
steps: Segment landing experiences by traffic certainty: cold or unfamiliar-category vs branded or high-intent
Increase the density and visibility of proof and authority cues on the cold, ambiguous paths
Trim or simplify proof cues on the high-intent branded path where the buyer has largely already decided
Track conversion rate separately for each segment after the change

test.method: Compare conversion rate on cold vs high-intent traffic before and after concentrating proof on the ambiguous steps.
test.read_point: One test cycle after the change

title: Audit your own checkout and pricing flow for lowball-shaped patterns
hypothesis: If your own checkout, pricing and gift-with-purchase copy is read and asked whether it would survive being named out loud for what it is, then a hidden fee, a shrinking discount, or a manufactured concession is fixed before a customer discovers it themselves.

signal.check: No one has recently checked whether a favorable price, gift or advantage shown early in the funnel survives unchanged through to checkout.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a self-audit, not a measured lift

risk.note: A copy and pricing-flow review; fixing a found issue is a real change and should be treated as its own project.

prerequisites: Full visibility into the checkout flow from landing offer through final charge
steps: Walk the funnel end to end as a new customer would, from the first offer to the final charge
Note any price, gift or advantage that shrinks, disappears, or gets a fee attached before checkout completes
Ask whether each one would survive being described out loud to the customer for what it is
Fix any pattern that would not survive that description
Repeat the audit whenever pricing, shipping fees or offer copy changes

test.method: Re-run the walkthrough after any pricing or offer change and count issues found.
test.read_point: At every pricing or offer change, and quarterly otherwise

title: Run a would-we-greenlight-it-again gut check in every launch post-mortem
hypothesis: If every launch, channel or influencer-bet post-mortem starts with 'knowing what we now know, would we make this call again,' read before the group's rationalizations arrive, then a genuinely bad bet is caught instead of defended because money or reputation is already committed to it.

signal.check: A launch, channel or influencer bet is being continued or expanded in a post-mortem without first asking whether the team would choose it again knowing what they know now.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a decision-process change, not a measured lift

risk.note: A meeting-process change; no cost.

prerequisites: A scheduled post-mortem or review for the launch, channel or bet in question
steps: Open every launch or channel post-mortem with the time-travel question, before discussing next steps
Ask each stakeholder to answer individually first, in writing, before group discussion
Compare the individual answers to the group's eventual recommendation
Flag any gap between a private 'no' and a public decision to continue

test.method: Track how often the private gut-check answer diverges from the eventual team decision.
test.measure: share of post-mortems where the gut check changed the recommendation

title: Resolve a genuine customer concern before presenting a paid add-on
hypothesis: If a real, verifiable concern (an honest sizing note, a true 'runs small' flag) is resolved for the customer before a complementary paid add-on is offered, then the add-on is presented at the exact moment credibility is highest, instead of competing with an unresolved doubt.

signal.check: Upsell or cross-sell offers are shown without first addressing a known, real point of buyer hesitation for that product.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a sequencing change, not a measured lift

risk.note: A PDP or post-add-to-cart content change; requires an honest, real concern to resolve, not an invented one.

prerequisites: A known, real customer concern for the product (sizing, fit, compatibility, durability)
steps: Identify the single most common real concern customers have about the product, from reviews or support tickets
Address that concern honestly and specifically right before or alongside the add-to-cart step
Present the complementary paid add-on immediately after the concern is resolved, while trust is highest
Track add-on take rate before and after adding the honest resolution step

test.method: Compare add-on take rate with and without the honest concern-resolution step placed first.

title: Send bad-news transactional messages through a distinct identity from marketing
hypothesis: If delayed-shipment, backorder and price-increase notices go out under a distinct sending identity or template from best-news marketing sends, without hiding the brand's own responsibility, then the marketing sender identity does not become associated with disappointment every time something goes wrong.

signal.check: Delay, backorder or price-change notices go out from the same sender name and template as promotional marketing email, with no separation.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a routing and template change, not a measured lift

risk.note: An email and SMS template and sender-identity change; must still disclose the brand's real responsibility for the issue.

prerequisites: Separate email or SMS templates or sender profiles available for transactional vs marketing sends
steps: Identify every 'bad news' transactional message type: delays, backorders, price increases, quality issues
Build or assign a distinct sender identity or template for these, separate from promotional sends
Keep the brand's own responsibility for the issue clearly and honestly stated, not hidden behind the separate identity
Track open rate and unsubscribe rate on marketing sends before and after separating the two

test.method: Compare marketing-send engagement and unsubscribe rate before and after separating bad-news messages.
test.measure: email_click_rate and unsubscribe rate on marketing sends

title: Show a real live concurrent-shopper or cart count instead of a countdown
hypothesis: If a genuine, system-generated count of how many people currently have an item in their cart or are viewing it replaces a manufactured urgency countdown, then the page keeps the same social-proof-plus-scarcity effect without a claim that could be shown to be false.

signal.check: A PDP uses a countdown timer or 'X left' claim that is not tied to real, live inventory or session data.

expected_effect.size: unknown; an honest-signal swap, not a measured lift

risk.note: Requires a real data feed (live sessions or cart adds); must never fall back to a fabricated number when traffic is low.

prerequisites: Live session or cart data that can be surfaced accurately
Engineering time to build the real-time display
steps: Confirm the platform can generate a real, live count of concurrent viewers or cart-holders for a given SKU
Replace any countdown or 'X left' claim not backed by real data with this live count
Suppress the display entirely when the real count is too low to be meaningful, rather than inventing a number
Track conversion rate on SKUs with the real live count versus the prior manufactured claim

test.method: A or B test the honest live count against the prior countdown or static claim.

title: Test whether value holds after a disclosed introductory incentive ends
hypothesis: If usage, engagement or repeat purchase is measured after a disclosed introductory discount or incentive expires, then the brand learns whether the product itself is holding the customer, or only the incentive was, before scaling the acquisition offer further.

signal.check: A welcome discount, trial price or introductory incentive is used at scale to acquire customers with no tracked read on retention after it ends.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a measurement addition, not a guaranteed lift

risk.note: A cohort-tracking exercise; no live change to the incentive itself.

prerequisites: Cohort tracking that can separate customers by acquisition offer and follow them past the incentive's end date
steps: Tag customers acquired via the introductory incentive as their own cohort
Track repeat purchase, engagement or subscription retention for that cohort past the incentive's end date
Compare against a cohort acquired without the incentive, if one exists
If retention drops sharply once the incentive ends, treat that as a signal the offer is buying trial, not loyalty

test.method: Compare 90-day repeat rate or churn for incentive-acquired cohorts against non-incentive cohorts.

title: Build a genuine back-in-stock waitlist instead of a fake 'almost sold out' claim
hypothesis: If a real stockout is met with a genuine back-in-stock waitlist that states true availability and lets the customer opt in to be notified, then the same urgency and anticipation the source documents is earned honestly, with no fabricated scarcity claim to be caught out on.

signal.check: A product page shows 'almost sold out' or similar urgency language that is not tied to a real, current stock count.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a genuine-scarcity replacement, not a measured lift

risk.note: Requires accurate, real-time inventory data; must not claim a wait or urgency that stock data does not support.

prerequisites: Real-time inventory data
A waitlist or back-in-stock notification mechanism
steps: Confirm real-time stock data is accurate for the SKUs in question
Replace any unverified urgency claim with the true stock count or an honest out-of-stock state
Add a back-in-stock waitlist opt-in for out-of-stock SKUs
Notify waitlisted customers promptly and honestly when stock actually returns

test.method: Track waitlist signup rate and conversion once restocked, versus the prior unverified urgency claim.
test.measure: other:waitlist_signups and conversion rate on restock

title: Price flat creator fees from your own Meta CPM, not a rate card
hypothesis: If a creator's flat fee is set from your own recent Meta CPM and the creator's trailing view average, discounted for audience mismatch, then the price paid tracks what the impressions are actually worth to you instead of a generic follower-count rate card.

signal.check: Creator fees are negotiated from follower count or an external rate card, with no reference to the brand's own CPM or the creator's actual delivered views.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a pricing method, not a measured lift

risk.note: A negotiation and budgeting method; no live spend change beyond how existing creator budget is allocated.

prerequisites: A recent, representative Meta CPM figure
The creator's trailing 10-video average view count
steps: Pull a recent, representative Meta CPM for the brand
Set a target creator CPM at roughly half that figure as a starting point
Pull the creator's trailing 10-video average views, not follower count, as the expected impression base
Calculate the maximum flat fee as expected views times target CPM divided by 1,000
Discount the fee proportionally for audience mismatch in geography or demographic skew
Track delivered views per paid post and recompute actual CPM to correct future offers

test.method: Compare actual delivered CPM against the target CPM used to set each creator's fee.
test.read_point: After each paid creator post, reviewed monthly

title: Give creators loose briefs limited to non-negotiables; withhold scripts
hypothesis: If a creator brief states only product facts, legal claim limits, disclosure requirements and logistics, leaving hook, tone, pacing and format to the creator, then the resulting content keeps the native feel that a fully scripted brief tends to flatten.

signal.check: Creator briefs currently include a written script or tightly directed lines for the creator to read, outside a regulated-claims category that requires it.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a briefing-process change, not a measured lift

risk.note: A creative-process change; regulated-claims categories should keep tighter briefs.

prerequisites: A vetted creator pool with genuine product affinity
A written list of non-negotiable claims and disclosure rules
steps: Write the brief with only non-negotiables: product facts, legal claim limits, disclosure rules, logistics
Leave hook, tone, pacing and format entirely to the creator
Review submitted content only for compliance and brand safety, not creative substance
After the campaign, extract themes (not scripts) from what performed for the next round of briefs
Keep tighter, more directed briefs for any regulated-claims category

test.method: Compare hook rate and hold rate on loosely briefed content against previously scripted content.
test.measure: hook_rate on loose-brief vs scripted content

title: Validate a new product or flavor with a structured in-person tasting panel
hypothesis: If a new product or flavor is tested on a structured in-person panel of verified ICP tasters, with answers recorded in a comparable format, then real product signal is captured instead of a small vocal online comment thread that can look like demand and is not.

signal.check: A new flavor or product variant decision is being made from online comment volume or internal opinion, with no structured in-person panel of verified target customers.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a validation-method change, not a measured lift

risk.note: Requires an in-person venue and real target-customer tasters; a small or unrepresentative panel can still mislead.

prerequisites: Access to an in-person event, office or sampling moment
A way to confirm tasters match the actual target customer
steps: Bring multiple candidate variants to an in-person event or sampling moment
Ask direct, structured questions and record answers in a comparable format across sessions
Confirm each taster actually matches the target customer profile before counting their vote
Weight results by ICP fit, not raw comment volume or headcount
Cross-check the panel's favorite against sales and reorder data before scaling production

test.method: Compare panel-predicted winners against actual sell-through and reorder rate after launch.

title: Treat large in-person events as content-production budget, not attendance
hypothesis: If a large in-person event's budget is judged by the reusable digital assets it produces rather than attendance, then a mediocre event that generates strong content counts as a win, and a great event that generates no content is treated as close to a failure.

signal.check: An in-person event's budget and success are judged by headcount or atmosphere, with no shot list or content plan built in before booking the venue.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a budgeting-lens change, not a measured lift

risk.note: Requires bringing cameras and creators to the event; adds production coordination on top of the event itself.

prerequisites: A planned in-person event with enough scale to justify content production
steps: Set the shot list, attending creators and footage needs before booking the venue
Bring cameras and creators so one event produces vertical video, stills and paid-creative assets together
Judge the event primarily by the volume and quality of reusable content produced, not attendance
Distribute the resulting assets across organic, paid, retail decks and investor material afterward

test.method: Track cost per reusable asset produced from the event against the event's total budget.
test.read_point: Within one month of the event

title: Re-earn a retail buyer's shelf space every quarter, not just at signing
hypothesis: If the relationship with a retail buyer is built and re-proven every quarter with the named human buyer, not the account, then shelf space is defended on current performance instead of assumed safe because of what was true when the deal was signed.

signal.check: A retail relationship is managed only at the account level, or performance updates to the buyer stop after the initial deal is signed.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a relationship-management cadence, not a measured lift

risk.note: A relationship-management practice; no cost beyond time.

prerequisites: A named contact at each retail account, and current sell-through data to share
steps: Identify the specific named buyer at each retail account, not just the account name
Bring a fresh, current sell-through or performance update to that buyer every quarter
Treat the relationship as re-earned each quarter, not secured by the original deal
Track shelf-space or door-count changes against the cadence of buyer contact

test.method: Track shelf-space retention and expansion against the frequency of buyer touchpoints.

title: Generate visible local demand in a buyer's city before pitching retail
hypothesis: If visible social proof and targeted ads or creators are run in a target retail buyer's own city before the pitch, then the buyer initiates contact on their own instead of the brand cold-pitching with no local evidence of demand.

signal.check: A retail pitch is being prepared with no prior local demand-generation activity in the target buyer's city or region.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a tactic the source itself flags as needing re-verification for current ad targeting rules

risk.note: Requires budget and lead time; geo-targeting capability and disclosure norms should be re-checked before use.

prerequisites: Budget for a short, geo-targeted local campaign
A specific target retail buyer and city identified
steps: Identify the specific retail buyer and city being targeted
Run a short window of geo-targeted ads or local creator content in that city
Build visible social proof (reviews, local press, local creator content) ahead of any outreach
Let the resulting local buzz reach the buyer before a formal pitch is sent
Never disclose the tactic to the buyer once contact is made

test.method: Track whether buyer-initiated inquiries increase in cities that received the local demand-generation push.
test.read_point: One campaign cycle before a planned pitch

title: Segment retention effort by existing routine fit, not by customer age
hypothesis: If retention and subscription push is weighted toward customers who already practice a similar routine, rather than the youngest available audience, then subscription offers are aimed at the segment most likely to stick regardless of offer strength.

signal.check: Subscription and retention offers are targeted primarily by age or a broad demographic, with no check on whether the customer already has a matching routine.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a targeting change, not a measured lift on a real brand

risk.note: A targeting and segmentation change for retention campaigns; reversible.

prerequisites: A way to identify or infer existing routine behavior in customer data or survey responses
steps: Identify a proxy for existing routine fit (frequency of related purchases, survey response, category history)
Weight subscription and retention offers toward customers who show that routine fit
Test whether the youngest segment converts to subscription at a lower rate regardless of offer depth
Reallocate retention spend away from segments that decline subscription broadly

test.method: Compare subscription conversion and churn by routine-fit segment versus by age segment.
test.read_point: One quarter after resegmenting retention targeting

title: Plan for entry-product decline and migrate customers to newer products
hypothesis: If the original entry product is expected to decline as the portfolio grows, and customers are deliberately migrated to newer products through email, bundles and merchandising, then the brand does not waste effort trying to hold every customer on a product whose category attention has moved on.

signal.check: The original hero or entry product is declining in sales with no deliberate migration plan moving its existing customers toward newer products.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a migration strategy, not a measured lift

risk.note: A merchandising and lifecycle-email change; reversible.

prerequisites: A multi-product portfolio with at least one newer product to migrate customers toward
steps: Identify the declining entry product and the newer product best suited to replace it for existing customers
Build a migration flow (email, bundle offer, PDP cross-sell) that introduces the newer product to entry-product customers
Track how many entry-product customers convert to the newer product instead of churning entirely
Accept the entry product's decline rather than over-investing to defend it

test.method: Track the share of entry-product customers who migrate to a newer product versus churn.
test.measure: share of migrated customers vs churned customers from the declining SKU
test.read_point: Two quarters after launching the migration flow

title: Screen every hire with a repeatable taste-fit question
hypothesis: If every candidate, from executive assistant to brand team, is asked to name three brands they love and why, paired with a short industry conversation, then cultural and taste fit is screened consistently across roles instead of being judged informally or skipped.

signal.check: Hiring interviews have no consistent, repeatable question used across roles to screen for cultural or taste fit with the brand.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a screening-process addition, not a measured lift

risk.note: An interview-process addition; no cost.

prerequisites: A defined hiring process with room for one added standard question
steps: Add 'name three brands you love and why' as a standard question in every interview, across roles
Pair it with a short conversation about the industry or category
Score answers for genuine taste and reasoning, not brand-name recognition alone
Track how the answer correlates with later performance or culture fit for hired candidates

test.method: Track post-hire performance or retention against the taste-fit screening score.

title: Own the marketplace seller-of-record relationship on consumables
hypothesis: If a consumable brand sells directly to the marketplace as the seller of record rather than through a third-party reseller, then counterfeit and diversion risk on that SKU is reduced because the brand controls the listing and supply chain directly.

signal.check: A consumable product is sold on a marketplace through a third-party reseller rather than the brand's own seller account.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a channel-control change, not a measured lift

risk.note: May require new marketplace seller onboarding and logistics; changes existing reseller relationships.

prerequisites: Eligibility to register as a direct seller on the relevant marketplace
steps: Register or transition to a direct seller-of-record account on the marketplace for the consumable SKU
Audit current listings for third-party or unauthorized resellers
Report and pursue removal of unauthorized listings once selling directly
Track counterfeit or diversion complaints before and after the transition

test.method: Track counterfeit and diversion complaint volume before and after becoming the direct seller of record.

title: Build a paid-social creative pool from top organic creator posts
hypothesis: If top-performing organic creator content is flagged and amplified as paid creative instead of commissioning new agency scripts from scratch, then paid creative keeps the native look that performs, and the account builds a tested creative bank faster.

signal.check: Paid creative is commissioned from scratch on an agency or new-shoot basis, with no process for flagging and amplifying organic creator content that already performed.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a sourcing-process change, not a measured lift

risk.note: Requires usage-rights confirmation before amplifying any creator content as paid.

prerequisites: An active organic creator program with tracked post performance
Confirmed usage rights for amplifying creator content as paid
steps: Track organic creator post performance by hook, audience and format
Flag top-performing posts as paid-amplification candidates rather than briefing new paid scripts
Confirm usage rights for repurposing the content as paid before amplifying
Keep the native look when amplifying; avoid heavy re-editing
Organize the resulting library by hook, audience and format for future matching

test.method: Compare cost per tested creative asset when sourced from organic amplification versus new agency production.
test.read_point: One quarter after adopting the process

title: Run TikTok Shop affiliate as its own incremental track, not a replacement
hypothesis: If TikTok Shop affiliate runs as its own program with its own compensation logic and community, kept separate from the core content-first creator program, then affiliate is judged as incremental reach instead of quietly replacing relationship-based creator work.

signal.check: TikTok Shop affiliate activity is blended into the same program, budget and relationship management as the core organic creator program.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a program-structure change, not a measured lift

risk.note: Requires separate tracking and community management for the affiliate track.

prerequisites: An active organic creator program
The ability to run TikTok Shop affiliate as a distinct track
steps: Keep the core creator program content-first, with no affiliate links or codes
Stand up TikTok Shop affiliate as a separate track with its own compensation structure
Build a distinct community touchpoint for top affiliates, separate from core creator relationship management
Judge affiliate performance as incremental to, not a replacement for, the core program
Include any omni-channel halo effect when judging affiliate compensation, not on-platform margin alone

test.method: Compare combined reach and revenue with both tracks running separately versus blended.
test.measure: acquisition_volume from the affiliate track specifically
test.read_point: One quarter after separating the tracks

title: Concentrate limited creator budget in the 5,000 to 50,000 follower band
hypothesis: If a limited creator budget is concentrated in the 5,000 to 50,000 follower band, starting with creators the target avatar already follows in-niche, then early creator spend buys real relevance and reach instead of being diluted across too many tiers or spent chasing large accounts.

signal.check: A limited creator budget is spread across a wide range of follower sizes, including large accounts, with no deliberate tier concentration.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a budget-allocation rule, not a measured lift

risk.note: A budget-allocation rule for creator spend; reversible.

prerequisites: A defined creator budget and a list of candidate creators by follower count
steps: List candidate creators the target avatar already follows within the specific niche
Filter to the 5,000 to 50,000 follower band as the starting concentration
Track which platform is actually producing views and discovery for the avatar
Reallocate budget toward that platform rather than spreading evenly by default
Diversify tier mix only once budget and results justify scaling past this starting band

test.method: Compare reach and cost per view in the concentrated tier against a spread-tier baseline.

title: Target the household decision-maker in offer and bundle design
hypothesis: If bundles, subscription cadence and creative are designed around the actual household purchaser, corrected for syndicated data that can misattribute who buys, then offers fit the person actually clicking buy instead of the end user who never sees the checkout.

signal.check: Offer and bundle design targets the end user of the product without checking who the actual household purchaser is, especially where syndicated purchase data may misattribute the buyer.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a targeting correction, not a measured lift

risk.note: A targeting and offer-design change; reversible.

prerequisites: Purchase data or survey evidence on who actually completes checkout for the product
steps: Check purchase data or run a short survey to identify who actually completes checkout, not just who uses the product
Design bundle composition, subscription cadence and creative around that actual purchaser
Build the buying experience so that purchaser is comfortable, trusting the end user will follow
Re-check the assumption periodically as the customer base shifts

test.method: Compare aov and conversion rate on offers redesigned around the confirmed purchaser versus the end user.
test.read_point: One test cycle after redesigning the offer

title: Build a deliberate founder posting cadence to generate inbound, not sales
hypothesis: If the founder posts consistently about real build decisions, including occasional setbacks, and treats resulting inbound as a pipeline for partners, hires and retail interest rather than expecting direct attributed sales, then founder content is judged on the right outcome instead of a sales metric it was never built to move.

signal.check: Founder content is posted inconsistently or judged by direct attributed sales, with no process to route the resulting inbound into hiring, partnership or retail pipelines.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a content and process discipline, not a measured lift

risk.note: A content cadence and internal routing process; every public claim must stay verifiable.

prerequisites: A founder willing to post consistently and disclose real setbacks, not only wins
steps: Set a realistic, sustainable posting cadence for the founder, including occasional real setbacks
Keep every public claim verifiable, since public statements create public accountability
Build a simple intake process to route resulting inbound (partner interest, hires, retail contact) into the right pipeline
Judge founder content by inbound generated, not by direct attributed sales

test.method: Track inbound leads (partner, hire, retail) attributable to founder content over time.

title: Confirm regulatory and labeling requirements before entering a new category
hypothesis: If regulatory and labeling requirements for a new product category are confirmed before committing production, especially in food and beverage, then a launch does not get built on a claim, ingredient or label format that has to be reworked or pulled after manufacturing.

signal.check: A new product category is being planned or produced without a completed regulatory and labeling review for that category.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a compliance gate, not a measured lift

risk.note: A pre-launch compliance check; does not itself change the product.

prerequisites: Access to current regulatory and labeling rules for the target category and market
steps: Identify the specific regulatory body and labeling rules governing the new category
Review planned claims, ingredients and label copy against those rules before committing to production
Fix any conflict before finalizing packaging or placing a production order
Repeat the check for each new market the category launches into

test.method: Track compliance issues found before versus after production commitment.

title: Validate a new product with a zero-inventory digital pre-offer first
hypothesis: If a low-cost digital version of a new product idea, such as a guide, template or pre-order, is sold by direct payment before any physical stock is built, then real demand is proven with no inventory risk before committing cash to manufacturing.

signal.check: A new physical product idea is moving straight to a manufacturing commitment with no lower-risk digital or pre-order test of demand first.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a validation-sequencing change, not a measured lift

risk.note: Requires a genuine, deliverable digital offer or honest pre-order commitment, not a placeholder that misleads early buyers.

prerequisites: A digital or pre-order version of the product idea that can be sold honestly ahead of physical stock
steps: Build a low-cost digital version of the idea (guide, template, pre-order) that can be sold immediately
Bundle in disproportionate value, such as community access or extra content, so the offer builds an audience too
Personally support early buyers to generate verifiable proof points
Only commit to a physical production run once this digital or pre-order test proves real demand

test.method: Track pre-offer conversion rate and buyer engagement before deciding on the physical production run.
test.read_point: One pre-offer test window before the physical decision

title: Budget about 1 percent of marketing spend on measurement tooling
hypothesis: If roughly 1 percent of total marketing spend is set aside for attribution, media-mix or incrementality tooling once a brand runs multiple channels, then even a small resulting lift in media effectiveness pays the tooling back many times over.

signal.check: No deliberate budget line exists for measurement tooling, or the brand is deciding whether it can afford incrementality or attribution software.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a budgeting rule of thumb from one operator, not a calculation

risk.note: A budget-allocation decision; applies once a brand runs more than one paid channel profitably.

prerequisites: Multi-channel paid spend large enough that a measurement error could plausibly cost more than the tooling
steps: Calculate 1 percent of current total marketing spend as a reference tooling budget
Compare that figure against the cost of available attribution, MMM or incrementality tools
Adopt tooling only where the reference budget can plausibly cover a real fix to a real measurement gap
Re-check the allocation as total marketing spend grows

test.method: Track whether a measurement-tooling investment recovers its cost through a resulting spend reallocation.
test.read_point: Two quarters after adopting a new tool

title: Tag every ad with concept, hook, thumb-stop and edit variation
hypothesis: If every ad is tagged with its concept, hook, thumb-stop and edit variation and that tagging is loaded into whatever attribution tool is used, then creative performance can be compared across platforms on equal footing instead of being locked inside each platform's own naming.

signal.check: Ads are named inconsistently or only by launch batch, with no structured tagging for concept, hook, thumb-stop or edit variation.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a tagging convention, not a measured lift

risk.note: A naming and tagging convention; small teams can start with fewer fields (format, theme, hook) if a full taxonomy is too much overhead.

prerequisites: An attribution or reporting tool that can hold structured ad-level fields
steps: Define a fixed tagging schema: concept/angle, hook, thumb-stop, edit variation
Start smaller (format, theme, hook) if the full schema is too much overhead for the team size
Apply the tags to every new ad at launch
Load the tags into the attribution or reporting tool so creative units can be compared across platforms

test.method: Check whether creative performance can be compared across platforms using the tags six months after adoption.

title: Isolate one variable at a time in every creative test
hypothesis: If a creative test holds everything constant except the one variable under test, such as several hooks against the same body and CTA, then a winner can be read cleanly instead of being confounded by multiple simultaneous changes.

signal.check: Creative tests routinely change more than one variable at once (hook, body, CTA, format together), making it unclear which change drove a result.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a testing-discipline change, not a measured lift

risk.note: A testing-process rule; no cost beyond planning discipline.

prerequisites: A test plan that names the single variable being isolated before launch
steps: Before launching a creative test, name the single variable under test
Hold body, CTA, format and every other element constant across the test variants
Launch the variants together under the same conditions
Read the result only against the named variable, not as a general 'which ad won' comparison

test.method: Check how often a test result changes when re-run with a genuinely isolated variable versus a mixed-variable test.

title: Prioritize genuine creative contrast over minor tweaks at real scale
hypothesis: If creative production at high spend focuses on genuinely different concepts, casts, angles and pain points rather than minor palette or angle tweaks, then the ad system is less likely to treat near-duplicate variations as the same ad and starve them of fresh reach.

signal.check: An account running dozens to hundreds of concepts weekly is mostly producing minor variations (background, camera angle) of the same core idea rather than genuinely distinct concepts.

expected_effect.size: unknown; one operator's account observation, not a verified platform mechanic

risk.note: A creative-production prioritization; verify current platform behavior around similar-creative grouping before relying on it.

prerequisites: Enough creative volume and production capacity to build genuinely distinct concepts weekly
steps: Audit recent creative output for how many genuinely distinct concepts (cast, angle, pain point) it represents versus minor tweaks
Redirect production effort toward new casts, angles and pain points rather than palette or camera variations
Track whether genuinely distinct concepts get more fresh reach than near-duplicate variations
Re-verify current ad-ranking behavior around similar creative before relying on this pattern long-term

test.method: Compare reach and frequency decay on genuinely distinct concepts versus minor-variation ads.

title: Audit the existing raw-footage library before commissioning new UGC
hypothesis: If a central library of existing raw creator and UGC footage is audited and re-cut before commissioning new shoots, then in-house editing capacity becomes a bigger unlock than paying for more filming.

signal.check: New UGC or creator shoots are commissioned by default with no check of whether existing raw footage could be re-cut into new ads first.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a production-process change, not a measured lift

risk.note: Requires a searchable, centralized footage archive; may need an editor hire to realize the benefit.

prerequisites: A central archive of past raw creator and UGC footage, searchable by concept or creator
steps: Build or organize a central archive of raw footage from all past creator and UGC shoots
Before commissioning a new shoot, check whether existing footage can be re-cut to test the same concept
Bring in or reassign an in-house editor to re-cut archived footage into new ad variants
Track the ratio of new ads sourced from re-cuts versus new shoots

test.method: Compare cost per new tested ad sourced from re-cuts versus new commissioned shoots.
test.read_point: One quarter after building the archive process

title: Source new UGC creators cheaply through product gifting
hypothesis: If new UGC creators are sourced through low-cost product gifting, with the expectation that only a small share will produce content worth paying to run as an ad, then creator sourcing cost stays low while the working paid-creator roster still grows from the ones who prove out.

signal.check: New creator relationships are sourced only through paid outreach or agency placement, with no low-cost gifting funnel to find new talent cheaply.

expected_effect.size: unknown; one operator's own reported hit rate, not a benchmark

risk.note: Requires product inventory to gift and a review process to identify usable content.

prerequisites: Product units available to gift
A process to review gifted-creator content for ad usability
steps: Set up a low-cost gifting program to send product to prospective creators
Set an honest expectation for hit rate: budget for a small share of gifted creators producing usable content
Review gifted content for ad-worthiness and offer payment only to those who produce it
Build a working roster of paid creators from the gifting funnel's successes over time

test.method: Track the share of gifted creators who convert to paid, ad-worthy relationships.

title: Favor non-endemic sponsorships over endemic ones for cost efficiency
hypothesis: If sponsorship deals prioritize creators whose audience fits the buyer but whose content category does not directly compete with the product, then the brand can access relevant reach at a lower price than the scarcer, more expensive endemic slots.

signal.check: Sponsorship or creator-partnership budget is spent mainly on endemic category creators, without evaluating non-endemic creators whose audience still fits the buyer.

expected_effect.size: unknown; one operator's own pricing comparison, not a benchmarked rule

risk.note: A sourcing-priority change for sponsorship deals; reversible.

prerequisites: A defined target buyer profile that can be matched against non-endemic creator audiences
steps: Identify the target buyer's demographic and interest profile beyond the immediate product category
Source and quote both endemic and non-endemic creators whose audience matches that profile
Compare price per reach or per audience-fit point between the two
Prioritize non-endemic deals where they are meaningfully cheaper for comparable audience fit

test.method: Compare cost per relevant reach between endemic and non-endemic sponsorship deals.
test.measure: cpm by endemic vs non-endemic sponsorship

title: Judge sponsorship performance on long-tail revenue, not launch week
hypothesis: If every sponsorship gets a unique coupon code and a unique landing URL, and performance is judged on cumulative, long-tail revenue rather than launch-week numbers alone, then a creator who keeps selling years later is not undervalued against one with a big first week and nothing after.

signal.check: Sponsorship performance is judged only on launch-week revenue or clicks, with no unique tracking that persists to capture long-tail sales.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a measurement-window change, not a guaranteed lift

risk.note: A tracking-setup change; coupon codes can leak onto aggregator sites, so treat the resulting number as directional.

prerequisites: The ability to issue a unique code and landing URL per creator and track both over time
steps: Issue a unique coupon code and a unique landing URL for every sponsored creator
Track revenue attributed to each over a long window (at least a year), not just the launch week
Watch for code leakage onto coupon-aggregator sites and flag affected creators
Rank creators for renewal by cumulative long-tail revenue, not first-week numbers

test.method: Compare creator rankings by launch-week revenue versus 12-month cumulative revenue.

title: Consider a small creator-equity-plus-retainer deal to open retail doors
hypothesis: If a small equity stake plus an annual cash retainer is offered to a creator with real category credibility, then a brand can buy wholesale or retail distribution access that ad spend alone cannot reliably purchase.

signal.check: A brand wants to open new wholesale or retail distribution and has only considered standard paid sponsorship deals, not an equity-based partnership.

expected_effect.size: unknown; one named deal example, not a general benchmark

risk.note: Requires proper legal and tax structuring (such as profits-interest units) to avoid an unwanted taxable event or unnecessary dilution; legal counsel is required.

prerequisites: A creator with genuine category credibility and existing relationships with target retail accounts
Legal and tax structuring support
steps: Identify a creator whose credibility could plausibly open a specific, named retail or wholesale door
Structure a small equity stake plus an annual cash retainer with proper legal and tax advice
Tie the partnership explicitly to distribution goals, not only content output
Track new doors or accounts opened that are attributable to the partnership

test.method: Track new retail or wholesale accounts opened within a year of the partnership versus the prior run rate.

title: Classify every role as revenue-generating or cost-reducing to stay lean
hypothesis: If every role is classified as either 'makes money' (marketing, wholesale, creative) or 'saves money' (ops, finance, product/COGS), then ambiguous relay-information roles that do neither become visible and headcount can stay lean as revenue grows.

signal.check: Headcount planning has no clear classification of which roles directly generate revenue versus reduce cost, making ambiguous roles hard to evaluate.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a classification exercise, not a measured lift

risk.note: An organizational review; any resulting headcount change should follow the brand's own people process.

prerequisites: A current org chart and role descriptions
steps: List every current role and classify it as revenue-generating or cost-reducing
Flag any role that does neither, or only relays information between other roles
Review flagged roles for consolidation, automation or removal
Re-run the classification at each planning cycle as the org grows

test.method: Track headcount-to-revenue ratio before and after the classification review.

title: Leave a visible unexploited growth lever for a buyer before a sale
hypothesis: If a named, unentered channel or unlaunched product line is left visible rather than presenting a fully optimized business with no obvious next move, then a prospective buyer sees a concrete reason to expect future upside instead of pricing the business as fully mature.

signal.check: A business preparing for a sale process has optimized every visible channel and product line, leaving no obvious next move for a buyer to point to.

expected_effect.size: unknown; one operator's negotiating pattern, not a measured lift

risk.note: A pre-sale positioning decision; requires genuinely holding back a real, credible opportunity, not fabricating one.

prerequisites: A real, credible unentered channel or unlaunched product line that could plausibly exist
steps: Identify one or more real, credible unentered channels or unlaunched lines (wholesale, Amazon, a new category)
Deliberately leave it unexploited rather than launching it before the sale process starts
Present it to prospective buyers as a named, concrete next move
Confirm the opportunity is genuine and disclosed honestly, not an invented placeholder

test.method: Track buyer interest or offer terms with and without a visibly named growth lever presented.

title: Interrogate deal terms and buyer-imposed debt load before accepting an exit offer
hypothesis: If deal terms are read line by line, including what any promised upside participation actually means and what debt load a private-equity buyer will place on the business, then a founder does not accept a headline price that hides a structure the business cannot survive under.

signal.check: An exit offer is being evaluated mainly on headline price, without a line-by-line review of participation clauses, earn-outs, EBITDA addbacks, or the debt load a buyer would place on the business.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a diligence checklist, not a measured lift

risk.note: Requires qualified legal and financial advice; this is a checklist prompt, not a substitute for that advice.

prerequisites: A term sheet or letter of intent to review
Access to legal and financial advisors
steps: Read every participation, earn-out and addback clause and ask what it actually guarantees, not what it implies
Get an independent, defensible EBITDA number before the buyer's own addbacks and subtractions are applied
Model the debt load the buyer would place on the business and whether it can survive a downturn under that load
Treat any promised 'second bite of the apple' as unlikely to materialize until proven otherwise
Get qualified legal and financial advice before signing

test.method: Compare the modeled downside case against the actual deal outcome after close.

title: Build an audience or content asset before launching a new product
hypothesis: If a founder builds an audience or content asset in the target category before launching a product into it, then the launch sells into an existing base of attention and credibility instead of starting acquisition from zero.

signal.check: A new product or brand is being planned with no prior audience, content presence or credibility built in the category before launch.

expected_effect.size: unknown; one operator's stated preference, not a measured lift

risk.note: A sequencing choice for a pre-launch founder; does not apply once a brand already exists and is deciding on its next move.

prerequisites: Founder time and willingness to build content and expertise publicly before the product exists
steps: Pick the target category and start publishing content or building expertise publicly in it
Grow a real audience or credibility base before committing to product development
Launch the product to that existing audience rather than cold
Track the share of launch-week revenue attributable to the pre-built audience versus paid acquisition

test.method: Track launch-week revenue share from the pre-built audience versus cold paid acquisition.
test.measure: share of launch revenue from the pre-built audience

title: Mine competitor 1 to 3 star reviews for the single highest-emotion complaint
hypothesis: If 1 to 3 star reviews of popular competitor products are clustered into recurring complaint themes and the single most emotionally charged theme is solved directly in a new hero SKU, then the product's core selling claim is built from proven, real frustration instead of a guessed positioning.

signal.check: A new hero product's positioning is chosen from internal opinion or a broad feature list rather than from clustered competitor complaint data.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a product-design method, not a measured lift

risk.note: A research exercise before product development; does not itself change a live product.

prerequisites: Access to competitor products' 1 to 3 star reviews on a marketplace or review platform
steps: Pull 1 to 3 star reviews for the leading competitor products in the category
Cluster complaints into recurring themes (fit, price, durability, comfort, and similar)
Rank themes by emotional intensity and frequency, not just frequency alone
Design or spec the new SKU to solve the single top theme directly, not every complaint at once
Write the product's core marketing claim directly from that theme

test.method: Compare conversion rate and review sentiment on the new SKU against the category's typical launch.
test.measure: cvr_pdp_to_cart and review_rating on the new SKU

title: Durability-test candidate products a fixed number of times before launch
hypothesis: If every candidate product is put through a fixed number of durability or wash-and-wear test cycles before launch, and sent back to development on failure, then a product that will generate returns or defect complaints is caught before it ever reaches a customer.

signal.check: A new product moves to launch without a fixed, repeatable durability or wear-test protocol, or with an ad hoc one that varies by SKU.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a quality-gate practice, not a measured lift on a real brand

risk.note: A pre-launch quality-control step; delays launch for any product that fails and needs rework.

prerequisites: The ability to run repeated durability or wear tests on pre-production samples
steps: Define a fixed number of test cycles appropriate to the product category
Run every new candidate SKU through the same test protocol before committing to production
Send any SKU that fails back to development rather than launching it as-is
Track defect and return rate on tested versus untested historical SKUs

test.method: Compare defect_rate and return_rate on SKUs that passed the fixed test protocol against prior launches that skipped it.
test.measure: defect_rate and return_rate by tested vs untested SKU

title: Price a tiered upgrade product for a distinct occasion, not as a replacement
hypothesis: If an elevated product tier is built for a distinct occasion the core product does not serve, priced modestly above the core price and marketed as a different product, then the higher tier adds a new purchase reason instead of just cannibalizing or undermining the base SKU.

signal.check: A premium or elevated SKU is being added to a line with no distinct occasion defined for it, or it is priced or marketed in a way that could undersell the base product.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a pricing and positioning method, not a measured lift

risk.note: A product-line and pricing decision; reversible before launch, harder to unwind after.

prerequisites: A base product with an identifiable occasion the new tier does not currently serve
steps: Define the specific occasion or use case the base product does not serve well
Design the elevated tier specifically for that occasion
Price it modestly above the core MSRP, not at a large premium
Market it explicitly as a different product for a different moment, not an upgrade replacing the base SKU

test.method: Track whether the elevated tier adds incremental units or cannibalizes the base SKU's unit volume.
test.measure: aov and base-SKU unit volume after the tier launches

title: Run a company-wide idea channel with fast-kill and hard-escalate norms
hypothesis: If a low-friction, company-wide channel is open to every employee for submitting ideas, with a norm of fast-killing misses without drama and escalating clear winners hard, then good ideas from any level of the company get a real shot instead of dying in a single team's backlog.

signal.check: No company-wide, low-friction channel exists for employees outside the marketing or product team to submit ideas, or submitted ideas have no clear kill or escalate process.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a process practice, not a measured lift

risk.note: A communication-tooling and culture change; no direct cost.

prerequisites: A shared messaging tool (such as Slack) accessible to the whole company
steps: Create an open channel for any employee, including new hires, to post ideas
Set an explicit norm: fast, undramatic kills for misses and hard, visible escalation for clear winners
Assign someone to periodically review and respond to submissions so the channel stays active
Track how many submitted ideas actually ship, and from which parts of the company

test.method: Track the number and source of ideas that go from the channel to a shipped test.

title: Build a multi-tier gift-with-purchase ladder using a different category per tier
hypothesis: If a cart gift-with-purchase ladder has 2 to 4 ascending spend thresholds, and each tier's gift comes from a different product category than the buyer's main purchase, then higher spend is rewarded while also driving cross-category discovery for a future purchase.

signal.check: A gift-with-purchase offer has only one threshold, or every tier's gift comes from the same category as the buyer's main purchase.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a merchandising mechanic, not a measured lift

risk.note: A cart-offer and merchandising change; set thresholds and gift cost from the brand's own price points and margin.

prerequisites: At least two distinct product categories to draw gift items from
steps: Set 2 to 4 ascending spend thresholds based on the brand's own AOV distribution
Assign each tier's gift from a category different from the buyer's likely main purchase
Track which tier customers hit most and whether the cross-category gift drives a later purchase in that category
Adjust thresholds and gift assignments based on take rate and margin impact

test.method: Track aov and cross-category repeat-purchase rate for customers who received a cross-category gift.
test.measure: aov and repeat_rate_90d in the gifted category

title: Offer a pack-builder for customers to assemble their own multi-pack
hypothesis: If customers can assemble their own multi-pack through a pack-builder tool at a genuine per-unit discount, then multi-unit purchases increase because the customer gets the exact assortment they want, not a fixed bundle they have to compromise on.

signal.check: Multi-unit purchases are only available as fixed, pre-set bundles, with no tool letting the customer choose their own mix of items for the pack.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a merchandising tool, not a measured lift

risk.note: Requires a pack-builder interface on the PDP or a dedicated page; a genuine discount off single-unit price must be maintained.

prerequisites: A catalogue with enough SKU variety to make a self-built pack meaningful
A pack-builder app or custom build
steps: Build or install a pack-builder interface letting customers choose items for a multi-pack
Set genuine per-unit pricing below single-unit MSRP for the pack
Default to promoting multi-packs over single units where relevant
Track units-per-order and aov before and after the pack-builder launches

test.method: Compare units_per_order and aov before and after the pack-builder is available.

title: Use bulk-buy quantity tiers to lower a premium item's effective unit price
hypothesis: If a premium or elevated-tier item offers set bulk-buy quantities such as 6, 9 or 12 units at a lower effective unit price, then price-sensitive buyers who want the premium item can access it at a unit cost closer to the core product.

signal.check: A premium-tier item is sold only in single units with no bulk-quantity pricing, limiting it to buyers willing to pay full unit price.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a pricing mechanic, not a measured lift

risk.note: A pricing-tier change on the PDP; reversible.

prerequisites: A premium SKU with enough margin to absorb bulk-tier discounting
steps: Set fixed bulk quantities (such as 6, 9, 12 units) for the premium item
Price each tier at a genuine per-unit discount off the single-unit price
Feature the bulk tiers prominently on the PDP, not buried in a dropdown
Track unit volume and aov shift toward the premium SKU after adding bulk tiers

test.method: Compare unit volume on the premium SKU before and after bulk-buy tiers are added.
test.measure: units_per_order and aov on the premium SKU

title: Give the post-purchase upsell program a dedicated full-time owner
hypothesis: If the post-purchase upsell program has one dedicated person combining data analysis, marketing and consumer insight, rather than running unattended after setup, then the offer logic stays sharp and matched to the cart instead of decaying into a generic, static pitch.

signal.check: A post-purchase upsell app or flow was set up once and left running with no dedicated owner reviewing or updating its logic.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a staffing change, not a measured lift

risk.note: A staffing or role-allocation decision; requires enough post-purchase revenue to justify a dedicated owner.

prerequisites: An existing post-purchase upsell app or flow
Someone able to own it as a defined responsibility
steps: Assign one person as the named owner of the post-purchase upsell program
Have that owner review offer logic against what is actually in the cart, not a generic static offer
Restrict offers to high-margin or clearance-friendly products, and keep it to a single offer, not stacked offers
Review and update offer logic on a fixed cadence rather than leaving it static

test.method: Track post-purchase upsell revenue per visit before and after assigning a dedicated owner.
test.measure: other:post_purchase_rpv before and after dedicated ownership

title: Organize the always-on creative pipeline into three fixed content buckets
hypothesis: If always-on creative output is organized into three fixed buckets, side-by-side comparisons, top-of-funnel comedy or parody, and straight DR or UGC selling content, and winning formats are repeated across product categories, then creative planning has a repeatable structure instead of ad hoc production.

signal.check: Creative production has no fixed content-bucket structure, and winning formats are not deliberately repeated across other product categories.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a planning structure, not a measured lift

risk.note: A creative-planning framework; no live spend change on its own.

prerequisites: Enough creative volume and categories to make bucket repetition meaningful
steps: Define the three buckets: value-prop comparisons, top-of-funnel comedy or parody, and DR or UGC selling content
Plan a mix of new creative across all three buckets each cycle rather than defaulting to one
When a format wins in one bucket for one category, deliberately re-test it in another product category
Track win rate by bucket and by category to refine the mix

test.method: Track win rate by content bucket and how often a winning format repeats successfully across categories.
test.measure: hit rate by bucket, and by category when a format is repeated
test.read_point: One quarter after adopting the structure

title: Reuse a winning paid-ad creative format directly on owned PDP and collection pages
hypothesis: If a winning paid-ad creative format, such as a side-by-side comparison, is placed directly on collection pages and PDPs, then the same argument that won attention in the ad also does the selling work on-site instead of a shopper landing on a page with a different, weaker story.

signal.check: A winning paid-ad creative format is used only in ads, with no version of it placed on the corresponding PDP or collection page.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a creative-reuse tactic, not a measured lift

risk.note: A page-content change; reuses existing creative assets rather than commissioning new ones.

prerequisites: A proven winning ad creative format and access to edit PDP or collection page content
steps: Identify the current best-performing ad creative format for a given product
Adapt the same visual argument (such as a side-by-side comparison) for the PDP or collection page
Place it prominently on the page, not buried below the fold
Compare conversion rate on pages with and without the reused creative

test.method: A or B test the PDP with and without the reused ad-style creative.

title: Enforce a numeric internal creative quality bar before anything ships
hypothesis: If every piece of creative is scored against a fixed numeric quality bar before it ships, and the team has the hard conversation when something falls short instead of rationalizing it, then weak creative does not reach spend just because it exists.

signal.check: Creative ships to live spend with no consistent numeric quality standard, or a known-weak piece is rationalized into launch rather than fixed or killed.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a review-process gate, not a measured lift

risk.note: A creative-review process change; no cost beyond review time.

prerequisites: A defined quality rubric or scoring scale the team agrees on
steps: Set a specific numeric quality bar (for example, a score out of 10) creative must clear before it ships
Score every piece against the bar before launch, including agency-delivered creative
Have the explicit, hard conversation when something scores below the bar instead of shipping it anyway
Decide whether the internal team can raise a below-bar piece itself, and build that capability if so

test.method: Track the share of creative shipped below the quality bar before and after enforcing the gate.

title: Reshoot top-performing creative with local actors instead of subtitling it
hypothesis: If a high-performing comedy or narrative ad format is reshot with local actors in the destination market's own language, rather than subtitled, then the format's comedic or emotional timing survives the translation instead of being flattened by a dubbed or subtitled version.

signal.check: A high-performing creative format is being localized for a new market by subtitling or dubbing the original, rather than reshooting it with local actors.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a localization method, not a measured lift

risk.note: Requires local production capability or a local agency partner in the new market.

prerequisites: Local production capacity or a partner agency in the destination market
steps: Identify the highest-performing comedy or narrative format from the home market
Localize the script and direction for the destination market's culture and language
Reshoot with local actors rather than subtitling or dubbing the original
Compare performance of the reshot version against a subtitled version if one exists

test.method: Compare hook_rate and ctr on reshot local creative versus a subtitled version of the same format.
test.measure: hook_rate and ctr, reshot vs subtitled
test.read_point: One test cycle per new market

title: Pre-commit a fallback plan before shifting spend toward brand awareness
hypothesis: If a fallback plan to revert to the prior direct-response spend mix is written down before shifting a portion of spend toward brand-awareness content, then the team can make the bet without risking an open-ended, undefined exposure if it does not pay off.

signal.check: A shift of spend toward brand-awareness content is being made with no pre-agreed fallback plan or trigger for reverting to the prior mix.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a planning discipline, not a measured lift

risk.note: A planning step before a spend-mix change; no cost.

prerequisites: A currently working direct-response spend mix to revert to if needed
steps: Set a specific window and spend amount for the brand-awareness test
Write the fallback plan and revert trigger before the spend shift begins
Set expectations up front that same-platform, day-one ROAS will look worse during the test
Judge results on the widened attribution window and P&L, not daily platform ROAS, before deciding to continue or revert

test.method: Track whether the team follows the pre-committed fallback plan when the test underperforms.
test.measure: other:downside_risk realized vs the pre-committed plan
test.read_point: At the end of the planned test window

title: Sanity-check post-purchase survey share against each channel's spend share
hypothesis: If a post-purchase 'how did you hear about us' survey's attribution share is checked against each channel's share of total spend, then a channel whose survey share is far out of line with its spend share flags a real measurement or channel-mix problem to investigate.

signal.check: A post-purchase attribution survey is run with no regular check of whether each channel's survey share roughly matches its spend share.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a reconciliation check, not a measured lift

risk.note: A reporting and reconciliation step; no live spend change on its own.

prerequisites: A post-purchase attribution survey
Spend-share data by channel
steps: Pull each channel's share of total ad spend for the period
Pull the same period's post-purchase survey response share by channel
Compare the two; a channel far above its spend share in survey response may be under-credited in platform reporting, and vice versa
Investigate and rebalance budget or platform-reporting trust where the gap is large and persistent

test.method: Track the gap between spend share and survey share by channel over time.

title: Negotiate fan-facing sponsorship moments instead of static logo placement
