hypothesis: If a live-event or team sponsorship is negotiated for fan-facing moments, such as seat upgrades or trigger-event giveaways, instead of static logo or signage placement, then the sponsorship produces a memorable brand moment instead of ignorable background branding.

signal.check: A sponsorship deal is being negotiated around standard logo or signage placement with no fan-facing activation included.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a negotiation tactic, not a measured lift

risk.note: An upper-funnel bet with weak direct trackability; treat results as a survey-trend read, not a platform ROAS number.

prerequisites: Budget for a sponsorship deal and a venue or event partner open to activation-style terms
steps: Identify a target event or team sponsorship opportunity
Negotiate for fan-facing activation moments (seat upgrades, in-game trigger giveaways) instead of only logo placement
Set expectations that direct trackability will be weak and the result will be read via survey trend
Track post-purchase survey mentions of the event or sponsorship over the following months

test.method: Track post-purchase survey mentions attributable to the sponsorship in the months following the event.
test.read_point: One to three months after the event

title: Build a paid membership club and invite a select subset into a research panel
hypothesis: If a paid membership club aggregates the brand's highest-LTV, most-repeat customers with real perks, and a small, selective subset of that club is invited into a higher-engagement private community, then the brand gets both a retention asset and a genuine product research panel from its best customers.

signal.check: No paid membership or loyalty tier exists for the highest-LTV customers, or one exists but is not used as a source of product or merchandising research.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a program structure, not a measured lift

risk.note: Requires enough repeat-customer volume to justify a paid tier and a smaller invite-only community on top of it.

prerequisites: A base of repeat, high-LTV customers
A platform for a paid membership and a private community
steps: Define the paid membership tier's perks (such as ongoing savings or free shipping) for top-LTV customers
Launch the paid membership and track enrollment among eligible customers
Invite a small, selective, high-engagement subset into a private community
Use the private community explicitly as a research panel for product and merchandising decisions, not as a marketing channel

test.method: Track membership retention and how often research-panel input leads to a shipped change.

title: Validate one vocal community member's idea across the wider group before acting
hypothesis: If a single loud community member's idea is tested against the wider group before it is acted on, and the loop is closed publicly when a member-sourced idea does ship, then the brand avoids over-indexing on one voice while still reinforcing that member participation matters.

signal.check: A single vocal customer or community member's suggestion is acted on directly, with no check against the wider community first.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a process discipline, not a measured lift

risk.note: A community-management process; no cost.

prerequisites: An active customer community or feedback channel with more than a handful of engaged members
steps: When one member raises a notable idea, poll or survey the wider community before acting
Only proceed if the wider group also responds positively
When a member-sourced idea does ship, publicly credit and close the loop with the community
Track how often single-voice ideas are validated versus rejected by the wider group

test.method: Track the validation rate of single-member ideas against the wider community and community engagement after loop-closing posts.

title: Track word-of-mouth survey share as the measure of a gifting program
hypothesis: If the post-purchase survey's word-of-mouth response share is tracked over time as the specific measure of a product-gifting or philanthropy program, then the gifting loop's real effect on new customers is visible instead of the program being funded on faith alone.

signal.check: A product-gifting or philanthropy program is running with no specific tracked measure of its effect on word-of-mouth acquisition.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a measurement addition, not a guaranteed lift

risk.note: A survey-question and reporting addition; no cost.

prerequisites: A post-purchase attribution survey with a word-of-mouth or referral response option
steps: Confirm the post-purchase survey includes a word-of-mouth or 'told by a friend' response option
Track that response share as its own trend line over time
Compare the trend against periods of active gifting or philanthropy activity
Use the trend, not a single point-in-time number, to judge whether the gifting program is working

test.method: Track word-of-mouth survey share before, during and after gifting program activity.

title: Use a retail-as-a-service partner to test stores before owned capex
hypothesis: If one or two physical stores are opened through a retail-as-a-service partner before committing capital to owned stores, then the brand learns whether physical retail works for it without the fixed lease and buildout costs of owned locations.

signal.check: A brand is considering opening owned physical retail stores with no prior lower-risk test through a retail-as-a-service or similar partner.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a de-risking method, not a measured lift

risk.note: Requires finding and vetting a retail-as-a-service partner; verify current vendors and terms before committing.

prerequisites: A retail-as-a-service partner or similar low-commitment retail model available in the target market
steps: Identify a retail-as-a-service partner or similar low-commitment retail option
Open one or two test locations through that partner rather than owned capex
Track break-even-in-four-walls and foot-traffic conversion at the test locations
Only commit to owned stores once the test locations demonstrate a viable model

test.method: Track break-even performance at retail-as-a-service test locations before any owned-store commitment.
test.read_point: One full retail season per test location

title: Sequence marketplace entry: ship-direct integration, then a limited test, then rollout
hypothesis: If a new marketplace or big-box wholesale partner is entered through a digital ship-direct integration first, then a limited assortment test, then a full rollout once sell-through is proven, then the brand avoids overcommitting inventory and assortment before the channel is proven.

signal.check: A new marketplace or wholesale account moves straight to a full assortment rollout with no digital integration or limited test phase first.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a sequencing method, not a measured lift

risk.note: Requires the retailer or marketplace to support a phased or digital-integration entry path.

prerequisites: A retailer or marketplace partner willing to support a phased entry
Digital-integration capability (such as a direct-ship setup)
steps: Start with a digital-marketplace or ship-direct integration so orders fulfill directly with minimal upfront inventory commitment
Move to a limited, small-assortment physical or in-marketplace test once the integration is proven
Expand to a full assortment rollout only once sell-through is proven at the limited-test stage
Track sell-through and reorder rate at each stage before advancing to the next

test.method: Track sell-through rate at each stage of the phased entry before advancing.

title: Fight for control of in-store and in-marketplace display
hypothesis: If a brand negotiates for control over its in-store or in-marketplace display rather than accepting a retailer's default placement, then the side-by-side comparison or value story that actually converts customers gets told, instead of being left out by a display the retailer built without it.

signal.check: A retail or marketplace listing uses the retailer's default display or template, with no brand-controlled comparison or value-story element included.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a negotiation practice, not a measured lift

risk.note: A retail-relationship negotiation; requires enough leverage or volume to request display control.

prerequisites: An existing or pending retail or marketplace listing
A proven value-story creative asset to adapt for display
steps: Identify the retail or marketplace accounts where display is currently retailer-controlled
Prepare a proven value-story or comparison asset adapted for that display format
Negotiate for control or influence over the display as part of the account relationship
Track sell-through at locations or listings with brand-controlled display versus default display

test.method: Compare sell-through at accounts with brand-controlled display versus default retailer display.
test.measure: marketplace_share and sell-through by display type

title: Add a long-horizon hail-mary discount email for never-purchased subscribers
hypothesis: If subscribers who still have not purchased after roughly 120 days get one deeper, longer-horizon discount email, then the list finds out whether that segment will ever convert as customers at all, instead of being emailed forever at the standard offer depth with no resolution.

signal.check: Subscribers who never converted after the welcome flow ends continue receiving standard offers indefinitely, with no distinct, deeper long-horizon offer testing whether they will ever convert.

expected_effect.size: 10 to 20 percent depth range cited by adjacent sources for welcome offers; this specific email's depth is the brand's own to set

risk.note: An email-flow addition; the offer should be clearly time-bound and not repeated indefinitely.

prerequisites: A segmented list of subscribers who have never purchased, with tenure tracked
steps: Identify subscribers who have not purchased roughly 120 days after joining the list
Send one distinct, deeper discount offer specifically to this segment
Track the conversion rate of this segment against the standard welcome-offer conversion rate
Treat non-conversion after this email as a signal to stop emailing this segment at the standard cadence

test.method: Track conversion rate of the never-purchased segment after the hail-mary email versus their prior non-response.

title: Give customer service a standing budget for off-catalog surprise gifts
hypothesis: If customer service has a fixed, standing budget to send genuine, off-catalog surprise gifts to high-LTV customers pulled from CRM, then service recovery and loyalty moments feel like a real surprise instead of another branded discount the customer has already seen.

signal.check: Customer service has no dedicated, standing budget for surprise gestures to high-LTV customers, or surprises are limited to the brand's own product line.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a budget-line addition, not a measured lift

risk.note: A budget-line and process addition; sized to the brand's own CRM data and cash position.

prerequisites: CRM data identifying high-LTV customers
A standing budget line for off-catalog gifts
steps: Set a fixed, recurring budget line for customer-service surprise gifts
Pull high-LTV customers from CRM to identify surprise-gift candidates
Choose gifts genuinely outside the brand's own product line for a real surprise effect
Track csat and repeat purchase for surprised customers against a comparable, non-surprised cohort

test.method: Compare csat and repeat purchase rate for surprised high-LTV customers against a comparable cohort.
test.measure: csat and repeat_rate_365d for surprised customers
test.read_point: One quarter after the budget line starts

title: Restrict AI in customer service to routing, not full conversations
hypothesis: If AI in customer service is used only to bucket and route a query to the right specialist rep, rather than to handle the full conversation end to end, then customers still get a human-quality resolution while the team gets the routing efficiency AI is good at.

signal.check: AI is used to handle full customer-service conversations end to end, with no human review or handoff for anything beyond simple routing.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a scope-limiting rule, not a measured lift

risk.note: A tooling-configuration and policy change; existing AI tooling can often be scoped down rather than replaced.

prerequisites: An AI customer-service tool currently in use or under evaluation
A documented customer-service knowledge base or 'bible' for human reps
steps: Scope the AI tool to classification and routing only: identify the query type and route to the right specialist
Keep the actual resolution conversation staffed by trained human reps
Maintain a documented customer-service knowledge base tied to the brand's core values for reps to work from
Track csat and first-reply time under the routing-only scope versus a fuller AI-handled scope, if one was tested

test.method: Compare csat and first_reply_hours under AI-routing-only versus AI-handled-conversation configurations.

title: Run a regular all-hands call centered on a real customer's experience
hypothesis: If the whole company regularly listens to a real customer describe their actual experience with the brand, then customer obsession stays a lived, company-wide reality instead of a value statement only the customer-facing team hears about.

signal.check: No regular company-wide meeting includes a real customer's own account of their experience with the brand.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a culture practice, not a measured lift

risk.note: A meeting-format addition; requires sourcing a willing customer or a recorded account each time.

prerequisites: A recurring all-hands or company meeting
A process to source a customer willing to share their experience
steps: Add a segment to a recurring all-hands where a real customer's experience is shared, live or recorded
Rotate between positive and constructive (not only glowing) customer accounts
Let the team ask questions or discuss what the account implies for their own work
Track whether the practice surfaces recurring themes worth acting on

test.method: Track whether issues raised in these sessions lead to a tracked fix or process change.
test.measure: count of fixes traced back to an all-hands customer story

title: Use a live, role-specific homework assignment in hiring
hypothesis: If a candidate for a key role is given a role-specific homework assignment, such as sketching next year's roadmap, and required to present it live, then the hiring process weighs actual intentionality and granularity of thinking over generic interview answers.

signal.check: Hiring for a key role relies only on standard interview questions, with no role-specific working exercise required before an offer.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a hiring-process addition, not a measured lift

risk.note: A hiring-process addition; budget extra time in the process for candidates to complete and present the assignment.

prerequisites: A defined key role with a clear, assignable exercise related to its real responsibilities
steps: Design a role-specific assignment that mirrors real, near-term work for the role
Require the candidate to present the assignment live, not just submit it in writing
Score the presentation for intentionality and granularity of thinking, not just polish
Track how the assignment score correlates with the hire's later performance

test.method: Track post-hire performance against the assignment score for hires who went through the exercise.

title: Delay adopting a formal operating system until process scale justifies it
hypothesis: If a formal management operating system is adopted only once the team and processes have grown enough to actually internalize it, then the company avoids imposing a heavyweight system on a small team that would just add process overhead with no matching benefit.

signal.check: A formal operating system or management framework is being adopted at an early stage, before the team or process complexity has grown enough to need it.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a timing judgment, not a measured lift

risk.note: A timing decision for an organizational change; reversible by adopting later.

prerequisites: A current headcount and process-complexity picture to judge readiness against
steps: Assess current headcount, process complexity and where communication is actually breaking down
Delay adopting a formal operating system until those breakdowns are frequent and costly enough to justify the overhead
Run with lighter, ad hoc coordination in the meantime
Reassess readiness at each major growth stage

test.method: Track how often coordination or process breakdowns occur before and after adopting a formal system.

title: Run a decaying weekly peer-recognition budget tied to core values
hypothesis: If every employee gets a fixed number of recognition coins each week that expire if unused, tagged to a specific core value with a short note, and convertible to cash or gift cards, then values-based peer recognition happens continuously instead of only at formal review time.

signal.check: No peer-recognition system exists, or an existing one has no expiring budget or explicit tie to named core values.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a culture practice, not a measured lift

risk.note: A fixed weekly budget line and a lightweight tool (such as a Slack app); budget it explicitly on the P&L.

prerequisites: A messaging tool that can support a recognition app or a manual equivalent
A defined, fixed weekly budget
steps: Give each employee a fixed number of recognition coins per week that expire if unused
Require the giver to tag a specific core value and add a short note when giving
Let coins convert to cash or gift cards at a fixed rate
Budget the program as a fixed weekly P&L line and track participation rate

test.method: Track participation rate and which core values get tagged most often over time.

title: Build an empathy avatar feed to study the customer before creating content
hypothesis: If a separate social account follows the accounts a customer avatar already follows, and the team studies the resulting feed's content type, mood and timing before writing anything, then new content starts from real observed customer taste instead of the team's own creative instinct.

signal.check: New content or creative briefs are written from the team's own taste or a generic persona document, with no direct observation of what the target avatar actually consumes.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a research method, not a measured lift

risk.note: A research exercise; requires picking 1 to 2 concrete avatars, not a broad demographic.

prerequisites: 1 to 2 defined customer avatars
A spare social account to build the feed on
steps: Pick 1 to 2 specific customer avatars to study
Open a separate social account and follow the accounts each avatar likely follows
Study the resulting feed for content type, mood and time-of-day patterns
Brief new content from these observed patterns before writing from personal instinct

test.method: Compare hook_rate on content briefed from the avatar feed against content briefed without it.
test.measure: hook_rate on avatar-fed vs instinct-briefed content

title: Rebuild a spiking organic hook two ways before paid amplification
hypothesis: If a spiking organic post is either run as-is through whitelisting or has only its hook kept and the back half rebuilt into a product promo, then a viral moment with no product tie-in still has a real path into paid without wasting the hook that already proved it stops the scroll.

signal.check: An organic post spikes with no clear commercial angle, and the team either ignores it for paid or forces the whole piece into an ad without rebuilding the non-working half.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a repurposing method, not a measured lift

risk.note: A creative-repurposing decision; requires whitelisting or ad-code access to run the organic account's content as paid.

prerequisites: A spiking organic post
Whitelisting or ad-code access to the originating account
steps: Identify a spiking organic post with a strong hook but weak or no product tie-in
Option A: run the whole piece as-is via whitelisting or an ad code
Option B: keep only the hook and rebuild the back half into a direct product promo
Test both approaches against the flat baseline of not amplifying the post at all

test.method: Compare paid performance of the as-is version against the hook-plus-rebuilt-promo version.
test.measure: hook_rate and roas_prospecting by rebuild approach

title: Add a tribe-narrowing qualifier to hooks and mirror it on the landing page
hypothesis: If a broad hook topic is narrowed with a specific qualifier in the first three seconds, and that same qualifier is mirrored on the landing-page headline, then a viewer who self-identifies with the narrower group arrives at a page that confirms they landed in the right place.

signal.check: Ad hooks use a broad topic with no narrowing qualifier, and the landing page headline does not echo any qualifier language used in the ad.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a copy technique, not a measured lift

risk.note: A copywriting change on both the ad hook and the landing page; reversible.

prerequisites: A broad topic hook that can be narrowed with a specific audience qualifier
steps: Take an existing broad hook and add a specific qualifier that narrows it to a subgroup
Mirror the exact same qualifier language in the landing page headline
Launch the qualified hook against the unqualified version as a test
Check message match: does the visitor feel like they landed on the right page

test.method: A or B test the qualified hook and matching landing page against the unqualified version.

title: Use a direct polarizing comparison format anchored to a real differentiator
hypothesis: If a direct, polarizing good versus bad comparison is built around a real, verifiable product differentiator, then the format stops the scroll and self-selects higher-intent viewers instead of a softer, non-committal message that everyone can politely ignore.

signal.check: Ad creative avoids direct comparison framing even where the brand has a real, honest differentiator worth contrasting against the category norm.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a creative format, not a measured lift

risk.note: A creative-format choice; the comparison must be built on a real, honest differentiator, not an invented one.

prerequisites: A real, verifiable product differentiator worth contrasting against a category norm
steps: Identify one real, honest differentiator the product has against typical category alternatives
Build a direct, polarizing good versus bad comparison format around it
Test it against a softer, non-comparison version of the same message
Confirm every claim in the comparison is checkable and true

test.method: A or B test the comparison format against a non-comparison version of the same core message.

title: Structure a lean two-person media pod: one analyst, one creative
hypothesis: If the marketing team pairs one analytical or briefing person with one creative person, and the creative person is exempt from meetings and spreadsheets, then output stays high because the creative role's time is protected for shooting and editing, not administration.

signal.check: The marketing team structure mixes analytical and creative work across the same people, or requires the creative person to attend the same meetings and reporting as the analyst.

expected_effect.size: unknown; an org-design pattern, not a measured lift

risk.note: An organizational-structure change; fits a small team, not a fully staffed department.

prerequisites: At least two people who can split analytical and creative responsibilities
steps: Assign one person the analytical and briefing role: meetings, data, posting priorities
Assign the other the creative role: shoots, edits, or being on camera
Explicitly exempt the creative role from meetings and spreadsheet reporting
Track creative output volume before and after the split

test.method: Track weekly creative output volume before and after adopting the pod structure.
test.read_point: One month after adopting the structure

title: Mine your own customer data to find existing customers who are influencers
hypothesis: If a data tool cross-references the customer or email database to identify which existing customers are also influencers or creators, and the top tier is contacted personally with a non-templated message, then a brand finds free, already-loyal advocates it would otherwise never discover by manual searching.

signal.check: Influencer and creator identification only looks outward at unknown accounts, with no process to check whether existing customers are already influencers.

expected_effect.size: unknown; one operator's tool-assisted example, not a benchmark

risk.note: Requires a data tool or manual process capable of matching customer records to social accounts.

prerequisites: Customer or email database
A tool or process to match records to social/influencer accounts
steps: Cross-reference the customer or email database against social accounts to find existing influencers
Rank matches by follower count or engagement to find the top tier
Contact the top tier personally and specifically, not with a templated outreach message
Offer product seeding, feedback requests or content collaboration

test.method: Track how many identified customer-influencers convert into active advocates or content creators.

title: Weight top-of-funnel versus mid-funnel posting mix by current reach
hypothesis: If organic posting mix shifts toward more top-of-funnel, provocative content when reach is low and toward more mid-funnel, tactical content once reach is already strong, then content strategy matches the account's actual current stage instead of running one fixed ratio regardless of audience size.

signal.check: Organic content mix uses a fixed top-of-funnel-to-mid-funnel ratio regardless of the account's current reach level.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a mix heuristic, not a measured lift

risk.note: A content-planning ratio change; reversible weekly.

prerequisites: A way to track current organic reach trend to decide which mix applies
steps: Assess current organic reach trend: growing from a low base, or already established
If reach is low, weight the mix toward more top-of-funnel, provocative or tribal content
If reach is already strong, shift toward mostly mid-funnel, educational or tactical content
Re-check the mix on a fixed cadence as reach changes

test.method: Track organic reach growth under the reach-weighted mix versus a fixed ratio.
test.read_point: One quarter after adopting the reach-weighted mix

title: Set a pre-approved trend-response path with fixed budget and turnaround
hypothesis: If a trend-response path is pre-approved with a named fast-turnaround creator, a fixed budget and a fixed delivery window, then the team can actually act inside a trend's short relevance window instead of losing days to ad hoc approval each time.

signal.check: Responding to a trending format or topic requires ad hoc approval and creator sourcing each time, causing the brand to consistently miss the trend's relevance window.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a process pre-approval, not a measured lift

risk.note: A standing process and budget pre-approval; only useful once basic content formats are already proven.

prerequisites: At least one proven working content format
A fast-turnaround creator relationship
steps: Identify a fast-turnaround creator who can execute on short notice
Pre-approve a fixed budget for trend-response content
Set a fixed delivery window target appropriate to the category's trend speed
Only trend-jack once existing formats are already proven, not as a first strategy

test.method: Track turnaround time and hit rate on trend-response content before and after pre-approval.

title: Set up a two-tier creator brief system by trust level
hypothesis: If creator briefs run through a standard tier with full legal and brand review or a lighter, trusted tier with an explicit no-go list and no legal gate, then creator content volume can scale without every single brief bottlenecking on full review.

signal.check: Every creator brief goes through the same full legal and brand review regardless of the creator or campaign's risk level, limiting how many briefs the team can process.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a process-tiering change, not a measured lift

risk.note: A process change; the trusted tier's no-go list must be genuinely clear to avoid compliance gaps.

prerequisites: A pool of creators or campaign types trusted enough to skip full legal review
A written no-go list for the lighter tier
steps: Define the standard tier: full legal and brand review required
Define a lighter, trusted tier with an explicit, short no-go list and no legal gate
Assign creators or campaign types to the appropriate tier based on trust and risk
Bring in a working creator or content-literate advisor if briefs keep failing, rather than tightening review further

test.method: Track brief turnaround time and issue rate by tier.
test.read_point: One quarter after adopting the tiers

title: Anchor a creator-seeding campaign with one bigger creator, then layer smaller ones
hypothesis: If a large creator-seeding push starts with one bigger creator to kick off excitement and then layers in many smaller creators, then the campaign gets an initial spark of visibility that the smaller creators can then amplify at volume.

signal.check: A creator-seeding campaign either relies on one big creator alone or spreads budget evenly across many small creators with no anchor moment to kick it off.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a sequencing tactic, not a measured lift

risk.note: A campaign-sequencing decision; requires budget for at least one meaningful anchor creator plus a broader seeding pool.

prerequisites: Budget for one anchor creator plus a broader pool of smaller creators to seed
steps: Book one bigger, credible creator to anchor and kick off the campaign
Time the anchor creator's content to launch first
Layer in many smaller seeded creators once the anchor moment has landed
Track post rate and engagement of the layered wave against the anchor's initial reach

test.method: Track post rate and engagement of the seeded wave following the anchor creator's launch.

title: Cancel creative-review meetings that a KPI alone should settle
hypothesis: If a creative decision has a clear, measurable KPI (such as a button color's effect on conversion rate), the review meeting for it is cancelled and the decision is left with the person doing the measurable work, then a group of people without a real, informed opinion stops slowing down decisions that data can already answer.

signal.check: A creative or on-page decision with a clear measurable outcome is still debated in a multi-person review meeting instead of being resolved by the responsible person's own data.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a governance change, not a measured lift

risk.note: A meeting and decision-rights policy change; applies only to genuinely KPI-measurable decisions, not subjective creative calls.

prerequisites: A clear KPI that the decision in question can be judged against
steps: List recurring review meetings and sort decisions into 'KPI-measurable' and 'genuinely subjective'
Cancel the meeting for KPI-measurable decisions and give ownership to the person doing that measurable work
Keep group review only for genuinely subjective creative calls
Track cycle time on decisions before and after removing the unnecessary meetings

test.method: Track decision cycle time on KPI-measurable calls before and after removing the review meeting.

title: Judge broad and targeted creators on different metrics
hypothesis: If broad-reach creators are judged on view volume at an acceptable CPM and targeted creators are judged on saves, shares and buying intent, then neither type of creator gets penalized for underperforming on a metric it was never suited to move.

signal.check: All sponsored creators are judged on the same metric (typically view count or direct attributed sales) regardless of whether their role is broad awareness or targeted intent.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a measurement-matching change, not a measured lift

risk.note: A reporting and evaluation change; no live spend change on its own.

prerequisites: A way to classify each creator relationship as broad-reach or targeted-intent
steps: Classify each active creator relationship as broad-reach or targeted-intent
Judge broad-reach creators on view volume at an acceptable CPM
Judge targeted-intent creators on saves, shares and estimated buying intent, not view count
Re-negotiate or drop creators who cannot deliver on the metric their category should be judged by

test.method: Track renewal decisions made under the matched-metric system versus a single blended metric.

title: Mandate AI-workflow documentation so knowledge does not live in individuals
hypothesis: If every team member documents their AI-assisted workflows into a shared, queryable resource, then institutional experimentation knowledge survives staff turnover instead of leaving with whoever discovered the working process.

signal.check: Team members use AI tools individually with no shared documentation of what workflows and prompts actually work.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a knowledge-management practice, not a measured lift

risk.note: A process and tooling requirement; needs a shared, searchable location for documentation.

prerequisites: A shared, searchable location (wiki, shared doc, internal tool) for workflow documentation
steps: Require each team member to document their AI-assisted workflows as they develop them
Store documentation in one shared, searchable location
Review and prune documentation periodically for what still works
Track how often documented workflows get reused by someone other than their author

test.method: Track reuse rate of documented workflows by people other than the original author.

title: Check whether AI-generated content's negative comments actually move revenue
hypothesis: If negative comment volume on AI-generated visual content is checked against actual revenue or subscriber movement before scaling it further, then the brand does not overreact to visible online criticism that never actually affected the business.

signal.check: AI-generated visual or hero content is paused or scaled back purely because of negative comment volume, with no check on whether revenue or subscribers actually moved.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a measurement check, not a guaranteed outcome

risk.note: A measurement check before a content-strategy decision; no cost.

prerequisites: Revenue and subscriber or list-growth data around the period the AI content ran
steps: When AI-generated content draws negative comments, pull revenue and subscriber data for the same period
Check whether either metric actually moved, not just comment sentiment
If neither moved, treat the backlash as noise and continue testing rather than reflexively pulling the content
If a metric did move, treat that as the real signal and adjust

test.method: Compare revenue and subscriber movement against comment-sentiment volume for AI-generated content.

title: Spot rising creators early and lock in a generous deal before their price rises
hypothesis: If a creator judged likely to grow quickly is identified while still small and offered a simple, generous early deal, then the brand secures a relationship at a low rate before that creator's price rises once they hit a bigger following.

signal.check: Creator partnerships are only pursued once a creator already has a large, proven following and a correspondingly high rate.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a sourcing-timing tactic, not a measured lift

risk.note: Requires judgment to identify creators likely to grow, which carries real prediction risk.

prerequisites: A team member with genuine familiarity with the relevant creator niche to judge growth potential
steps: Have a team member familiar with the niche identify smaller creators likely to grow quickly
Offer a simple, generous early deal before the creator's rate rises with their following
Track the return on early-locked deals against later, higher-priced deals with comparable creators
Treat this as a portfolio bet, expecting some picks not to pan out

test.method: Compare cost per reach on early-locked creator deals versus deals made after the creator had already grown.
test.read_point: Six months to one year after each early deal

title: Tie every large brand campaign to a measurable capture path
hypothesis: If every large brand campaign includes a measurable capture path, such as a landing page, guide download or lead form, then the campaign's reach produces trackable leads on top of awareness instead of attention with nothing to show for it afterward.

signal.check: A large brand-awareness campaign is planned or has run with no attached landing page, lead capture or other measurable path for the resulting attention.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a campaign-design requirement, not a measured lift

risk.note: A campaign-design requirement; does not reduce the campaign's awareness goal, only adds a capture layer.

prerequisites: Budget and capability to build a landing page, download or lead form alongside the campaign
steps: Require every large campaign brief to name its capture path before approval
Build the landing page, guide download or lead form alongside the awareness creative
Track leads or downloads captured as a campaign KPI alongside reach and impressions
Review campaigns retrospectively for whether the capture path was actually promoted, not just built

test.method: Track leads or downloads captured per large campaign against its reach.

title: Set a 40 to 50 percent true DTC gross margin gate before launch
hypothesis: If a new DTC product's true gross margin, after final-mile shipping, pick-pack fees and payment costs, is confirmed at 40 to 50 percent before committing to launch, then a structurally unprofitable product is fixed on paper (price, pack size, channel) instead of discovered after scale.

signal.check: A new DTC product is nearing launch with a margin model that only accounts for ingredients or unit cost, not full landed and fulfillment cost.

expected_effect.size: 40 to 50 percent true gross margin, per the source's own DTC CPG benchmark

risk.note: A pre-launch financial modeling gate; does not itself change a live product.

prerequisites: A full landed-cost model including shipping, 3PL fees and payment or marketplace fees
steps: Build the true cost model: ingredients or unit cost, plus final-mile shipping, pick-pack fee and transaction fees
Calculate the resulting true gross margin at the planned launch price
If margin is below 40 to 50 percent, change price, pack size or channel mix before launch
Do not commit to launch on the strength of a margin model that omits fulfillment costs

test.method: Recompute true gross margin at 90 days post-launch against the pre-launch model.
test.measure: gross_margin at launch vs 90 days post-launch
test.read_point: Before launch, and again at 90 days

title: Budget free sampling as a fixed percent of marketing spend, sized by LTV math
hypothesis: If free product sampling is budgeted as a fixed share of marketing spend and sized by how many free units convert to one paying customer on LTV terms, then sampling is funded like a real channel with real economics instead of tracked loosely as an untracked giveaway.

signal.check: Free product sampling has no fixed budget line or LTV-based sizing, and is either untracked or treated as pure marketing cost with no return model.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a budgeting method, not a measured lift

risk.note: Works best for cheap, shelf-stable, easily-sampled products; harder for frozen, heavy or beverage formats.

prerequisites: Estimated LTV per converted customer
A product cheap and stable enough to sample widely
steps: Calculate how many free units can be given away per resulting buyer and still profit on LTV
Set a fixed percent of marketing budget for sampling based on that math
Sample across retail floor, influencers and organic giveaways rather than one channel
Track conversion rate from sampled units to paying customers to refine the budget over time

test.method: Track conversion rate from sampled units to first purchase against the LTV assumption used to size the budget.

title: Generate campaign ideas with a non-obvious-but-true test
hypothesis: If a campaign idea is rejected unless it is both non-obvious and backed by a real, defensible fact, then marketing avoids both the trap of an obvious idea nobody notices and a clever idea nobody can verify.

signal.check: Campaign ideas are chosen for being clever or on-trend without a check for whether they are both non-obvious and factually true and defensible.

expected_effect.size: unknown; an ideation filter, not a measured lift

risk.note: A creative-brief and approval filter; no live spend change on its own.

prerequisites: A real, defensible fact about the product worth dramatizing
steps: List the obvious campaign ideas the category or brand name suggests, and reject them outright
Find one true, defensible, verifiable fact about the product
Dramatize that fact in a way nobody would predict
Run roughly one such idea per quarter rather than trying to do it constantly

test.method: Track recall or engagement on non-obvious-but-true campaigns versus the prior standard campaign approach.

title: Fix a confusing brand name with packaging, not a full rebrand
hypothesis: If a name that reads confusingly is fixed through packaging hierarchy, shrinking the name visually and leading with the most valuable plain-language description, then the brand avoids the cost and existing-customer risk of a full rebrand while still fixing the actual confusion.

signal.check: A brand's name is known to confuse or mis-signal what the product is, and a full rebrand is being considered as the only fix.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a packaging-hierarchy fix, not a measured lift

risk.note: A packaging and design change; weigh the cost and existing-customer confusion risk against a full rebrand before choosing this path.

prerequisites: A clear diagnosis of what the current name communicates versus what it needs to communicate
steps: Diagnose specifically what the current name signals to a new shopper versus what it should signal
Weigh a full rebrand's cost and risk of alienating existing customers against a packaging fix
Shrink the name visually using negative space and lead with the most valuable plain-language description
Keep any numeric or technical claim as a secondary, supporting line, not the headline

test.method: Compare shelf or PDP conversion rate before and after the packaging hierarchy change.
test.measure: cvr_pdp_to_cart before and after the packaging change

title: Brief a naming or creative agency with explicit strategic variables
hypothesis: If a naming or creative agency brief states the positioning tension, brand-DNA references and non-negotiable elements explicitly, rather than asking the agency to 'go make something,' then a weak creative outcome is traceable to the brief, and the agency has real constraints to work from.

signal.check: A creative or naming agency brief is open-ended, with no stated positioning tension, brand-DNA references or non-negotiable elements.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a briefing-discipline change, not a measured lift

risk.note: A briefing-process change; no cost beyond the time to write a more detailed brief.

prerequisites: A defined positioning tension and any non-negotiable brand elements
steps: State the positioning tension explicitly (what the brand is and deliberately is not)
Give brand-DNA references (comparable brands or figures that capture the intended feel)
List non-negotiable elements the agency must keep
Treat a weak result as a brief-quality issue to fix, not solely the agency's failure

test.method: Track the number of revision rounds needed on agency deliverables before and after using a structured brief.

title: Assemble a cross-functional war room within 24 hours for a fast-moving crisis
hypothesis: If a fast-moving reputational risk gets a small cross-functional team assembled in-office within about 24 hours, rather than routed through a normal approval cycle, then the brand can respond while the moment is still live instead of publishing a response after public attention has moved on.

signal.check: A fast-moving, unrelated reputational event is being handled through the normal approval process with no defined rapid cross-functional response team.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a response-process change, not a measured lift

risk.note: Legal and PR counsel should still be involved for serious matters; this is for genuinely fast-moving, lower-stakes moments.

prerequisites: In-house content or creative capability that can move fast
A pre-identified small cross-functional team
steps: Pre-identify who belongs on a rapid-response team (founder, creative, legal contact, comms)
When a fast-moving event hits, assemble that team in person within about 24 hours
Move from event to a published response inside that same window
Reserve the slower, normal process for anything genuinely serious or legally complex

test.method: Track time from event to published response before and after adopting the war-room process.

title: Choose evidence-based specialist credibility partners over celebrity endorsement
hypothesis: If nutrition or technical credibility comes from named specialist doctors and thought leaders rather than athletic or lifestyle celebrities, then an evidence-based category gets factual credibility that a purely aspirational endorsement cannot provide.

signal.check: A brand in an evidence-based category (health, nutrition, technical performance) is choosing or already using athletic or lifestyle celebrity endorsement as its primary credibility signal.

expected_effect.size: unknown; one operator's opinion, not a benchmarked comparison

risk.note: Celebrity and specialist choices both carry key-person reputational risk; check that risk before committing.

prerequisites: Access to relevant named specialists or thought leaders in the product's evidence base
steps: Identify named specialists or thought leaders with genuine relevant expertise
Prioritize them over athletic or lifestyle celebrities for factual, evidence-based credibility claims
Disclose the partnership honestly and keep claims within what the specialist can actually support
Track whether the resulting content improves trust signals such as review sentiment or conversion on claim-heavy pages

test.method: Compare conversion or trust signals on pages using specialist credibility versus celebrity endorsement.
test.measure: cvr_pdp_to_cart and review sentiment by endorsement type

title: Stay deliberately under-visible in syndicated retail data while young
hypothesis: If a young brand leans on DTC, Amazon and specialty retail that syndicated retail-tracking data under-reports, then its true scale stays harder for fast-follower competitors to see until the brand is already large enough to withstand a copycat.

signal.check: A young, category-pioneering brand's full sales picture is easily visible to competitors through syndicated retail data, inviting fast followers before the brand has scale to defend its position.

expected_effect.size: unknown; one operator's own case, not a general strategy

risk.note: A channel-mix consideration; should not be the sole reason to avoid retail data providers a brand would otherwise want.

prerequisites: A channel mix that already includes meaningful DTC or Amazon sales alongside any tracked retail
steps: Assess how much of current sales runs through channels that syndicated retail data actually tracks
Where category-pioneer status is a real asset, weigh keeping a heavier DTC and Amazon mix before large mass-retail expansion
Track whether competitor fast-follower activity increases once retail visibility grows
Revisit the tradeoff once the brand has enough scale that visibility is no longer a competitive risk

test.method: Track fast-follower competitor activity against the brand's retail-data visibility over time.

title: Attend a trade show only when buyer access is the real unmet need
hypothesis: If trade-show attendance is gated on whether buyer access is genuinely the unmet need, and skipped once existing retailer relationships already provide that access, then company energy and budget are not spent on a channel that has stopped adding anything new.

signal.check: Trade-show attendance continues by default or habit, without checking whether the brand still lacks the buyer relationships the show would provide.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a resource-allocation gate, not a measured lift

risk.note: A budget and calendar decision; reversible each year.

prerequisites: A current list of target retail buyer relationships and which ones already exist
steps: List the buyers a given trade show would realistically provide access to
Check how many of those relationships already exist through other channels
Skip the show if existing relationships already cover the realistic buyer list
Attend only when a genuine, currently-missing buyer relationship is the goal

test.method: Track new buyer relationships actually gained per trade show attended.
test.measure: other:trade_show_roi as new relationships per show

title: Over-deliver on a service failure fix and accept some policy abuse
hypothesis: If a damaged or negative delivery experience is met with an over-delivered fix, such as a full free replacement, rather than a minimal remedy, then some of those customers convert into vocal advocates, and the brand accepts a small rate of policy abuse as the cost of that conversion.

signal.check: Service-recovery policy defaults to the minimal remedy for a damaged or negative delivery experience, with no test of an over-delivered fix.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a policy-generosity change, not a measured lift

risk.note: Requires accepting a higher cost per resolved case and some abuse of the generous policy.

prerequisites: A support process able to authorize a full replacement or equivalent over-delivery
steps: Identify a segment of service-failure cases to test a full, over-delivered fix on
Track whether these customers later leave positive reviews or make repeat purchases
Accept a small, bounded rate of abuse of the generous policy rather than tightening it for everyone
Compare cost of over-delivery against the value of resulting advocacy and repeat purchase

test.method: Compare repeat purchase and review sentiment for over-delivered fixes against the standard minimal remedy.
test.measure: repeat_rate_90d and review_rating by fix type

title: Run a structured pre-launch sequence: anticipation, hype-channel test, email list
hypothesis: If a launch is preceded by months of public anticipation on owned channels, a small hypothesis-tested giveaway on the chosen hype channel, and a growing owned email list, then day-one demand is pre-loaded instead of starting cold on launch day.

signal.check: A launch date is set with no deliberate pre-launch anticipation sequence, hype-channel test, or email-list build ahead of it.

expected_effect.size: unknown; works better for a founder with existing credibility; a first-time founder may need product-market fit first

risk.note: Works better for a second-time or already-credible founder; a first-time founder should validate product-market fit before leaning on this.

prerequisites: Founder or brand channels with some existing audience
A firm launch date
steps: Seed the idea publicly on founder or brand-owned channels roughly 6 months before launch
Pick a firm launch date and build anticipation toward it
Test the intended hype channel with a small, hypothesis-driven giveaway before committing full spend to it
Grow an owned email list through the anticipation period so day-one traffic has a warm audience

test.method: Track email list size and day-one launch revenue against the pre-launch sequence's stated goals.
test.measure: list_size at launch and day-one revenue

title: Get accounting audit-ready and stay transparent through a sale process
hypothesis: If accounting is kept fast, accurate and audit-ready as a standing practice, and prospective buyers are shown weak points honestly rather than hidden, then a sale process does not stall or collapse when diligence finds what transparency would have already surfaced.

signal.check: Accounting is not kept audit-ready on an ongoing basis, or a pending sale process is being approached by minimizing visibility into known weak points.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a readiness practice, not a measured lift

risk.note: An ongoing accounting-hygiene practice; the transparency norm applies specifically once a real sale process begins.

prerequisites: Accounting function capable of producing audit-ready statements on a standing basis
steps: Keep raw-material inventory, finished-goods inventory, net revenue and cost of goods as standing weekly numbers
Maintain accounting practices that could pass an audit at any time, not only before a planned sale
During a sale process, invite buyers to see real operations and introduce the team rather than hiding weak points
Track diligence findings that surprise the seller as a signal of where readiness was incomplete

test.method: Track the number and severity of diligence findings that were not already known and disclosed by the seller.

title: Run a competitive sell-side process with 8 to 10 mixed buyers
hypothesis: If a sale process invites roughly 8 to 10 mixed strategic and private-equity buyers with a pitch segmented by buyer type, then real competitive tension sets the price, instead of a single-buyer negotiation with no leverage or a too-broad process that wastes time.

signal.check: A sale process is being run with only one interested buyer, or with an unfocused, very large buyer list, and no pitch segmentation by buyer type.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a process-design tactic, not a measured lift

risk.note: Requires an investment bank or advisor to design and run the process, and real deadlines to prevent drag.

prerequisites: An investment banker or advisor to coordinate the process
A realistic buyer list of both strategics and private equity
steps: Engage a banker or advisor to design the process and set firm deadlines
Invite roughly 8 to 10 potential buyers mixing strategics and private equity
Segment the pitch: strategics get an earnings-accretion and synergy story, private equity gets an IRR and leveraged-buyout story
Stay personally engaged as CEO through closing, since the banker runs the process but does not sell the company

test.method: Track final deal terms achieved against the terms implied by the first offer received.
test.measure: other:deal_competitive_tension realized in final terms vs first offer

title: Deliberately teach judgment and agency to avoid a founder decision bottleneck
hypothesis: If a founder deliberately teaches judgment and decision-making to the team instead of solving every problem personally, then decisions stop floating up to the founder as the company scales, and the team keeps its own capability instead of losing it through habitual rescue.

signal.check: A founder or leader routinely makes decisions the team could learn to make themselves, causing decisions to bottleneck at the top as the company grows.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a leadership practice, not a measured lift

risk.note: A leadership-behavior change; requires the founder to tolerate some near-term slower or imperfect decisions while judgment develops.

prerequisites: A team with room to take on more decision-making responsibility
steps: Identify recurring decision types that currently always reach the founder
Deliberately hand a subset of those decisions to the relevant team member, with guidance rather than a direct answer
Cycle between close involvement on genuinely high-stakes items and stepping back on the rest
Track how many decisions of that type get resolved without the founder over time

test.method: Track the share of a defined decision type resolved without founder involvement over successive quarters.
